10491-practice-book-leland-powers-school:
Leland Powers School issued this practice book in 1909, for students of vocal expression and reading aloud. Powers thanks publishers for permission to reprint pieces by Webster, Tennyson, Browning, Emerson, Ruskin, and others. The book serves a school that taught speech as an art, not merely as reading.

Exercises for elemental vocal expression and for transition, drawn from Lewis B. Monroe's Sixth Reader, fill much of the volume. Poems like The Brook, Cavalier Tunes, Columbus, and Elaine give students words to speak with feeling. Readers get a historic elocution manual, useful for students of early speech training.
1057-poems-with-the-ballad-of-reading-ga:
Oscar Wilde's poems gather here beside his last great work, "The Ballad of Reading Gaol," written after his release from prison. The early lyrics praise beauty, Rome, and art, while the Ballad tells of a fellow prisoner hanged for murder and of the pity Wilde learned inside.

The contrast gives the book its force: the young aesthete's lush verse against the older man's stark lines on shame and mercy. "Each man kills the thing he loves" runs through the Ballad like a bell. The volume stands as Wilde's poetic testament, and it moves readers still.
10598-the-lives-of-the-poets-of-great-br:
The first volume of The Lives of the Poets of Great Britain and Ireland, printed in 1753 and compiled by Mr. Cibber, opens the series with the earliest English poets. Its lives run from Chaucer, Langland, and Gower through Lydgate, Skelton, More, Wyatt, and Sackville, down to writers of the sixteenth century. Notes left by the collector Thomas Coxeter supplied much of the material.

Each life sketches birth, education, career, and works, with stories about reputation and character. The volume shows how eighteenth-century readers traced English poetry back to its medieval roots. For students of early literature, it remains a useful, readable source on poets long before Shakespeare.
10622-the-lives-of-the-poets-of-great-br:
Printed in 1753, this third volume of The Lives of the Poets of Great Britain and Ireland was compiled by Mr. Cibber and other hands. It gathers short lives of poets from the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, drawing on books and on manuscript notes left by earlier collectors. Poets covered here include Denham, Aphra Behn, Dryden, Rowe, and Wycherley.

Each life gives birth, schooling, career, and writings in compact form, often with anecdotes about character and reputation. The volume works as a reference for readers tracing how English poetry grew from the age of Charles I to the age of Queen Anne. It also shows what eighteenth-century readers thought worth remembering about their poets.
10635-stories-from-the-italian-poets-wit:
Leigh Hunt, the English poet and essayist, retold the Italian poets for English readers in Stories from the Italian Poets, and this second volume, dated 1846, covers Boiardo, Ariosto, and Tasso. Each poet gets a critical notice of life and genius, followed by stories drawn from his great poem. Angelica's adventures, Astolfo's journey to the moon, and the loves of Rinaldo and Armida are among them.

Hunt writes in a lively, companionable style, translating and retelling rather than copying the verse. His aim is to open Italian romance to readers who know no Italian. The volume offers a pleasant door into the Orlando poems and Jerusalem Delivered, guided by a critic who loved them.
10885-stories-from-the-italian-poets-wit:
Leigh Hunt retold tales from Italy's great narrative poets in prose, adding short lives of each writer. Volume one draws on Dante, Pulci, Boiardo, Ariosto, and Tasso, keeping as much of the original poetry's spirit as prose allows. Notes explain hard passages, and favourite passages appear in the original alongside Hunt's versions.

Readers meet Angelica, Armida, and other figures of Italian romance, with tangled quests smoothed into single, continuous stories. Hunt also gives an abstract of Dante's whole poem, so newcomers can follow its shape. The book works both as an introduction to Italian poetry and as a pleasant story collection in its own right.
10902-big-and-little-sisters-a-story-of-:
Theodora R. Jenness wrote Big and Little Sisters as a story of an Indian mission school in Dakota. It opens on a Saturday morning in December, as two young Sioux girls, Hannah Straight Tree and Cordelia Running Bird, climb the stairs for cleaning duty. The great unplastered mission building is chilly, halls drafty from wind sweeping the plains through doors where restless children pass.

The girls, aprons over heads and shoulders, dread the work as they shiver on the landing. Jenness follows mission school life through Native girls' eyes, with sympathy and period detail. Readers get a rare children's story set among Sioux pupils, earnest and humane for its time.
10981-child-s-new-story-book-or-tales-an:
Tales and dialogues for little folks fill this 1849 story book, meant to teach truth while entertaining children. A boy sails a cork ship in a basin, imagining the North Pacific and Captain Cook's Friendly Islands, while a friend asks where Cook was born. A little girl listens to a shell and hears, as her uncle promised, the whisper of the sea.

Other pieces follow Robert and John on a May morning, a boy tempted by cowslips on the way to school, and children on a frosty morning by a frozen pond. Dialogues let children hear good conduct modelled in conversation. The book's tone is gentle and instructive, typical of early Victorian children's literature, where play, nature, and duty sit side by side.
11017-samuel-f-b-morse-his-letters-and-j:
Volume one of Edward Lind Morse's edition follows Samuel F. B. Morse from birth on April 27, 1791, through Yale, to a painting career in England. Letters from his parents, his teachers, and his friends trace a studious boy who longed to travel, loved electricity, and wished to sail with the artist Washington Allston. Morse enters a bookshop as a clerk, paints the Landing of the Pilgrims, and sails on the Lydia for London.

Later chapters cover study under Benjamin West, meetings with George III's circle, and early longing for a telegraph, alongside portraits painted at Charleston and family letters from Concord. The volume shows Morse first as an artist, before invention took over his life. Readers get the inventor's youth in his own letters and his son's notes.
11018-samuel-f-b-morse-his-letters-and-j:
Edward Lind Morse edited his father's letters and journals in this second volume, published in 1914 with reproductions of paintings and diagrams of the telegraph. Chapters run from October 1832, when Morse first conceived the telegraph aboard the packet Sully, through his painting career, his appointment at the University of the City of New York.

Later chapters cover Alfred Vail, Joseph Henry, Leonard Gale, the Morse alphabet read by sound, and the long patent lawsuits that followed success. Morse's own letters show an artist turned inventor, defending priority against rivals such as Charles Jackson. The volume serves readers of invention history and of American art, in the inventor's own words.
11066-graf-von-loeben-and-the-legend-of-:
Allen Wilson Porterfield wrote this 1915 Modern Philology article on Graf von Loeben and the legend of the Lorelei. Porterfield likens poets to athletes at Olympia: some, like Goethe, win often, some, like Immermann, win once, and some, like Loeben, compete loyally for twenty-five years without ever winning a lasting work. Loeben, prolific and popular in his day, is now obscure, named in only six of twenty best-known German literary histories.

Porterfield argues that students have given Loeben too much credit for the Lorelei, a legend Brentano created, not merely revived, from echo poetry and older tales such as Frau Holla. The article traces influence among German romantics with care. It suits readers of German literary history and of how legends are made, borrowed, and credited.
12014-the-lives-of-the-poets-of-great-br:
Volume 4 of The Lives of the Poets of Great Britain and Ireland, by Mr. Cibber and other hands, appeared in 1753 and gathers short lives of poets from Motteux and Manley to Congreve, Vanbrugh, Steele, and Gay. The volume's list runs through Prior, Centlivre, Stepney, Pack, and many lesser-known names, with women poets such as Mrs. Brady and Mrs. Fenton included.

Cibber's lives mix biography with literary judgment, anecdote, and quotation, in the manner of eighteenth-century literary history. The fourth volume is valuable less for any single life than for its range: it preserves the reputations, quarrels. Works of a generation of poets as their contemporaries and near-contemporaries understood them.
12090-the-lives-of-the-poets-of-great-br:
Printed in 1753, this fifth volume of The Lives of the Poets gathers short biographies of British and Irish writers, under the name of Mr. Cibber with other hands. It belongs to a multi-volume reference work that tried to record every poet of note up to its day.

Entries run from Aaron Hill and Addison through Behn, Butler, Chaucer, Congreve, Dryden, and many lesser-known names, each with life facts, anecdotes, and a judgment of the verse. The tone is gossipy and partisan, and modern scholars treat some claims with care. Still, the volume preserves stage lore and literary gossip that would otherwise be lost, and it shows how the eighteenth century ranked its own poets.
12112-the-boy-scouts-of-the-eagle-patrol:
Lieutenant Howard Payson wrote this boys adventure book in the early Boy Scout era, when the movement was new in America. The Eagle Patrol, led by a seventeen-year-old patrol leader near Hampton, Long Island, spends its summer on trails, boats, and camps.

Chapters follow a cruise to an island, a rescue, stolen uniforms, a hydroplane race, a storm at sea, and the hunt for a missing tenderfoot named Joe Digby. A local bully provides trouble, and the patrol answers with teamwork, first aid, and pluck. The book preaches the Scout code through action, not lectures. It now reads as a period piece, full of khaki, campfires, and early faith in organized boyhood.
12166-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Walter Scott edited this second volume of John Dryden collected works, published in 1808 as part of an eighteen-volume set. Dryden, poet laureate under Charles II and James II, dominated English letters in the Restoration, and Scott text draws on Congreve earlier edition checked against quarto and folio originals.

The volume holds early plays: The Wild Gallant, The Rival Ladies, The Indian Queen, The Indian Emperor, and Secret Love, or the Maiden Queen, with dedications and Scott notes. Plots run from Mexican conquest to court intrigue and mistaken love. Read together, they show Dryden learning his craft in the theater, mixing heroic tragedy with comedy, before his later fame as satirist and translator.
12816-the-devil-s-pool:
George Sand's Devil's Pool, in George B. Ives's 1901 translation, opens her rustic tales under the title Hemp-Beater's Tales. Sand says she had no theory and no plan for a literary revolution, only a love of country life as the dream of cities and courts. The romance of rustic manners, she notes, has lived in all ages.

The story follows Marie, a little shepherdess watching three sheep on the common, and a young man carrying partridges and a hare as a gift for his future father-in-law. Marie cooks a partridge in ashes so it will not smell of smoke. The novel charms as a pastoral of French country life.
12928-three-expeditions-into-the-interio:
Major T. L. Mitchell's Three Expeditions into the Interior of Eastern Australia, volume one, second edition, records journeys that opened Australia Felix and New South Wales. Mitchell wrote his journals at day's end, exhausted in mind and body, and asks readers to pardon defects from that labour. A new, vast country without classical associations still claims attention, he argues.

A Gwydir passage shows the work: smoke ahead, grass burning both sides of the route, wheel tracks obliterated by naked feet, and a long cooey signalling arrival among numerous tribes. Mitchell surveys with care and colonial confidence. The volume remains a key record of inland exploration.
13033-three-expeditions-into-the-interio:
Major T. L. Mitchell, surveyor-general, published this second, revised edition in two volumes; this is volume two, covering his 1836 expedition to the Darling and Murray rivers. Mitchell lists his route, gear, men, and Native guide, then records the march day by day. Chapters note corroboree dances, limestone caves, dry creeks, broken wheels, and snakes.

The journal is full of plain survey detail: rainwater in clay plains, lagoons with pelicans and ducks, bullocks watered without unyoking, and carts sunk deep in swampy ground. Mitchell names the rich black soil and tall grass of Australia Felix with open delight. The volume stands as a first-hand record of inland exploration, made by the man who mapped much of it.
13351-the-life-of-thomas-lord-cochrane-t:
Thomas, eleventh Earl of Dundonald, with H. R. Fox Bourne, completes his father's story in this 1869 first volume. It carries on from the Autobiography of a Seaman and recounts the public life of Thomas, tenth Earl, admiral of the Red and rear-admiral of the fleet. The book is dedicated to Angela Burdett Coutts, whose father backed Cochrane through his career.

Speeches, grievances, and quarrels with ministers fill the pages, including Cochrane's attack on a Regent's advisers for hiding the true state of the country. Later passages follow service under a foreign emperor, broken contracts, and an offer to resign rather than serve under such treatment. Naval daring and political trouble run side by side throughout.
14517-france-and-england-in-north-americ:
Francis Parkman's Montcalm and Wolfe, part six of his France and England in North America, tells the story of the Seven Years' War in America, from 1745 to the fall of Quebec. This Collier edition reprints the 1884 text with a new introduction by Samuel Eliot Morison.

Parkman contrasts England and France in the eighteenth century, then follows Washington's Virginia regiment guarding a long frontier, the campaigns of Montcalm, and Wolfe's victory. His footnotes cite French and English sources at length. The book remains the classic narrative of the war for Canada, vivid and partisan in the old manner.
14567-the-reconstructed-school:
Francis B. Pearson, Ohio's chief of public schools, put out The Reconstructed School in 1921 as a book on school reform. Pearson had written on the teacher and the high school problem.

Chapters survey the school's task, past and future, then treat honesty, thanks, hope, drive, dreams, awe, duty, freedom, and calm as aims. Pearson shows thanks at work when Keats takes joy in Spenser's sea whales. The book argues that good character is the school's true fruit, in plain, hopeful prose. Pearson wrote for teachers and school boards after the war, and his chapters still read well today.
14859-daddy-takes-us-to-the-garden-the-d:
Howard R. Garis, author of Uncle Wiggily books, sends a little boy and girl to the garden with their dear Daddy in this 1914 volume of the Daddy series for little folks. Each book in the series takes children to a new place and teaches something of value about nature, outdoor sports or animal life.

Camping, fishing, circus, skating, coasting, farm and garden visits follow the same pattern, priced at fifty cents a volume and illustrated by Eva Dean. In the garden, planting, growing and watching living things become lessons told as family fun. Garis writes simply and warmly, for children learning how a garden works and why it matters.
14947-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Volume sixteen of the works of John Dryden was printed in London in 1808. Dryden's works were first collected in eighteen volumes, with notes historical, critical and explanatory and a life of the author by Walter Scott. Its contents open with the life of Saint Francis Xavier, of the Society of Jesus, apostle of the Indies and of Japan.

A dedication to the queen and an author's advertisement to the reader follow, with notes on the king of Portugal and the blessed father. Scott's edition set a standard for Dryden scholarship, gathering poems, plays and prose with commentary. This volume shows Dryden as translator and biographer of a missionary saint, a side of his work less known than his satire.
15123-david-lockwin-the-people-s-idol:
John McGovern's 1889 Chicago novel follows David Lockwin, a people's idol whose rise runs through primaries, beer kegs, and election nights. Books trace Davy, then Esther Lockwin, then Robert Chalmers and George Harpwood, through Georgian Bay, Cape Croker, and the South Side. A balcony cheer opens the tale.

Politics, lynch law threats, disguise, and heroic acts mix with love and patronage in a broad, crowded plot. McGovern writes with a newspaperman's eye for crowds and deals. The novel offers a lively, if dated, picture of Gilded Age Chicago politics and the men who rode popular favor to power.
15349-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Walter Scott edited this fourth volume of John Dryden's collected works, printed in London in 1808. It gathers three plays with their dedications and two short essays on drama. Scott's notes, drawn from history and past criticism, run through the whole volume.

The main play is the two-part heroic tragedy about Almanzor and Almahide and the fall of Granada to Spain. An essay defends heroic plays, while a second essay looks back at the drama of the last age. Marriage-a-la-Mode and The Assignation, a comedy set in a nunnery, complete the set. Readers get Dryden the working playwright, not just the poet, with his own arguments for the grand, high-flown stage style he favored.
15839-the-rebel-of-the-school:
A school story by Mrs. L. T. Meade, author of Miss Nonentity and Merry Girls of England, issued in Chicago by M. A. Donohue and Company. Meade's series, uniform with this volume, includes Bad Little Hannah, A Bunch of Cherries, and The Honorable Miss. The rebel of the title defies school rules and school opinion alike. Meade writes for girls who liked plucky heroines.

Lessons, friendships, and scrapes fill the term, as the rebel learns when to fight and when to yield. Teachers, prefects, and schoolmates press her from all sides. Kindness and courage, Meade holds, matter more than mere obedience. The book charms as a period school tale: spirited, moral, and full of girls' talk and trouble.
16109-don-a-clarines-y-man-ana-de-sol:
Heath's Modern Language Series published Dona Clarines y Manana de Sol in 1915, two plays by the brothers Serafin and Joaquin Alvarez Quintero. S. Griswold Morley of the University of California edited the volume with introduction, notes, and vocabulary for American students of Spanish. The introduction draws on a semi-serious autobiography from Alma Espanola of 1904, since the brothers kept their private lives quiet.

Serafin, born in 1871, and Joaquin, born in 1873, grew up in Utrera and Seville, where they attended the Instituto and showed early dramatic talent. Their plays, full of Andalusian wit and feeling, became favorites of the Spanish stage. Students reading Spanish will find this a friendly, well-aided entry to their work.
16124-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
December 1880 brings Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science, entered by J. B. Lippincott of Philadelphia. Its lead piece, An Historical Rocky-Mountain Outpost, opens on a balmy Colorado day, with snow ranges, leafless cottonwoods along the Fontaine qui Bouille, and sombre plains to the east. The town in view is Pueblo, whose history holds greater contrasts than even earth and sky.

Other pages in Lippincott's manner mixed fiction, travel, science, and essays for a general American audience. The magazine aimed to entertain and instruct in one monthly sitting, without academic dryness. This number offers a pleasant sample of Gilded Age magazine writing from the Rocky Mountain West.
16161-the-seven-great-monarchies-of-the-:
George Rawlinson, Camden professor of ancient history at Oxford, opens his great history of the ancient East with Chaldaea, the first monarchy. Volume one, with maps and illustrations, surveys the country's geography, climate, people, language, arts, manners, religion, and chronology in eight chapters. A preface notes that ancient history must be rewritten as travelers and scholars bring new discoveries to light.

Rawlinson writes for general readers as well as students, turning cuneiform finds and classical authors into a clear narrative. The volume sets the stage for Assyria, Media, Babylonia, and Persia in the series that follows. Students of the ancient Near East will still value its scope, maps, and careful summary.
16162-the-seven-great-monarchies-of-the-:
Assyria, the second monarchy of Rawlinson's ancient East, occupied the upper Mesopotamian valley, with capitals strung along the middle Tigris. The heart of the country lay between the thirty-fifth and thirty-seventh parallels, though the name Assyria grew by degrees to cover a vast, ill-defined tract on every side. Herodotus counted Babylonia a mere district of Assyria, while Pliny added all Mesopotamia and Strabo more besides.

This volume, first in the New Persian Empire set's Assyrian portion, opens with a description of the country before moving to people, arts, and history. Maps and illustrations support the survey. Readers of ancient history will find a clear, old-style account of the empire that once ruled the Near East.
16163-the-seven-great-monarchies-of-the-:
Volume two of George Rawlinson's history of the ancient East takes Media, the third monarchy, as its subject. The opening chapter maps a vast highland east of the Mesopotamian plain. It rises nowhere less than three thousand feet above the sea. Lofty ridges stand on the north and west, and a high table-land runs south to the Indian Ocean and east toward Afghan country. Six or seven parallel ridges shape its western mountains.

Later chapters in Rawlinson's pattern will cover Media's people, language, arts, religion, and history, with maps and illustrations to guide the reader. The Oxford professor writes with the same clear, learned ease as in his Chaldaea volume. Students of ancient empires will find a solid, readable account of a power that helped shape the Near East.
16164-the-seven-great-monarchies-of-the-:
Babylonia Proper, an alluvial tract toward the mouths of the Tigris and Euphrates, anchors the fourth monarchy in Rawlinson's history. It lies between the Arabian desert on one side and higher ground on the other, nearly the same ground already described under Chaldaea. A verse from Daniel about a great tree reaching to heaven opens the chapter on the empire's extent.

This volume follows Babylonia's kings, cities, and power from a small river plain to a wide empire, with maps and illustrations to guide the reader. Rawlinson writes with an Oxford scholar's clarity for a general audience. Students of the ancient Near East will find a solid survey of Babylon's rise and reach.
16165-the-seven-great-monarchies-of-the-:
George Rawlinson's Persia volume, the second of his three-volume New Persian Empire set, treats the fifth monarchy of the ancient East. Persia Proper itself was narrow and poor, barely five hundred miles at its greatest length, yet the Persian kings ruled an empire fifty-six degrees long and in places more than twenty wide. Its bounds ran from the Indus and the desert of Tibet to the Mediterranean, the Danube, and the Caspian.

Maps and illustrations support Rawlinson's survey of extent, government, and power, written with an Oxford professor's clarity for general readers. The volume shows how a small homeland grew into the largest empire the ancient East had yet seen. Students of Persia, Greece, and the ancient world will find it a solid, readable survey.
16166-the-seven-great-monarchies-of-the-:
Parthia's story opens in a desert east of the Caspian Sea, stretching fifteen hundred miles from the Mougbojar hills to the Indian Ocean. About midway, a strip of territory breaks the waste, a region of beauty some three hundred twenty miles east to west and nearly two hundred north to south. A mountain chain south of the Caspian skirts the great plateau of Iran on the north and frames the land.

This third volume of Rawlinson's New Persian Empire set traces Parthia's geography, climate, and neighbors before its kings and wars. Maps of Parthia proper guide the reader through a country often overshadowed by Rome and Persia. Students of ancient empires will find a clear account of a power that held the East for centuries.
16167-the-seven-great-monarchies-of-the-:
Volume three of George Rawlinson's ancient history covers the seventh monarchy, the Sassanian or New Persian Empire. Its opening chapter traces the Persians under Alexander's successors and then under the Parthians, who at first honored their religion and let them keep kings of their own. Parthian policy hardened, priests lost favor, and oppression of the Magi helped spark the insurrection of Artaxerxes.

Rawlinson, Camden professor at Oxford, builds the story from classical authors and newer finds, with maps and illustrations to guide readers. The volume explains how a subject people rose to found a great empire of their own. Students of Rome, Persia, and the ancient Near East will value its clear, learned narrative.
16402-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Walter Scott edited this seventh volume of Dryden's collected works, printed in London in 1808. It holds The Duke of Guise, a tragedy written when stage plays served party factions under Charles II. A vindication of the play, the opera Albion and Albanius, and the tragedy Don Sebastian complete the volume. Epistles to the Earls of Rochester and Leicester open two of the pieces.

Scott's notes, historical and critical, frame each work and explain its moment. The volume shows Dryden as a working playwright in stormy political times, not merely as a poet of high verse. Scholars of Restoration drama will find it a rich, well-annotated source.
16456-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Walter Scott's sixth volume of Dryden's works, printed in 1808, holds three plays: Limberham, or the Kind Keeper, a comedy; Oedipus, a tragedy; and The Spanish Friar, or the Double Discovery. Epistles to Lord Vaughan and Lord Haughton open two of the pieces. Scott's notes frame each play with history and criticism.

The editor notes Limberham's coarseness, which offended even in its own day, while praising the age's frank stage. The volume shows Dryden working across comedy and tragedy at full stretch. Students of Restoration drama will find it a valuable, well-annotated slice of the collected works.
16469-the-lives-of-the-poets-of-great-br:
Theophilus Cibber's Lives of the Poets, volume two of the 1753 set, gets a facsimile reprint here from a Gottingen library copy. The title page of volume one promised four volumes, but a fifth of the same date continues the work, all by Cibber and other hands for R. Griffiths. Old spelling, punctuation, and quirks are kept.

The lives cover British and Irish poets with anecdote, verse, and gossip of the age. As a reprint, the volume serves scholars of eighteenth-century letters who want the text as it first stood. General readers will enjoy its chatty, old-fashioned biographies of poets now half-forgotten.
16550-the-prose-works-of-william-wordswo:
Alexander B. Grosart collected Wordsworth's prose for the first time in this 1876 volume, the first of three, covering political and ethical writings. An apology for the French Revolution, the Convention of Cintra with De Quincey's appendix, and letters on military policy lead the contents. A dedication to the Queen opens the book, with a poem sent to Windsor Castle.

Grosart adds notes and unpublished manuscripts, giving readers Wordsworth the prose writer, not only the poet. The politics are earnest and high-minded, from revolution to national defense. Wordsworth scholars will find the volume essential, and general readers will meet a thinker too often hidden behind the poems.
17227-rod-of-the-lone-patrol:
H. A. Cody's 1916 boys' book, dedicated to three little boys keen to become Boy Scouts, follows Rod of the Lone Patrol. Parson Dan sips cocoa by an open fire on a wild October night as the tale opens with a waif of the night. Chapters follow Rodney's growth, Captain Josh, chums to the rescue, good turns, scout work, an island adventure, first aid, and a night run.

Cody writes in warm, Canadian scout-story style, with duty, pluck, and kindness at its heart. Rod's best good turn closes the moral arc. Young readers who like scout tales will enjoy a gentle, old-style adventure of a lone patrol boy who earns his place among friends.
17302-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
This volume of the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers, founded in 1852, prints a technical paper on the Pennsylvania Railroad's New York tunnel extension. Paper number 1156, by B. F. Cresson Jr., covers Terminal Station-West, the ground between Ninth and Tenth Avenues and 31st and 33rd Streets in Manhattan, about six acres in all.

The paper sets out the site limits, then turns to house wrecking, since ninety-four dwellings, apartment houses, and church buildings stood on the ground to be cleared. Readers get a detailed engineer's record of how a great rail terminal was planted in a crowded city, from survey lines to demolition. It suits readers of civil engineering and of New York's building past.
17588-the-vitalized-school:
Francis B. Pearson, superintendent of public instruction of Ohio, published this work on schooling with Macmillan in February 1917. He was author of books on the teacher and the high school problem, and the book was reprinted in January 1918. His contents run from teaching school, the teacher, and the child, through the child of the future and the teacher-politician, to sublime chaos, democracy, patriotism, and work and life.

Later chapters cover words and their content, complete living, the time element, the artist teacher, the socialised recitation, agriculture, the school and the community, poetry and life, and a sense of humour. A closing chapter pictures a typical vitalized school. Readers get a progressive-era call to make schools live, not merely run.
17776-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
This volume of the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers carries paper number 1168, Tests of Creosoted Timber, by W. B. Gregory. The Society, founded in 1852, printed such papers for working engineers who built with wood, iron, and stone.

Gregory tested southern pine beams that had served 26 years in a rail trestle near New Orleans, cut from 30-foot stringers into shorter lengths. He asked how time, weather, and heavy trains had worn timber treated with creosote oil. The paper gives plain facts for bridge and trestle builders, and it shows how early engineers checked a new preservative in the field.
17777-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
The Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers, founded in 1852, prints paper number 1176 in this volume. It covers reinforced concrete pier construction, by Eugene Klapp, with discussion by William Arthur Payne and Klapp. The paper opens with a private yacht pier built near Glen Cove, Long Island, a small structure that raised points of wider interest.

Klapp argues that the pier, though of no great moment in itself, shows how means may be fitted to ends in concrete work. Readers get a technical record of early reinforced concrete practice on the American coast. The paper suits civil engineers and historians of building technology.
17871-a-slave-girl-s-story-being-an-auto:
Kate Drumgoold wrote A Slave Girl's Story in Brooklyn in 1898, telling her own life from bondage to freedom. She writes for those who prayed that slaves might be freed, schooled, and taught to read and write for themselves.

Drumgoold recalls a brother lost to war, a mother sold and sought, and a family that found its way north to schools and books. She speaks with faith, pride, and a teacher's zeal for her race's children. The book is short, plain, and strong, a first-hand voice of Black freedom, and a call to learn, teach, and rise.
18012-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
This volume of the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers carries paper number 1153, The New York Tunnel Extension of the Pennsylvania Railroad, by E. B. Temple. The paper covers the Meadows Division and the Harrison transfer yard, a key link in the great rail scheme.

Temple sets out how the new tunnels and yards were planned and built, for engineers who would judge, copy, or learn from the work. The prose is plain and technical, with figures and detail for the trade. It is a solid period record of a vast city rail project, and a useful source for historians of New York transit.
18019-the-luckiest-girl-in-the-school:
Angela Brazil wrote The Luckiest Girl in the School, first printed in the United States in 1922 by A. L. Burt, by arrangement with Frederick A. Stokes. Brazil, author of many schoolgirl books, here gives Winona a great change and a new school to conquer.

Chapters run from an entrance examination and Seaton High School to a symposium, Aunt Harriet, a crisis, an autumn foray, and a camera. Winona falters over papers that are not hers, and pluck must see her through. Brazil writes bright, loyal school tales. It is a cheerful girls' book, full of chums, scrapes, and school pride.
18065-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
Alfred Noble wrote this paper for the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers, number 1152, on the East River Division of the New York tunnel extension. Noble, a past president of the Society, links the first general outline to the detailed work of the resident engineers.

The paper traces borings begun in late 1901, from a pile-driver boat in the East River, through Manhattan and Long Island City. Wash and core borings mapped rock, reefs, and channels, and profiles were drawn for the tunnel lines. It is a plain, technical note on a vast project, and a key record for historians of New York's rail tunnels.
18229-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
Charles W. Raymond wrote paper number 1150 in the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers, on the New York tunnel extension of the Pennsylvania Railroad. Raymond recalls President A. J. Cassatt's refusal to accept that a great railroad should be kept from the most populous city in the country by a river less than one mile wide. That thought became the tunnel project.

An earlier steam tunnel near Christopher Street had failed, but electric traction changed the case. Electric trains avoided the ventilation troubles of steam in tunnels and allowed grades that steam locomotives could not climb. Readers get a civil engineering record: how a bold crossing under the Hudson became workable, and what new power made an old plan possible at last.
18287-songs-of-the-springtides-and-birth:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's Songs of the Springtides, with a Birthday Ode, appears here as taken from volume three of his collected poetical works. Heinemann published the volume in London in 1917, reprinting a book first printed by Chatto in 1904. The volume sits beside Poems and Ballads in the collected order, with Songs Before Sunrise and Songs of Two Nations nearby.

Songs of the Springtides opens with a dedication to Edward John Trelawny, followed by Thalassius and other spring poems. The birthday ode adds a public, celebratory note to the seasonal lyrics. Readers get Swinburne in his lyrical mode: musical, classical, and full of sea and spring, in a late collected form that gathers his shorter poems for a new generation.
18408-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
George C. Clarke wrote paper number 1157 in the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers, on the site of the terminal station for the New York tunnel extension of the Pennsylvania Railroad. Clarke describes the preliminary work for the Manhattan station site built under the chief engineer of the East River Division. It covers disposal of material dug from the terminal works and the East River tunnels.

Following General Charles W. Raymond's outline, Clarke maps the track yard from Tenth Avenue eastward into 32nd and 33rd Streets, with north and south areas about 170 and 160 feet wide at the house line. Tail tracks and double-track tunnels under Ninth Avenue add room. Readers get engineering in detail: how a great station site was cleared, dug, and shaped beneath a crowded city.
18448-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
Herbert M. Wilson wrote paper number 1171 in the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers, on federal investigations of mine accidents, structural materials, and fuels. Discussion by Kenneth Allen, Henry Kreisinger, Walter O. Snelling, and others follows the paper. Wilson opens with the Cherry, Illinois, mine disaster of November 13, 1909.

On that day 527 men were in the mine, 330 were entombed, and 310 were killed. Twenty men were rescued alive after a week underground, when hope had nearly been abandoned. The disaster, Wilson says, focused public attention as even three great disasters in 1907 had not. Readers get engineering turned to public safety: how Congress ordered investigation of mines, materials, and fuels after a catastrophe.
18548-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
This volume of the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers, founded in 1852, opens with a major paper on the New York tunnel extension of the Pennsylvania Railroad. Chief engineer Charles M. Jacobs describes the North River division, from Ninth Avenue in New York to the Hackensack Portal west of the Palisades. His paper traces how the road sought a direct rail link into Manhattan.

Jacobs recalls early talks from 1890 on, surveys and borings, and the shift from a Brooklyn tunnel plan to a direct Pennsylvania line. Later papers in the volume, by assistant and resident engineers, detail the work as built. The volume is a key record of one of America's great early tunnel projects.
18641-hunter-patrol:
H. Beam Piper and John J. McGuire wrote this short story for Amazing Stories in May 1959. Its hero, Benson, leads a dozen UN regulars and Turkish partisans on a raid against a Pan-Soviet supply dump, faking a paratroop attack to pull foe troops from the front. At 0539, with a barrage due in eleven minutes, he hurries down a dry ravine toward friendly lines on his last patrol before rotation home.

Faint tank tracks that end against a vine-clad slope warn him something is wrong, and he dives for cover as the tale turns strange. The cover line asks if one man with power to bring world peace could be afforded at any price. The story is a taut mix of war tale and science fiction idea.
18722-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
Paper 1159 of the American Society of Civil Engineers' Transactions describes the East River tunnels of the Pennsylvania Railroad's New York tunnel extension. James H. Brace, Francis Mason, and S. H. Woodard wrote the paper, presented in December 1909.

Four single cast-iron tube tunnels, each about 6,000 feet long, run from shafts in Manhattan under the river to Long Island City. Shields drove east from Manhattan and west from Long Island City to meet mid-river, while a land section ran from East Avenue to the river shafts. S. Pearson and Son built the work under a profit-sharing contract, breaking ground in May 1904 and finishing five years later to the day.
18747-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
This volume of the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers opens with Paper 1172 by Beverly S. Randolph on locomotive performance on grades of various lengths. Randolph studies train resistance from grades and curves, using Baldwin Locomotive Works data and figures from roads direct. His tables give the share of driver weight used in draft for grades before 1880 and for 1908 to 1910.

A striking finding is that an 1871 Lehigh Valley Consolidation matched the latest Great Northern Mallet compounds in steam-to-weight ratio, suggesting forty years of little change. Discussion by Purdon, Trautwine, and Randolph follows the paper. The volume is a solid record of railway engineering practice.
18748-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
Paper 1173 of the American Society of Civil Engineers' Transactions, by A. Kempkey Jr., describes a concrete water tower at Victoria, on Vancouver Island. The paper, with discussion by four fellow engineers, grows out of a full remodeling of Victoria's water system.

Water drawn from Elk Lake, five miles north, flows to a pumping station and then to consumers across a fast-growing city of about thirty-five thousand. The remodeling raised the lake's capacity, replaced miles of main, added a large pumping engine, and built a twenty-million-gallon concrete-lined reservoir. Its crowning piece, the elevated tank on the city's highest hill, gave high-level service through pumps that started and stopped on their own as the water rose and fell.
18785-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
Paper 1177 of the American Society of Civil Engineers' Transactions gives the final report of the Special Committee on Rail Sections, dated June 1910. The committee, appointed in 1902, had reported to the society in 1903, 1905, 1906, 1907, 1908, and 1909.

Its members ask to be discharged, feeling they have nothing to add to their earlier reports, whose cardinal principles are already followed in used and proposed rail sections. A note by William R. Webster approves the report in connection with an attached specification, calling it too condensed for those new to the rail question. The paper offers a revised specification, including one for open-hearth steel rails with a sliding scale for carbon and phosphorus.
18795-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
This volume of the American Society of Civil Engineers' Transactions opens with Paper 1178, the presidential address John A. Bensel gave at the society's forty-second annual convention in Chicago on June 21, 1910. Bensel warns his fellow engineers that, for all their great works, they lag behind other professions in spirit and in joint effort for their calling.

He looks back to John Smeaton, who first used the terms engineer and civil engineer in 1761, and to the vast change in the built world over the hundred years since. His plea is plain: a calling as old as building itself should act together, not only build well. The address sets a professional theme the volume's record of proceedings then carries forward.
18885-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science for August 1878 opens along the Danube, at Ada-Kalé, a Turkish fortress rising from the river where three quarrelsome races meet. The fortress, long the first glimpse of the Orient for travelers from Western Europe on the way to Constantinople, is to be razed to the water's edge. The treaty between Russia and Turkey ordains it.

Its writer passes an old Turk fishing from a small boat near the Roumanian bank, rowed by two soldiers. A Wallachian sentry watches idly six hundred feet away, even as Turkish guns bombard Kalafat across the river. The scene sums up a land where, the writer jokes, it is always afternoon. River and rail journeys on toward Orsova complete a traveler's Danube sketch.
19037-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
James H. Brace and Francis Mason describe the cross-town tunnels of the Pennsylvania Railroad's New York tunnel extension, in a paper published in the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers. The paper covers the tunnels running east from the Terminal Station toward shafts east of First Avenue, beneath Thirty-second and Thirty-third Streets and then curving under private property.

Work began under a 1905 contract, with excavation driven from several shafts. The shafts were the First Avenue shafts, intermediate shafts on private ground, and later west shafts between Sixth and Seventh Avenues, plus open-cut sections west of Sixth Avenue. The paper records shaft sinking, excavation methods in good and bad ground, roof support, lining, and progress, illustrated with plates and tables. It stands as a detailed engineering record of how a major Manhattan rail tunnel was actually built.
19337-a-christmas-carol:
Charles Dickens wrote this short Christmas tale, here in an early nineteen hundreds edition with pictures by George Alfred Williams. Ebenezer Scrooge, a miser who hates Christmas, is visited on Christmas Eve by the ghost of his dead partner Marley. Then three spirits show him his past, his present, and his future.

Each visit strips away one more of Scrooge's excuses, from lonely boyhood to the cold house he will leave behind if he does not change. The final stave turns the tale toward warmth and giving, which is why the story has stayed at the heart of Christmas reading ever since.
19944-the-yotsuya-kwaidan-or-o-iwa-inari:
The Yotsuya Kwaidan is Japan's most famous ghost story, retold here from the Tokugawa era. This edition's maps follow the Edo Sunago of 1866. District details come from an Edo map published in 1857. The Go Edo Zusetsu Shuran supplies further topography. Such care grounds a ghost tale in real streets. Oiwa, the wronged wife, haunts those streets forever in Japanese tradition.

James de Benneville retold Tokugawa tales for English readers. The kwaidan, or weird tale, was his specialty. Oiwa's story mixes murder, betrayal, and relentless haunting. It still anchors Japanese horror today. The maps show Edo as the tale's first audience knew it. This volume is folklore and city history together.
20144-the-fourth-book-of-virgil-s-aeneid:
Virgil's Aeneid, book four, tells of Dido and Aeneas in Carthage. This volume pairs it with book nine of another famed classical work. The pages discuss the stuff from which such poems were built. Critics, it notes, were not always fair in judging the results.

Book four of the Aeneid holds one of the great love tragedies in verse. Dido's passion and death have moved readers for two thousand years. School and college readers long met Virgil in volumes like this one. Readers get Latin epic with the aids and notes students once used daily.
20390-elements-of-structural-and-systema:
Douglas Houghton Campbell wrote Elements of Structural and Systematic Botany as a textbook for high school and college courses. It teaches both how plants are built and how they are sorted into groups. Clear terms and steady order guide the student through each topic.

Campbell adds only as much classification as will make the links between plant groups clear. He explains the rules on which the sorting rests. The aim is practical. Students should be able to recognize the commoner types of the different groups, in the field or the laboratory.
20661-the-romance-of-an-old-fool:
The Romance of an Old Fool, published in 1902, is a novel told through the diary of its elderly hero. From childhood he has kept a diary, a running comment on the daily incidents of his pleasant but uneventful life. Into that quiet record, love arrives absurdly late.

He confesses his small revenges in its pages. When Bunsey's society seemed too assertive and familiar, he punished the offender by retreating to his diary. The old fool's romance is watched by the whole town, and by himself, with a mix of shame and delight. The book treats late love gently and comically.
20730-for-the-sake-of-the-school:
Angela Brazil helped shape the classic British school story, and For the Sake of the School opens in a rush of travel. A porter shouts for girls to stand back on a crowded platform. Pupils bound for Glanafon and Graigwen swarm with boxes, talk, and nerves at the start of term.

School loyalty gives the book its title and its core test. Brazil's girls face scrapes, strains in friendship, and calls to put the school first. Her tales made boarding-school life vivid for generations of young readers. This one keeps her usual mix of fun, feeling, and firm school spirit.
20734-roman-antiquities-and-ancient-myth:
Roman Antiquities and Ancient Mythology was made for classical schools, to teach the daily world behind Latin texts. The preface notes fresh changes, with some parts cut so the book kept its size. Questions were dropped to make room for new matter.

Inside, pupils found Roman customs, offices, dress, houses, and gods set out in clear order. Such manuals once stood on every Latin student's desk. They turned dry grammar work into a picture of real life in Rome. This volume shows how schools in that era taught the ancient world as a full way of life, not just a language.
20750-journal-of-the-proceedings-of-the-:
Crustacean shells open the third zoology volume of the Linnean Society's journal proceedings. Spence Bate argues that shell structure can settle doubtful species. He applies the point to the genus Galathea and names a new species there.

Learned papers like this one built Victorian natural science piece by piece. Each claim rests on close looking at real specimens. The Linnean Society, named for the great classifier Linnaeus, spread such work worldwide. Modern readers can watch taxonomy grow in real time, one crab shell and one careful note at a time, across these dense pages.
21034-the-corner-house-girls-at-school:
Dot, the youngest Corner House girl, knows Allie Neuman of Willow Street well, she ventures. Grace Brooks Hill sends the sisters back to school in this 1915 tale. Allie will share Dot's grade at school, past Mrs. Adams's house on the way.

Ruth, Agnes, Tess, and Dot fill the Corner House set with sisterly life. School terms, new friends, scrapes, and home joys drive this volume's plot. Hill writes warm tales of girls who work, play, and stick fast together. This school entry shows the sisters beyond their famous house, in classrooms where their bond meets fresh tests.
21083-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
Paper No. Paper No. 1154 in the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers reports on the Bergen Hill tunnels. They formed part of the Pennsylvania Railroad's New York Tunnel Extension. Engineer F. Lavis presented it in April 1910. The tunnels form the section west of the Hudson River, known as Section K.

Bergen Hill is a hard trap-rock ridge, the lower end of the Hudson Palisades. Lavis describes two parallel single-track tunnels driven through it, on a line near 32nd Street in New York. Plates, figures, grades, and rock conditions fill the paper. It records how American rail engineers pushed a main line under a river and hill.
21324-recollections-of-old-liverpool:
A nonagenarian who was born in Liverpool and remembered into his nineties published these recollections in 1863, with a view of the city in 1813. His chapters roam widely. They cover the ducking stool and the Flashes in Marybone, the launch of ships, the inside of a slave ship, and the town's privateers. The salt trade gets pages of its own.

John Howard the prison reformer, the Borough Gaol, fairs, footpads, and country walks to Everton all appear. Later chapters turn to elections, with George Canning and Henry Brougham stirring divisions. Few books preserve a port city's everyday past so personally, from a man who watched Liverpool grow across two centuries.
21656-the-princess-of-the-school:
Angela Brazil opens The Princess of the School with a Christmas rush dodged, in a tale copyrighted in 1920. Miss Walters packs her pupils off by the first trains to beat the crowds. The girls themselves raise no objection to the early start.

Chapters promise a stolen joy-ride, a Valentine party, and a girl disinherited. Princess Carmel arrives as the new owner's kin, and a secret society forms. Sicily, the Casa Bianca, and the high seas widen the tale beyond the school. Frank Wiles draws the pictures. Brazil, queen of the school story, mixes lessons, larks, and loyalty in her known bright style.
21847-dr-wortle-s-school:
A school scandal tests a proud headmaster in Anthony Trollope's Dr. Wortle's School, published in two volumes in 1881. Dr. Jeffrey Wortle, rector of Bowick and master of its school, was esteemed by others and by himself. He had taught at Eton for ten years before taking the living. Into his ordered world comes a new usher, Mr. Peacocke, and with him a mystery.

The doctor asks his question, and the story is told: a secret in the usher's past that polite society cannot forgive. The bishop, the Stantiloup family, and Lord Carstairs all take their parts. Trollope treats the matter with his usual fairness, letting every side speak. It is one of his shorter, sharper novels of character under pressure.
21955-the-secret-wireless-or-the-spy-hun:
Boy wireless operators hunt German spies in Lewis E. Theiss's The Secret Wireless, published in 1918 while the Great War still raged. Henry Harper sits in the doorway of his father's backyard workshop, where the Camp Brady Wireless Club has its headquarters, reading the morning paper. Suddenly he springs up, fist clenched. His idea sets the patrol preparing for action.

A message in cipher, a pursuit in the dark, and a clue from the air fill the chapters. Theiss dedicated the book to a Bucknell professor of electrics who helped him keep the wireless work true. The boys change ciphers, race too late, and at last capture the spies. It is wartime adventure for the first radio generation, patriotic and proud of its sparks.
21993-the-devil-s-pool:
French peasant love is told with a poet's care in George Sand's The Devil's Pool. Jane Minot Sedgwick and Ellery Sedgwick Englished it in 1894. Sand opens with Holbein's plowman, urged on by a skeleton with a whip through stony soil. Then her own tale softens the picture: Germain, a skilled husbandman and widower, is sent to find a new wife. He travels with little Marie and his small son Petit-Pierre across the heath.

The devil's pool of the title waits in the woods where the travelers lose their way at night. An appendix describes a country wedding in full, favors, feast, and cabbage rite. Sand loved the Berry countryside and its people. This short novel is her tenderest portrait of them.
22101-wood-folk-at-school:
William J. Long, a minister and naturalist, wrote the Wood Folk books to teach children about animals. In Wood Folk at School he takes readers into a deep hollow in the big woods. A fallen tree bridges the stream, and Long sits on the mossy trunk to watch. Bridges, he says, are for crossing, so every neighbour must pass his seat.

Foxes, deer, birds, and small beasts come by, each with lessons to learn. Long treats the woods as a school where the young are trained by their parents. His stories blend sharp watching with kindly invention. Critics of his day argued over how much he made up, but young readers loved the wood folk then and the books stayed in print.
22113-peggy-stewart-at-school:
Gabrielle E. Jackson's Peggy Stewart at School, published in 1918, belongs to her Peggy Stewart series for girls. Peggy, the daughter of a naval officer, goes away to boarding school. The book opens in fierce August heat at home, with dry grass and dust over everything. Indoors, all is cool and inviting by contrast, but school waits.

At school Peggy meets new girls, new rules, and the small politics of dormitory life. Jackson writes about lessons, friendships, scrapes, and homesickness. Her heroine is lively, loyal, and quick to take the lead. Such girls' school stories were a thriving kind in 1918, and Peggy Stewart was among their popular heroines.
22208-cruel-barbara-allen-from-coals-of-:
Cruel Barbara Allen takes its title from the old ballad of the hard-hearted Barbara. David Christie Murray's tale, from his Coals of Fire set, opens on a man remarkable for nothing but dreamy eyes. Those eyes could flash with inward lightnings at times. His hair was lank, his figure thin and ungraceful, and his clothes sat awkwardly on him.

Neighbours thought him sulky, and some found his voice bumptious. Murray builds the story on the gap between that outside and the life within. The ballad's theme, love scorned until too late, hangs over the plot. It is a moody piece, showing Murray's interest in misjudged, solitary men.
22250-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science was a Philadelphia monthly that mixed fiction with fact. This volume gathers issues from the 1870s, when the magazine was in its prime. One travel piece describes a city ringed by the Atlas mountains, extremely picturesque. Steamers stay only a few hours at each port, the writer laments, leaving scarcely time to enjoy the views.

Serial novels, poems, science notes, and essays share the volume's thick pages. Lippincott's later became famous for printing The Picture of Dorian Gray entire in one issue. The bound volumes show the respectable middle of American magazine culture: improving, various, and built to be kept.
22601-hiawatha-and-the-iroquois-confeder:
Horatio Hale wrote Hiawatha and the Iroquois Confederation, a study in anthropology about the founding legend of the Five Nations. The catalog record gives no year. Hale, a linguist and ethnologist, treated Native traditions as serious historical evidence at a time when many scholars did not.

The sample weighs deep questions about the antiquity of human types, arguing that people appeared on earth with much the same body and mind they keep today. Around such arguments, Hale examines the Hiawatha story and the league it credits him with founding. The book stands as an early, respectful attempt to read Iroquois tradition as history. It still rewards readers interested in the roots of anthropology and in the confederation itself.
22609-the-writings-of-james-russell-lowe:
James Russell Lowell's Political Essays form one volume of his collected writings in prose and poetry. The catalog record gives no year. Lowell, poet, editor, and diplomat, was among the most feared political pens of nineteenth-century America, and this volume gathers his essays on public men and public questions.

The sample shows his manner at full stretch. A ruler, pressed by the needs of his position, slides by degrees into crime and luxury. Those were the very sins that once horrified him in his hermitage days. Lowell's prose mixes learning, wit, and moral judgment in long, rolling sentences. These essays let modern readers watch a leading American man of letters judge the politics of his age, from slavery to Reconstruction and beyond.
22995-miss-pat-at-school:
Pemberton Ginther's Miss Pat at School, published in 1915, opens on a confession. Her friend confesses that her calm face is a fraud. Inside, she admits, she is more stirred up than ever before in her life. The feeling runs too deep for words, and none will come.

Miss Pat belongs to the era's boarding-school series for girls, where new terms bring new rivals, secrets, and loyalties. Ginther keeps the excitement in the emotional register her excerpt shows, feelings too deep for words at the school gate. Lessons, pranks, and friendships fill the chapters between. The book preserves the hopes such fiction sold its readers, that school would test them gently and friendship would see them through.
23240-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-no-:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 336, for October 1843, is an issue of the famous monthly review. Its critics could be severe about heavy books. One review in this issue grants that a work is abstract, calls for unbroken attention, and offers little in the way of lighter or amusing matter.

Yet the same review praises searching thought and clear views, aptly expressed. That balance was Blackwood's trademark: sharp judgement in lively prose. Readers get a sample of Victorian reviewing at full strength, where a dull subject could still earn respect if the thinking was strong and the writing lucid.
23763-fred-fenton-on-the-track-or-the-at:
Allen Chapman published Fred Fenton on the Track in 1913, one of his athletic stories for boys. Fred, already known as a pitcher, now runs for Riverport School, and the book follows the cross-country runners through training, races, and schoolboy rivalry.

Early chapters bring a strange sound from a well, a rescue out of the depths, and a shock for Fred. Chapman, who also wrote the Tom Fairfield and Darewell Chums series, keeps the pace brisk and the sportsmanship clean. It is a school story in the classic mold: pluck, teamwork, and a finish worth running for.
24022-a-christmas-carol:
Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol, in the edition illustrated by Arthur Rackham and published by J. B. Lippincott, first appeared in that form in 1915 and was reprinted many times through 1973. Its character list names the whole company of the tale, from the grasping, covetous old man himself to the smallest Cratchit.

Ebenezer Scrooge, surviving partner of Scrooge and Marley, employs Bob Cratchit, father of Peter, Belinda, Martha, and Tiny Tim, the cripple. Fred is Scrooge's nephew, Fezziwig the kind-hearted old merchant, and Belle the comely old sweetheart. The ghost of Jacob Marley, the ghosts of Christmas Past, Present, and Yet to Come, Mrs. Dilber the laundress, and Fan, Scrooge's sister, complete a cast that has haunted Christmas ever since.
24153-gloria-crucis-addresses-delivered-:
The Reverend J. H. Beibitz, vice-principal of the Theological College at Lichfield, gave these addresses in Lichfield Cathedral during Holy Week and on Good Friday 1907. Longmans, Green, and Company published them in 1908 under the title Gloria Crucis, the glory of the cross. The first address takes its text from Galatians, that a Christian should glory only in the cross of Christ.

Beibitz argues that the cross is often treated as the weak point of Christianity, attacked from outside and accepted on blind faith within. He rejects harsh pictures of the atonement as a price to calm an angry God, and seeks a rational account instead. Readers get sober Holy Week preaching, plain in style and serious in aim.
24203-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
This number of Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science is dated November 1873. It opens with The New Hyperion, a travel serial from Paris to Marly by way of the Rhine, here in its fifth part, In Pursuit of a Passport. The narrator crosses the storied Rhine in an engineer's coach, listening to a canal-digger's legend as they roll from pavement to bridge.

The legend tells how Louis XIV took Strasburg in 1681 in peacetime. Alsatians held the Grand Monarch a bit of a magician, keeping a tiny yellow demon in an ebony casket chained at his praying-chair. The goblin ran errands swift as lightning for three hemp seeds a meal. Readers get travel, legend, and period wit in one magazine number.
24286-the-birds-christmas-carol:
Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote this Christmas story, published by Houghton Mifflin Company in Boston and New York, reaching its eight hundredth thousand printing. It is dedicated to the three dearest children in the world, Bertha, Lucy, and Horatio. Chapters run from A Little Snow Bird and Drooping Wings through The Birds' Nest. Birds of a Feather Flock Together follows, with Some Other Birds Are Taught to Fly. When the Pie Was Opened the Birds Began to Sing comes next, and The Birdling Flies Away closes the book.

It opens very early on Christmas morning, snow falling on housetops, with a little child born in the Bird household. The family meant to name a girl Lucy, but a real Christmas baby must not be lightly named. Readers get a tender holiday tale of a frail child, a window school, and a carol shared.
24329-st-winifred-s-or-the-world-of-scho:
Frederic W. Farrar wrote this school story, set in a Victorian boys' boarding school. Farrar himself attended such a school. He then served as assistant master at Harrow and head master of Marlborough College. His book is judged by its producer better in some ways than his far more famous Eric. It holds a number of well-written, moving episodes, though Farrar's habit of Latin and Greek quotations mars it for some readers.

It opens with Walter's home, where his mother and a fair-haired, blue-eyed two-year-old cry goodbye as Walter springs into a waiting carriage for the station. Mr. Evson takes his son to a large public school, the first time Walter has left home. Readers get the intimate details of school life, its friendships, faults, and farewells.
24688-the-making-of-a-trade-school:
Mary Schenck Woolman, director of the Manhattan Trade School for Girls and professor at Teachers College, Columbia, wrote this account of making a trade school, published at Boston in 1910. The school began its work in November 1902, in a building chosen for its classes. Woolman's book tells how it grew.

Parts cover organisation and work, representative problems, equipment and support, and detailed accounts of department work. Woolman argues that girls deserve real training for real trades, not mere accomplishments. Her book remains a landmark of vocational education, practical, idealistic, and full of classroom detail.
24714-fairy-tales-from-brazil-how-and-wh:
Elsie Spicer Eells wrote these fairy tales from Brazil, how and why tales from Brazilian folk-lore, published at Chicago in 1917 with pictures by Helen M. Barton. The special edition came by arrangement with Dodd, Mead. Its contents open with how night came, and how the rabbit lost his tail, in the pattern of just-so stories.

Later tales explain Brazilian animals, plants, and customs through folk fancy, with humour and charm. Eells collected her tales from Brazilian sources, retelling them for American children. Young readers get a bright doorway into South American folklore, full of animals, tricksters, and wonder.
24851-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for August 1880 opens with American Aeronauts, a celebration of balloonists as modern knights-errant. From Pilatre de Rozier to Gaston Tissandier, who rose seven miles into the upper air, the piece praises daring men. They take the wings of the morning for daring's sake, not for science or profit.

The same issue ranges widely, as the magazine's title promises: popular tales, science notes, and a study of Scottish music, bagpipes, and the drone's key of A minor. The mix shows a Victorian monthly at its best, feeding curious readers on many subjects at once. It remains a fine sample of 1880s magazine culture.
24858-the-story-of-wool:
Sara Ware Bassett wrote The Story of Wool in 1913, with pictures by Elizabeth Otis. Donald Clark, an eastern city boy, gets a puzzling telegram and heads west to a sheep ranch, where Sandy the herder becomes his teacher. Chapters follow the dipping, the shearing, and two adventures on the range, with a narrow escape and a prediction that comes true.

Bassett, who thanked the United States Department of Agriculture for help, mixes a boy's story with real ranch work: dogs, bells, dust, and long quiet days under a huge sky. Donald ends by choosing his own path. The book gives young readers a clear, lively look at how wool goes from sheep to cloth.
24923-the-variation-of-animals-and-plant:
Charles Darwin's first volume on variation under domestication gathers the evidence behind his theory of how breeders reshape living things. Domestic dogs and cats open the survey, showing how selection, habit, and crossing produce breeds far removed from their wild kin. Pigeons receive the closest study, with careful measurements of bones, beaks, and plumage across many fancy varieties.

One recorded detail shows the method at work: in certain pigeons the crest stands more prominent while the scapula runs about a fifth of an inch shorter than in the wild rock-pigeon. Such small, counted differences, piled up breed by breed, build Darwin's case that domestication can move a species a long way. The volume remains a patient foundation stone for the argument of natural selection.
25030-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science for November 1878 leads with Seawanhaka, the Island of Shells, illustrated by the wreck of the Circassian. The article weighs what Long Island was called by its aboriginal dwellers. The Canarsees met Hudson in Gravesend Bay in 1609, and Rockaways, Montauks, Shinecocs, and Patchogues lead to Pequots and Narragansetts. Old names include Mattenwake, Paumanacke, Mattanwake for good or pleasant land, Pamunke, and Meitowax, but none equals Seawanhaka for an island whose sunny shores are strewn with shells.

The same number recalls the old stagecoach creeping from Brooklyn to Sag Harbor in two days and a half, against the modern whirl of a few hours. It ranges to Caucasian folklore, where karts are female ogres with cannibal tastes. Narts are giants of protean shape, and mysterious equestrians are called hare riders. The magazine mixes antiquarian curiosity with popular science.
25072-the-new-england-magazine-volume-1-:
The April 1886 number of the New England Magazine and Bay State Monthly gathers local history, biography, and fiction with a strong New England flavor. Its leading articles profile Andover, James Otis Jr., and the Webster family, alongside a romance set during King Philip's War.

Shorter pieces cover New England manners in the poet Bryant's youth, the founding of the New England Library, and the region's schools and churches. The issue reads as a regional portrait in itself, showing how New Englanders of the 1880s remembered their past and argued about their character.
25116-the-new-england-magazine-volume-1-:
The 1886 fifth number of the New England Magazine and Bay State Monthly continues the regional miscellany begun in the previous issue. Its leading article profiles Trinity College in Hartford, with portraits of its presidents and views of its buildings across the century.

Other pieces continue the Webster family history and Fanny Bullock Workman's romance of King Philip's War. A poem honors Oliver Wendell Holmes on his departure for Europe, and a sketch describes New Bedford, its whalers, wharves, and churches. The number shows a magazine building a loyal New England readership out of local pride and local history.
25475-the-knickerbocker-or-new-york-mont:
The June 1844 Knickerbocker, volume 23, number 6, opens with an eye-witness account of plague at Constantinople. The writer lived in Galata in 1837, near enough to the deaths to know them well, yet apart from the Turkish quarters. He kept rigid quarantine with the widowed owner of his house, her daughter Aleukâ, and her little son Petraki. Out of doors he wore an oil-cloth cloak and kept dogs off with his cane.

Later pages turn to lighter matter, including a tale of Professor Shaw, his bugs and specimens, and three days in limbo after a townsman with a grudge calls him cracked. The number shows the Knickerbocker's mix of travel, humour, and magazine miscellany. Its pieces speak in the voice of a New York monthly at the height of its run.
25510-betty-vivian-a-story-of-haddo-cour:
Mrs. L. T. Meade sets this school story at Haddo Court, a large school for girls, where Betty Vivian must answer a hard question posed in the opening chapter, simply headed Yes or No. Betty, her sister, and friends such as Fanny face choices about loyalty, work, and conduct as term life unfolds.

Later chapters move from first reception at the school to an attic shared by the Vivians, a trip south, Scotch heather, and a special entertainment, each test shaping Betty's judgment. Meade, a veteran writer of girls' school tales, keeps the focus on friendship, rules, and growing resolve.
25870-a-world-of-girls-the-story-of-a-sc:
L. T. Meade tells a school story at Lavender House, where new girls, small tiffs, and a head mistress shape the term. Chapters move from good byes to the old life and traveling companions to little drawing rooms, a day at school, work and play, and a mystery found in a school desk. Talk in the chapel, a girl sent to Coventry, and sweets that prove poisoned raise the stakes.

The tale centers on Hester and her young charge Nan, whose illness brings grief and fear to the great hall. Mrs. Willis comforts Hester with an arm round her side and hope from the doctor, while schoolfellows are kept away lest the child be excited. Meade, a veteran writer of girls' books, mixes fun, feeling, and suspense in a world run by girls themselves.
26067-the-life-of-thomas-lord-cochrane-t:
The second volume of the life of Thomas, Lord Cochrane, tenth earl of Dundonald, completes his Autobiography of a Seaman. Written by Thomas, eleventh earl, with H. R. Fox Bourne, it opens in 1827 with Cochrane's arrival in Greece. He was welcomed at Hydra and Poros, and dealt with the Greek factions and National Assembly.

Chapters follow his commission as first admiral, the election of Capodistrias as president, and the siege of Athens. His memorial to the Lord High Admiral seeks justice for officers cut off from service. The volume mixes campaign narrative with letters and documents, closing the record of a career that ranged from British service to the Greek war of independence.
26122-five-little-peppers-at-school:
Margaret Sidney's school story, eighth in the Pepper books' order of publication, sends the Five Little Peppers to school under Mrs. Ferguson. Published in November 1903 and illustrated by Hermann Heyer, it follows the children's lessons, scrapes, and friendships in their new setting.

Miss Salisbury tells a tale of her own school days, when her father's telegram reached Mrs. Ferguson only because a storm delayed her party at the railroad station. Had the party not been delayed, her absence would have plunged the school in distress. Rickie, beaten too, shares the mishap in the frontispiece scene. The book keeps the Peppers' warmth, humor, and family loyalty at school.
26138-in-the-flash-ranging-service-obser:
Private Edward Alva Trueblood's 1919 memoir records his service with the American Expeditionary Forces in France, in the flash ranging service. The book relates his personal observations as a private soldier, from training beside French troops to taking over a section of the line.

The French stayed about ten days, long enough for the Americans to learn the work, and then the section passed to American hands. Provisions came in at night on men's backs, since a supply train by day would draw fire, and water ran short. Enemy guns shifted place after each attempt, keeping the Allies guessing. Trueblood's account is plain, direct, and grounded in daily hardship.
26154-the-joyous-adventures-of-aristide-:
William J. Locke's 1912 volume follows Aristide Pujol, a debonair Frenchman, through nine comic adventures. Chapter titles promise a fair patronne, an Arlesienne, a kind Mr. Smith, a foundling, a pig's head, Fleurette, a miracle, a fickle goddess, and a St. Martin's summer. Illustrations by Alec Ball catch scenes such as a father's entrance at the fourth kiss.

A narrator who knows Aristide tells the tales, with side figures such as Madame Bidoux adding local colour. Each adventure turns on charm, quick wit, and a scrape escaped by luck or nerve. The book offers light, sunny entertainment, and it shows Locke's gift for a hero who wins friends wherever his travels take him.
26392-the-hero-of-garside-school:
J. Harwood Panting's school story follows Harry Moncrief, who arrives at Garside and must win his place among boys quick to judge a newcomer. His friend Paul stands by him through a bad start to term, challenges from St. Bede's, and quarrels over the honour of the form. A little hunchback, a black book, and a forum debate add to the school's daily drama.

Adventure widens beyond the classroom with a raft on the river and a voyage. The mystery of the school's old flag, stolen from its turret, is traced through a mystic order of beetles and letters at the tuck-shop. Forgiveness proves the hero's hardest lesson, as friendship breaks and mends. The book closes with the flag's return and old bonds renewed.
26750-memorial-address-on-the-life-and-c:
George Bancroft delivered this memorial address on the life and character of Abraham Lincoln at the request of both houses of Congress. He spoke before them at the House of Representatives in Washington on February 12, 1866. The Government Printing Office published it the same year.

Bancroft opens with divine rule over human affairs, as certain as physical science, marshaling the great procession of nations through the ages. Kings are lifted up or thrown down, republics flourish and wither, and dynasties pass like a tale told, yet nothing is by chance. America, the child of the ages, drew nourishment from India, Greece, Rome, medieval municipalities, Teutonic representation, and English experience, washing the gold of political wisdom from sands, rocks, and ruins. Farmers left half-ploughed land for the musket, facing peril and death with hearts still on home.
27371-the-diplomatic-correspondence-of-t:
Jared Sparks edited this first volume of the diplomatic correspondence of the American Revolution, published in Boston in 1829. It came out under the direction of the President from the original manuscripts of the Department of State. Congress had ordered the publication by a resolution of 27 March 1818, so the letters appear as official papers rather than private memoirs.

The volume prints letters from Benjamin Franklin, Silas Deane, John Adams, John Jay, Arthur Lee, William Lee, Ralph Izard, and Francis Dana. Others follow, with replies from the Secret Committee of Congress and the Secretary of Foreign Affairs. Correspondence of the French ministers Gerard and Luzerne is included as well. It is a core source for how the United States won foreign support during the Revolution.
27372-the-diplomatic-correspondence-of-t:
Jared Sparks edited this eighth volume of the diplomatic correspondence of the American Revolution, published in Boston in 1830 by Nathan Hale and Gray and Bowen, with New York and Washington imprints. Like the first volume, it prints letters from the original manuscripts of the Department of State, under the congressional resolution of 27 March 1818.

This volume continues the correspondence of John Jay, opening with Robert R. Livingston writing from Philadelphia on 13 December 1781 about military operations in the South and asking for more frequent communications. Letters of Franklin, Adams, Jay, Lafayette, and others fill the series as a whole. Researchers get the Revolution's diplomacy in the writers' own words.
27632-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
This volume of the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers, instituted in 1852, prints society papers with their discussions. Paper number 1191, by E. D. Hardy, reports the results of operating the water purification plant in Washington, D.C.

The plant opened in October 1905, with a pumping station raising water from McMillan Park Reservoir up to the filters. It holds 29 filters of the slow sand type. When the first paper was written in November 1906, the plant had run about one year. Hardy now reviews five years of records on cost, efficiency, and methods of operation, with discussion by Allen Hazen, George A. Johnson, and others.
27879-the-diplomatic-correspondence-of-t:
Edited by Jared Sparks, this eleventh volume of the diplomatic correspondence of the American Revolution was published in Boston in 1830 under a resolution of Congress of March 27, 1818.
