It gathers letters of Franklin, Adams, Jay, the Lees, Laurens, Lafayette, Dumas, and others on foreign relations during the whole Revolution.

The volume continues the correspondence of the French minister Luzerne, with letters from Philadelphia in September 1781 on mediation, the admission of an American minister, and Dana's mission to St. Petersburg. It is a primary source for the diplomacy that won independence, printed from manuscripts in the Department of State.
28564-a-bunch-of-cherries-a-story-of-che:
Mrs. L. T. Meade's A Bunch of Cherries, published by M. A. Donohue and Company of Chicago in 1898, tells of Cherry Court School. The house is long, low, and rambling, partly a hundred years old, with square rooms and low ceilings. Behind it lies a walled garden two or three centuries old, covering at least three acres, famous for cherries from White Heart to black.

Mrs. Clavering's cherry feast, toward the end of June before vacation, is the event of the school year. Girls count the hours to it, and hard work quickens at its mention. Chapters follow the girls, a telegram, Sir John's great scheme, Florence, Kitty, ribbons, and a fairy box. Readers get a school story sweetened by fruit and friendship.
28693-tales-of-the-fish-patrol:
Jack London wrote this 1905 collection of stories about the fish patrol of San Francisco Bay. The narrator and his partner Charley enforce fishing laws against oyster pirates, Greek fishermen, and poachers. Their tales include White and Yellow, The King of the Greeks, A Raid on the Oyster Pirates, and The Siege of the Lancashire Queen. George Varian's pictures show the boats, the grappling irons, and the chases.

London drew on his own youth on the bay, and the stories mix adventure with close knowledge of tides, boats, and fishing work. The patrol's raids turn on nerve and seamanship rather than gunplay alone. Readers who know The Call of the Wild will find the same energy here. It turns to a true-life corner of California: the state's fight to protect its fisheries from men who fished out of season.
28749-the-madcap-of-the-school:
Angela Brazil wrote this school story about girls at a boarding school, where lessons, friendships, and pranks fill the term. The chapters move from a moated grange and a secret society called the Mystic Seven to a week working on the land, a camp, and a turn as amateur detectives. Balliol Salmon's pictures show the girls in their loudest and liveliest moments.

The heroine's high spirits keep getting her into scrapes, and the story follows how she and her friends sort them out without losing their fun. Brazil wrote many school tales, and this one follows her usual pattern: loyalty to the school, close friendships, and mischief that stops short of real harm. Young readers get a lively picture of English girls' school life.
28878-four-little-blossoms-at-oak-hill-s:
Mabel C. Hawley wrote this 1920 children's book about four little Blossoms at Oak Hill School, published by Saalfield in Akron and New York. The chapters open with the house that Bobby built, school supplies, and starting school, then move to a dead snake, another schoolroom, an unpleasant meeting, and a hard lesson. Later chapters bring a spoiled book, Bobby in trouble, and a monkey hunt.

Bobby, the elder brother, builds a bay window from a rocking chair while small Twaddles keeps pushing back into the game. The Blossoms' school days mix mischief with lessons, in the cheerful style of the series. Young readers get a gentle story of starting school, with a frontispiece of the children thrilled by clever beasts and performers.
28901-social-rights-and-duties-addresses:
Leslie Stephen wrote this first volume of Social Rights and Duties, addresses to the Ethical Societies of London, published in 1896. Some chapters first appeared in the International Journal of Ethics and the reviews. They treat the aims of ethical societies, science and politics, the sphere of political economy, the morality of competition, social equality, and ethics and the struggle for existence.

Stephen opens by warning his hearers not to overrate what a society can do, while insisting that the vital problems of the day deserve support. His addresses argue for honest thinking over party slogans. Readers interested in Victorian moral philosophy get a clear, unsentimental voice: a thinker who valued reason, fairness, and plain speech about society's hard questions.
28950-the-geneva-protocol:
David Hunter Miller wrote this 1925 study, The Geneva Protocol, published by Macmillan in New York. Miller, an American expert on world law, looks at the Geneva plan chapter by chapter. He covers how it would take effect, who signed it, how signers would treat each other, and how disputes would be settled.

Later chapters treat the status quo, home questions, pledges against war, aggression, and the Japanese amendment. Further chapters cover sanctions, separate defense pacts, the plan and article ten of the Covenant, and the disarmament talks. Annexes print the Covenant of the League of Nations. Readers keen on the League's failed effort to outlaw war get a careful study from the time, written by a lawyer who knew the diplomacy from inside.
28966-a-dear-little-girl-at-school:
Amy E. Blanchard wrote this 1910 school story about Edna, a dear little girl at school, published by Whitman in Racine, Wisconsin. The book opens with Edna and her big cousin Ben Barker on the back porch, where Ben works on his bicycle wheel for a long ride. Edna, ready to hand him tools or fetch rags and oil, asks where he is going, and Ben answers with jokes about Johnny-jump-up and dog-wood bark.

Blanchard writes for young girls with warmth and gentle humor, following Edna from home pastimes into school life and friendship. Cousin Ben's teasing talk sets the tone: kind, funny, and safe. Readers get a period girls' book of the simplest pleasures, porch talk, bicycles, and the first steps toward school, told in an easy, affectionate style.
28974-the-manor-house-school:
Angela Brazil wrote this school story, The Manor House School, published by Blackie and Son in London, Glasgow, and Bombay, with pictures by A. A. Dixon. The book opens in the first week of summer term at Winterburn Lodge, where preparation is over and girls stroll the playground till the tea bell. Tennis balls thud, three pianos practice in three keys, and two yellow heads and a brown one bend over a battered atlas.

Chapters follow Nora's news, an interesting stranger, a strong suspicion, and Haversleigh, through the plot thickening, a secret door, and the lantern room, to good-bye to the manor. Brazil writes her usual lively school tale of friendship and mystery. Readers get a cheerful period girls' book, with a frontispiece crying glorious news.
29343-three-addresses-to-girls-at-school:
J. M. Wilson, head master of Clifton College and vice-president of the Clifton High School for Girls, published these three addresses in London in 1890. Wilson first printed them for private circulation among their hearers, then published them at frequent request, keeping personal and local allusions he could not remove. His preface dates from Clifton College in September 1890.

The first address, on education, was given at Clifton High School on October 25, 1887. The second, on high school education for girls, was given at Bath and Clifton in December 1889. The third, on religion, was given at St. Leonard's School, St. Andrews, on April 13, 1890. Readers get a Victorian headmaster's case for girls' education, earnest and practical, from inside the schools themselves.
29395-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
J. B. Lippincott and Company published this October 1880 number of Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science. Its opening piece, A Chapter of American Exploration by William H. Rideing, compares the Rocky Mountains with the Alps. Adventurers seeking peril on the Aiguille Verte and the Matterhorn, Rideing argues, will not find such friable cliffs in the Rockies, where high summits may be reached with less danger.

The issue also carries the serial Adam and Eve through chapters thirty to thirty-two, and a piece titled Seven Weeks a Missionary. Readers get a month of a popular literary magazine, mixing western exploration with fiction and missionary narrative for a general audience.
29438-the-diplomatic-correspondence-of-t:
Jared Sparks edited this ninth volume of the Diplomatic Correspondence of the American Revolution. It was published under the direction of the President of the United States. Its sources are original manuscripts in the Department of State. Congress authorized the work by a resolution of March 27, 1818. The volume prints letters concerning the foreign relations of the United States during the whole Revolution.

Correspondents include Benjamin Franklin, Silas Deane, John Adams, John Jay, Arthur Lee, William Lee, Ralph Izard, Francis Dana, and William Carmichael, whose correspondence fills this volume. Henry Laurens, John Laurens, Lafayette, and Dumas also appear, with replies from the Secret Committee of Congress and the Secretary of Foreign Affairs. The entire correspondence of the French ministers Gerard and Luzerne with Congress is included. Readers get primary sources for Revolutionary diplomacy, in the founders' own letters.
29575-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Volume twenty of Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science, dated August 1877 and entered by J. B. Lippincott and Company, opens with a concluding paper down the Rhine. Coblenz, the writer says, first gave him associations with the river, from drives to a city of wide, calm flow, a low bridge of boats, and busy outskirts. That picture differs from the Rhine of German song and English ballad, all castles and poetry.

The old town, however, has many beauties, though its military character shows. The issue mixes travel, fiction, and science in Lippincott's popular manner. Readers of Victorian magazines will find a rich, well-illustrated number from a magazine that served general readers with both letters and learning.
29600-rural-life-and-the-rural-school:
Joseph Kennedy, dean of the School of Education at the University of North Dakota, wrote Rural Life and the Rural School. It was printed by the American Book Company of New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago. Its first chapter treats rural life a generation ago: chores and work, yearly routine, harvesting, threshing, and winter work, with women's condition unrelieved and the backward rural school as a central problem.

Later chapters trace the urban trend: cityward drift, city schools and churches, retired farmers, and educational centers. Kennedy argues the rural problem must be met with better schools and facilities. Students of education history will find a clear, early study of country life and the schools that served it.
301-the-ballad-of-reading-gaol:
Oscar Wilde, himself a prisoner at Reading, wrote of a trooper hanged for killing the woman he loved. The Ballad of Reading Gaol, dedicated to C. T. W., opens with a man in shabby grey who looks wistfully at the sky. Wilde walked another ring of pain beside him.

Two versions appear here, both tracking the condemned man's last days, the trial men, and the prison routine. Wilde turns pity for one killer into protest against all hanging. The ballad's refrain on each man killing the thing he loves became famous. It stands as Wilde's last great poem.
30112-development-of-the-phonograph-at-a:
Leslie J. Newville wrote Development of the Phonograph at Alexander Graham Bell's Volta Laboratory as paper five in Contributions from the Museum of History and Technology. It appeared in United States National Museum Bulletin 218, pages 69 to 79.

The fame of Thomas A. Edison, Newville opens, rests most firmly on his gift for turning other men's ideas to practical use. Yet the credit goes to Alexander Graham Bell, a longtime Smithsonian Regent and friend of S. P. Langley, its third Secretary. With his Volta Laboratory associates, he made practical the phonograph, called Edison's most original invention. How Bell became involved, with Charles Sumner Tainter and Chichester Bell, in making practical phonograph records is not so well known, though the story of his telephone has been told and retold.
30296-the-philosophy-of-teaching-the-tea:
Nathaniel Sands argues for the dignity of teaching in a Harper volume from New York in 1869, titled The Teacher, the Pupil, the School. Of all callings shaped by the division of labor, he says, none matches the true teacher for nobility or usefulness, yet neither teachers nor people at present grasp that truth. Among the Greeks, he notes, no calling was more honored than teaching, a lesson lost amid so-called classical studies.

Sands charges that precious time of youth has been wasted and young minds and morals perverted by those studies, while the teacher's proper honor went disregarded. What duty could be more responsible, he asks, than training the young in industry, truthfulness, economy, and sobriety, and giving knowledge and skill without which life becomes a burden. The book speaks to teachers, parents, and schools in plain, earnest terms.
30627-in-the-heart-of-a-fool:
William Allen White writes In the Heart of a Fool, published in New York in October 1918 by the Macmillan Company. It follows his earlier In Our Town, A Certain Rich Man, and The Martial Adventures of Henry and Me. Contents open with stage directions and a cast of characters, then introduce the fool and his lady fair.

A chapter considers the ladies, God bless them, and another notes that the Adams family Bible lies like a gentleman. Margaret Muller and further scenes follow in White's small-town saga. White, a Kansas editor and novelist, writes about ordinary people, folly, love, and moral choice with warmth, humor, and plain American speech.
30760-my-private-menagerie-from-the-work:
Théophile Gautier wrote this memoir of his own animals, translated and edited by Professor F. C. de Sumichrast for volume nineteen of Gautier's works, printed in 1902. Gautier admits he was fond of animals all his life, cats most of all. He says he was often drawn in Turkish dress on cushions, with cats climbing on his shoulders and head. He insists the joke held some truth.

Five short parts follow his pets in order: old memories, a white dynasty of cats, a black dynasty, dogs, and horses. He recalls coming to Paris from Tarbes at age three, homesick and speaking only his local speech, and he links each animal to a place or a time in his life. The result is a light, fond book for readers who like cats, dogs, and a writer's home life.
30860-ruby-at-school:
Minnie E. Paull wrote this 1894 girls' book, the third volume of the Ruby series, published by Estes and Lauriat in Boston. Paull had already written Ruth and Ruby and Ruby's Ups and Downs, and here Ruby moves from mischief at home toward boarding school. Early chapters show Ruby in mischief, carrying out her plan, and facing consequences, before preparations for school begin.

Later chapters follow the journey, making friends, an old acquaintance, getting settled, and school life itself, with Maude's troubles, misadventures, surprises, and a Christmas getting ready. A frontispiece shows Ruby filling her apron with crisp, fresh cookies. Note that the source book used for this text lacked pages 145 to 146 and 159 to 160, and many pictures, so the held copy has gaps at those points.
30938-polly-s-senior-year-at-boarding-sc:
Dorothy Whitehill wrote this 1917 girls' book, published by Barse and Hopkins in New York, with pictures by Charles L. Wrenn. It is the third book of the Polly Pendleton series, after Polly's First Year at Boarding School and Polly's Summer Vacation, with other volumes in preparation. The frontispiece shows a girl who has made little or no progress in unpacking her suitcase, since nothing is put away.

Chapters run from Seniors and A Class Meeting through Fanny, Basket-Ball Election, Thanksgiving, and Maud, into the rest of Polly's senior year at boarding school. Whitehill follows Polly and her classmates through school elections, holidays, and the duties of being seniors. It is a warm, old-fashioned school story for young readers, closing Polly's boarding-school years with friendship and fun.
3123-the-novel-and-the-common-school:
Warner writes here about American health, manners, and school reading within two generations. The physical state of the people has improved greatly, he says, more in the West than in the East, but markedly everywhere. A foreign traveler once blamed a dry, stirring climate and a feverish hunger for quick change for a decline in the race. That traveler would now find little to support his theory.

The essay links that bodily improvement to the common school and its books. Novels, Warner argues, belong in the education of ordinary readers, not kept from them. Well chosen fiction can train taste and morals for pupils who will never reach a college, and the school that scorns it wastes a plain tool for good.
31860-the-red-symbol:
John Ironside's novel The Red Symbol was published at Boston by Little, Brown and Company in April 1910, with copyright in 1909 and 1910. It opens with a telephone call to Maurice Wynn, a special correspondent of ten years' experience. Harding tells him Carson is ill, he must relieve him, and Lord Southbourne will give him instructions that night at Whitehall Gardens.

Wynn faces a sudden journey to St. Petersburg, a Savage Club dinner at the Hotel Cecil, and a frontispiece scene in which he hears a man mutter in French about the symbol. Readers get an Edwardian spy and mystery romance of London, Paris, and Russia, built on a red-haired woman, a blood-stained portrait, and murder most foul.
31985-perfect-control:
Richard Stockham's short story Perfect Control, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in January 1955, opens with Colonel Halter at his desk, bringing images on a telescreen into focus. Four booster tugs cling to the ancient derelict Alpha like barnacles. They swing her stern down toward Earth's bluish-white, moon-lit arc a thousand miles below.

When the control room of the old ship swims onto the screen, Halter sees a crew seated in a half circle at the control panel. Their faces are smooth and kind, with no lines of care or laughter, like faces of wax. Readers get a space mystery that asks why a man cannot go home again after years in space, and whether he can find the answer in time.
32093-loyal-to-the-school:
Angela Brazil's school story, published in London and Glasgow by Blackie and Son with drawings by H. L. Bacon, belongs to her long run of school tales. Brazil's name on the title page already carried books such as Monitress Merle, A Fortunate Term, and For the School Colours. Loyal to the School offers the same world: classrooms, cloakrooms, notice boards, and the small crises of a school term, told from inside a girls' community.

Its opening scenes show girls crowding a home-made poster in the hall, signed by M. Tatham. The poster calls the school to the gymnasium at half past two. New form lists will be read there, and new arrangements explained. Kathleen, Lesbia, Calla, and Aldora trade jokes and warnings about what may change. Readers get a light school story, where loyalty means facing new rules, forms, and friendships.
32239-dissertation-on-slavery-with-a-pro:
St. George Tucker's Dissertation on Slavery, with a proposal for the gradual abolition of it in the state of Virginia, was printed in Philadelphia for Mathew Carey in 1796. Tucker was professor of law at William and Mary and a judge of Virginia's General Court. He fronts the work with Montesquieu: slavery violates the laws of nature and civil society, and wounds the best forms of government.

In a democracy, Montesquieu's epigraph continues, where all men are equal, slavery is contrary to the spirit of the constitution. The dissertation itself proposes gradual abolition in Virginia, argued by a Virginia jurist from law, nature, and government. Its original spelling is maintained in this text, with short bibliographical notes set in brackets and longer footnotes renumbered. Readers get an early American abolition proposal, legal in form and revolutionary in implication.
32631-restricted-tool:
Malcolm B. Morehart Jr. tells of Richard Clark, a hunter who finds a strange metal gadget in a thorny shrub while chasing a rabbit. Two squat aliens soon confront him, one called Ursi, and explain that a careless crewman dropped the tool after scanner trouble hid Clark from view.

Clark dreams of a fortune making the device, which can lift and move heavy loads with ease. A farmer, however, already owns a general-purpose degrav tool and has used one for two years, so Clark's prize may be common goods in a world ahead of his own.
32892-women-of-america-woman-in-all-ages:
John Rouse Larus devotes the tenth volume of his series on woman in all ages and countries to the women of America. The Philadelphia volume, from George Barrie and Sons, is illustrated throughout. Its opening chapter treats the aboriginal woman of America.

Larus warns that broad generalities are nearly all that can be claimed, since Huron custom, Seminole custom, and Navajo custom differ widely. Later chapters move to the colonial foundations of New England and Virginia. A Pilgrim mother faces a mysterious wilderness that later bears terrible fruit at Salem. Another colonial chatelaine directs her garrison's guns herself against a superior enemy force.
32975-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica gathers the entries running from Calhoun to Camoens. Its articles include John Caldwell Calhoun, California and Lower California, the Caliph and the Caliphate, Callao, Callicott, Cambodia, and Camoens. Shorter entries on places, people, and terms that fall in the same alphabetical span sit alongside them. Transcriber's notes record corrections to the Caliph article, where Hajjaj had been misprinted.

Like other Britannica slices, this one mixes geography, history, biography, and science in the confident voice of early twentieth-century reference writing. Readers get the facts and judgments that educated readers of the day were expected to trust, from a state's history to a poet's life. As a reference text it is dated, but as a record of how knowledge was ordered a century ago, it remains a useful window.
32992-the-youngest-girl-in-the-school:
Evelyn Sharp's 1901 school story, reissued in 1906, follows the youngest girl in a school. She is a small newcomer among older girls who must learn the rules, the friendships, and the scrapes of boarding-school life. Illustrations by C. E. Brock catch its lively moments: a plea for a treat, a mop of tangled hair smoothed down, and children found where they should not be. Five heads pop up at an open window. The tone is warm and comic throughout.

Sharp, already known for The Making of a Schoolgirl, writes for girls who knew school from the inside. She treats teasing, loyalty, and small rebellions with sympathy rather than scolding. The youngest girl grows bolder as she finds her place, and the book's charm lies in that growth. It remains a pleasant period piece, and a good early example of the school story as a genre of its own.
33523-little-frankie-at-school:
Another volume in A. R. Baker's Little Frankie series, this book follows Frankie into the classroom. School brings new routines, lessons, teachers, and classmates, and Frankie must learn to sit, listen, recite, and get along with other children. Small incidents of the school day become occasions for lessons in diligence, honesty, and courtesy.

Written for very young readers, the book keeps its scenes short and its language plain, so that families can read it aloud or early readers can manage it alone. Like its companion volume on Frankie's plays, it reflects a nineteenth-century belief that everyday childhood experience, rightly guided, builds character. Its gentle tone makes it a sweet survival of early children's literature.
33530-dorothy-dale-at-glenwood-school:
Margaret Penrose's Dorothy Dale at Glenwood School, copyrighted in 1908, follows Dorothy to a new school, where a ranger commands proceed and Dorothy begins a thimble chase. Penrose, author of Dorothy Dale: A Girl of Today, writes of school life with warmth and humor, in a series that went on to further volumes. The book's frontispiece captures the thimble chase in full swing.

The tale's charm lies in its school detail, its lively girls, and its wholesome adventures, from classes to games. Its tone is bright and friendly, suited to young readers. For fans of girls' series books, Dorothy Dale at Glenwood School offers a pleasing, old-fashioned term with a heroine worth following.
34203-history-of-the-reign-of-philip-the:
William Prescott, the American historian, wrote this third volume of his History of the Reign of Philip the Second, King of Spain, bound here with his biographical and critical essays. The catalog title is a scrap from that pairing. Volume three opens with the Moors of Spain: their conquest of the land, the long struggle to win it back, and the mark that struggle left on the Spanish character.

Prescott then treats the forced conversion of the Moors under Philip, the harsh laws of 1563, and the suffering that followed. A front picture shows Don John of Austria from a painting at Madrid. Prescott wrote with a storyteller's gift and a scholar's care. His Philip remains a standard English history of Spain's great century.
34702-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
One slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica fills this file. Volume three, slice seven, runs from the Bible to Bisectrix. The edition calls itself a dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information. Hundreds of short entries stand between the long articles.

The list opens with the Bible in several forms. Entries treat the English Bible, Bible Christians, and Bible societies. Bibliography and bibliology follow, with bibliomancy beside them. Towns, rivers, and lives fill much of the slice. Bichat, Bickerstaffe, and the Biddle family all appear. Working topics include the bicycle, bimetallism, and the binary system. The slice ends among natural history entries. Binturong and the birch tree stand near the biography and biology articles.
35341-literature-in-the-elementary-schoo:
Literature in the Elementary School is a teaching book by Porter Lander MacClintock, issued by a university press at Chicago. Copyright pages date the work to 1907, and a long list of impressions follows it through 1914. That run of printings shows a book much used in its first years. The author dedicates it to friends and fellow students named on the page.

MacClintock writes for teachers of young children, on what written works belong in the early school years. Her university post and press point to a study grown out of training work. The steady reprinting, year after year, marks the book as a standard guide of its moment. Readers get a scholar's view of how stories and poems should meet a child at school.
35398-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
The hosted volume is one alphabet slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, running from Equation to Ethics. Its opening matter is the transcribers' notes, explaining how subscripts, superscripts, and Greek letters are rendered in plain text. A corrected list of small press errors in articles such as Estébanez Calderón and Etheredge follows.

The index of articles then marches in order: Equation of Time, Equator, Equilibrium, Equinox, Equity, and the lives of Erasmus and Eratosthenes among them. Escheat, the Escorial, and Escutcheon stand in the same run. The eleventh edition, issued in 1910 and 1911, is still prized as the high-water mark of the old scholarly encyclopedia. This slice preserves its entries exactly as the transcribers keyed them, chemical notation and all.
35519-joscelyn-cheshire-a-story-of-revol:
Sara Beaumont Kennedy sets a love story in the Revolutionary War in a novel issued in New York in 1901. Kennedy gives the book to her husband, Walker Kennedy. A front picture shows the heroine sweeping a courtesy full of open defiance and ridicule.

Chapter one, Cupid and Mars, brings young Richard Clevering home in a new Continental uniform of buff and blue. The tale moves through the march of the Continentals, Valley Forge, a fete at Philadelphia, and the field of Monmouth. Joscelyn faces peril in Clinton's tents, a prison road, Tarleton's toils, and a search of her lady's wardrobe. Readers get southern war romance, with battles, spies, and a maid's heart tried by both armies.
35730-peggy-parsons-at-prep-school:
Peggy Parsons at Prep School is a girls' school novel by Annabel Sharp, issued by the Donohue company of Chicago and New York. It opens with Peggy in her dorm room, braiding her curly hair and admiring a new blue silk kimono. The kimono was a gift from a cousin, labeled for midnight fudge parties. Her room-mate teases her that even yawning is not allowed at the school.

The fifteen chapters follow school life through a serenade, a bacon bat, a bean auction, and the inside of Gloomy House. Peggy manages Mrs. Forest, spends Christmas holidays away, meets a fortune teller, and plays Miss Robinson Crusoe. Spring brings Annapolis, water-sprites, and a close at Parsons Court.
35907-love-worship-and-death-some-render:
Sir Rennell Rodd made these renderings from the Greek Anthology, Love, Worship and Death, printed in London in 1916. Rodd, a diplomat and poet, sorts the old epigrams under his three heads. His index of authors runs from Mimnermus and Sappho to Callimachus and Leonidas of Tarentum.

Sappho gets four pieces: a bitter word, the beloved presence, Hesper the evening star, and out of reach. Simonides speaks for the Spartans and the Athenians who fell. Plato's grave in Persia and Anyte's shrine by the sea follow. One rendered voice warns that love and memory alike will leave the unloved dead to wander with the phantoms. Rodd's versions are smooth, musical English verse.
36838-camp-fires-of-the-wolf-patrol:
Alan Douglas, a scout master, wrote the first book of his Hickory Ridge Boy Scouts set, the tale of the Wolf Patrol. A roster at the front names the troop and its master, Roderic Garrabrant. The Wolf Patrol is led by Elmer Chenowith, a lad from the north west woods. His mates include Mark Cummings, Ted Burgoyne, and Toby Ellsworth Jones.

The series list at the front tells what this first book holds. The patrol goes on its first camp, and the boys get a chance to use their new scout craft in real work. Elmer amazes the rest with his grasp of camp life. The book is pitched as a clean, sound tale every boy should read. Later books in the set take the troop to woodcraft tests, a missing tenderfoot, a ball game, a great hike, and a trial of grit.
36957-social-rights-and-duties-addresses:
Leslie Stephen, the critic and man of letters, delivered these addresses to the ethical societies of London. The two-volume set came out in 1896, and this file holds volume two. Some pieces had already run in leading reviews, and Stephen thanks their owners for leave to reprint.

The five addresses treat heredity, punishment, luxury, the duties of authors, and the vanity of philosophising. A sixth honors forgotten benefactors. In the first, Stephen owns he has no science of value on heredity, and treats the word with care. The tone is that of a wise, dry speaker working out social duties before a serious audience.
37645-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Volume three of The Works of John Dryden is part of the first full set of his works, in eighteen volumes, with notes and a life by Walter Scott. William Miller printed it in London in 1808. Dryden was the great poet and playwright of Restoration England.

This volume holds plays, from Sir Martin Mar All, a comedy of feigned innocence, to The Tempest, reshaped from Shakespeare as a comedy. An Evening Love, or the Mock Astrologer, stands next, with a letter to the Duke of Newcastle. Tyrannic Love, a tragedy of a royal martyr, closes the set, with a letter to the Duke of Monmouth. Scott notes that Sir Martin came in part from Moliere and in part from the Duke of Newcastle. Drama readers get Dryden stage craft with Scott rich notes.
37898-the-diplomatic-correspondence-of-t:
The Diplomatic Correspondence of the American Revolution is a great set of letters on the foreign dealings of the United States during the war. Volume seven is hosted here, printed at Boston in 1830. Jared Sparks edited the whole work. It was published by direction of the President, from original papers in the Department of State, under a resolution of Congress of 1818.

The title page lists the writers: Franklin, Deane, Adams, Jay, the Lees, Izard, Dana, Carmichael, the Laurenses, Lafayette, and Dumas. Replies from the Secret Committee of Congress and the Secretary of Foreign Affairs stand alongside. So does the full correspondence of the French ministers Gerard and Luzerne with Congress. These letters show how a new nation begged, borrowed, and bargained its way to survival. Sparks's edition long served as the standard source for the diplomacy of the Revolution.
3842-memoirs-of-jean-franc-ois-paul-de-g:
Cardinal de Retz begins his memoirs with his birth and family, setting the stage for a life spent at the center of French trouble. The preface lists his titles, second Archbishop of Paris, Abbot of Saint Denis, and sovereign of Commercy. It traces his line from Albert de Gondi, duke and marshal, through his father Philippe Emanuel, general of the galleys. Retz was born at Montmirail in October 1614, into a house built for power.

The first book then follows his youth and entry into the church and the state, with Paris already stirring. A later passage shows a cardinal hurrying a count into civil war by chicanery, while the Duke of Bouillon presses for war whatever the cost. Readers who start here will meet Retz before the Fronde made him famous, ambitious, learned, and already dangerous.
3843-memoirs-of-jean-franc-ois-paul-de-g:
Cardinal de Retz opens his second book with a maxim for ambitious men, that they should begin public life with some notable act to strike the people's imagination. He recalls preaching on All Saints' Day before a crowd glad to see an archbishop in the pulpit. Then he faced an archbishopric sunk in temporals and spirituals by his uncle's sordidness and neglect. Retz owns frankly that his own corrupt inclinations would bear down honor and conscience.

The book then moves into the Fronde, as Paris example governs Guienne and Provence and everything shakes and totters. The queen shares the people's hatred with Cardinal Mazarin, while the Duke of Orleans shares their contempt with his favorite. Readers who like memoirs without varnish will find Retz a candid and cunning guide to civil war.
3844-memoirs-of-jean-franc-ois-paul-de-g:
Cardinal de Retz devotes his third book to the struggle between Mazarin and the Prince de Conde, who had saved the cardinal from the gallows. Mazarin, seeking to shed his debt, courts the house of Vendome, old opponents of Conde, while Paris fills with libels and ballads against the cardinal. Retz admits it suited his party to let attacks on Mazarin run, though attacks on the queen had to be stopped.

A grim scene follows, as two men condemned for libeling the queen cry from the scaffold that they die for verses against Mazarin, and the crowd rescues them from justice. Retz also confesses how fear of failure made him first refuse a cardinal's hat, then chase it with headlong haste. The book shows conspiracy from inside, told by a conspirator who admires his own craft.
3845-memoirs-of-jean-franc-ois-paul-de-g:
Cardinal de Retz covers the crisis of Mazarin's return in his fourth and fifth books. In December 1651 Parliament resolves to send deputies to the king, to forbid all governors to give the cardinal passage, and to warn foreign princes why he was removed. When a voice proposes setting a price on Mazarin's head, Retz and the other spiritual councillors retire, since canon law bars clergy from votes on life and death.

The narrative then follows the Duke of Orleans to Limours, where panic seizes him so hard that he takes musket fire for rejoicing as soldiers come to invest his palace. Messengers bring word that all is quiet, but he trusts no one and watches the window for drums. The books show a revolution eating its own leaders, with Retz at the center of the fear.
38534-the-great-musicians-rossini-and-hi:
H Sutherland Edwards treats Rossini and the modern Italian school in a volume of The Great Musicians series. Francis Hueffer edited the series, which also offered lives of Wagner, Weber, Mendelssohn, Schubert, Marcello, and Purcell. Each volume stands complete in itself, in a small cloth format.

The hosted pages open with the series list and a companion list of cheap lives of English philosophers. Edwards then turns to Rossini as the head of his school and the model of modern Italian opera. Readers get a Victorian life-and-works study of the composer of The Barber of Seville, written for general readers who wanted the great musicians in short, uniform volumes.
38631-the-monarchs-of-the-main-or-advent:
Thornbury's Monarchs of the Main tells the adventures of the buccaneers of the Caribbean. Hurst and Blackett published the first of its three volumes in London in 1855. The motto, from Much Ado About Nothing, gives the pirate character in a line: one foot on sea and one on shore, to one thing constant never.

The first chapter traces the precursors of the buccaneers on the island of Tortuga. French and English settlers conquered and lost it in turn. The hunters of Hispaniola, who cured meat over smoke and took their name from that practice, fill the second chapter. Thornbury describes their dress, their hunting, their duels, and their apprentices. Driven from the land at last, the hunters turned corsairs, and the great age of buccaneering begins.
38632-the-monarchs-of-the-main-or-advent:
George Thornbury wrote this history of the buccaneers in three volumes, and Hurst and Blackett published the second volume at London in 1855 under the title The Monarchs of the Main. Its motto, from Much Ado About Nothing, gives the buccaneer creed: one foot on sea and one on shore, to one thing constant never.

Volume two belongs chiefly to Sir Henry Morgan, the Welsh farmer's son who ran to sea and turned buccaneer. The contents follow him through the taking of Porto Bello and Maracaibo, the torturing of citizens for treasure, and the conquest and burning of Panama. Companions and successors follow: Esquemeling's escapes, Captain Cook, and the South Sea cruises of Sawkins and Sharp, who plundered Hillo and La Serena and took Arica. Trials for piracy and fresh seizures close the freebooters' round.
38633-the-monarchs-of-the-main-or-advent:
The Monarchs of the Main, volume III of 3, closes George W Thornbury's adventures of the buccaneers. Hurst and Blackett published it in London in 1855. An epigraph from Much Ado About Nothing sets the seamen's faithlessness. The first chapter follows Ravenau de Lussan. That young French officer joins De Graff at St Domingo. He crosses the isthmus, fights Greek mercenaries, and sacks towns from Leon to Granada.

The second chapter is titled The Last of the Brotherhood. Montauban cruises the Guinea coast and lives with a negro king. Laurence de Graff wins victories, then enters French service. Grammont takes Santiago, Maracaibo, and Cumana. The third chapter records the floating empire's destruction. The Peace of Ryswick tried to settle the buccaneers as planters. Instead they turned pirates outright. Blackbeard and Captain Avery people the final chapter. The pirates of New Providence and the kings of Madagascar end the brotherhood's story.
38642-the-diplomatic-correspondence-of-t:
Volume ten of The Diplomatic Correspondence of the American Revolution gathers letters by the young republic's envoys abroad. The title page names Franklin, Deane, Adams, Jay, and many more, plus the French ministers Gerard and Luzerne. The set was published under the direction of the President, from the first manuscripts in government hands.

Inside are letters to and from Congress and its secret committee, covering foreign ties through the whole war. Readers can watch aid, loans, treaties, and quarrels among the envoys unfold in their own words. For students of the Revolution, this volume is raw material of the best kind: the paper trail of how America won friends and funds abroad.
3884-memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoi:
Madame Campan, first lady in waiting to Marie Antoinette, opens her memoirs with a warning about Louis the Sixteenth. The king kept a crowd of confidants, advisers, and guides, chosen even from factions that attacked him, yet never fully disclosed himself to any one of them. He held the reins of secret intrigues in his own hand, and from that secrecy came the want of cooperation and weakness conspicuous in his measures.

The preface promises that chasms will appear in any detailed history of the Revolution for that reason, and Campan fills them from the queen's rooms. A Marly drawing room scene, where Lauzun teases a marshal about snuff taken with a chairman, shows her eye for rank and ridicule. Readers who like the queen's side of the story will find a loyal and observant witness.
3885-memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoi:
Madame Campan begins her memoirs at fifteen, when she was appointed reader to the king's daughters. She describes a court where Queen Maria Leczinska has just died, the dauphin died three years earlier, the Jesuits are suppressed, and Choiseul rules. Etiquette survives in all its Louis the Fourteenth forms, but dignity alone is wanting, and gaiety has fled to Paris, since the king thinks of nothing but the chase.

A duel pardon shows the young dauphiness at work. A grieving mother supplicates royal children for an hour and wins the culprit's life. A rival lady then sneers that even du Barry was solicited. Campan records the malice without comment. Readers who like Versailles before Marie Antoinette will find a sharp-eyed girl learning the court.
3886-memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoi:
Madame Campan's third volume follows Louis the Sixteenth in his first months, dwelling at La Muette, Marly, and Compiegne before settling at Versailles. The young king examines his grandfather's papers and promises the queen to share anything on the man in the iron mask, whose fame a celebrated writer's pen had fed. After research and talk with Maurepas, he reports no secret paper explains the prisoner, a dangerous intriguer and subject of Mantua, enticed to the frontier and held first at Pignerol.

Court life fills the rest, as young coxcombs imagine the queen notices them from her incognito theatre box, and Lamballe hands ushers the list of persons admitted to the queen's closet. Campan writes with a lady in waiting's precision. Readers who like Versailles before the storm will find a calm and detailed book.
3887-memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoi:
Madame Campan's fourth volume tours the royal visitors who came to Versailles in the last century's close. Northern sovereigns take a fancy for travel. The Grand Duke of Russia, later Paul the First, arrives with his wife as the Comte and Comtesse du Nord, presented on May 20, 1782. The queen receives them with grace, though nervous, and Louis speaks to Paul with more confidence than he showed Joseph the Second.

The comtesse, tall and stiff with German learning, fares less well at first. A lighter passage has the queen charging Campan to warn her when flowers cease to become her, and Campan refusing with a Gil Blas joke about the Archbishop of Granada. A jeweller's gathering diamonds hints at a darker story ahead. Readers who like court visits will find ceremony and wit in equal share.
3888-memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoi:
Madame Campan's fifth volume, the second book of her Revolution narrative, opens with the Tennis Court oath and the royal sitting of June 23. The king declares the orders must vote separately and threatens to act himself for the people's good. The queen counts Necker's absence as treachery, since he had promised to accompany the king and then disavowed the step. Insurrections on July 11, 12, and 14 open the disastrous drama, with the Bastille taken and Flesselles and Launay massacred.

The royal visit to Paris follows. The king speaks with firm grace of his pleasure among his good city's people, and the queen loudly corrects Bailly when he drops the word confidence from the speech. The Tuileries, unready and long given to courtiers, receives the family in haste. Readers who like the Revolution day by day will find Campan at her most urgent.
3889-memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoi:
Madame Campan's sixth volume covers the spring of 1791, when the royal family tries to leave Paris and cannot. The king, tired of the Tuileries, orders dinner at Saint Cloud, but guards mutiny at one o'clock, shut the gates, and refuse passage. Two men near the carriage are ill treated, Campan's father-in-law loses his sword, and the family returns indoors, seeing in the outrage a justification for escape in the people's eyes.

The queen has prepared since March, giving Campan secret orders for linen and gowns that Campan calls useless and dangerous. A tender scene follows, as the king taps at Campan's door to comfort her against injustice and calumny, noting that the royal family suffers the same. Readers who like the flight to Varennes from inside will find a book of plans, fear, and loyalty.
3890-memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoi:
Madame Campan's seventh volume follows the queen from the Tuileries to the Temple and toward the scaffold. Robbed of her purse on the way to the Feuillans, the queen borrows twenty five louis from Campan's sister. That loan later serves as pretense to arrest both women and leads to the sister's death. Campan herself, refused at the Feuillans gates on August 11 and again on the 12th despite tears and a deputy's intercession, cannot join her mistress.

The Temple chapters show drums beating, sections arming, and a rumored rescue by four or five hundred devoted men. Santerre arrives at eight in the morning, the king rises, and Clery carries his last farewell to his wife. Readers who like testimony at its gravest will find a book of loyalty, loss, and the Revolution's final cruelty.
39273-history-of-european-morals-from-au:
William Edward Hartpole Lecky wrote the History of European Morals from Augustus to Charlemagne. Longmans, Green and Company issued the ninth edition in London in 1890, in two volumes. This file holds volume one. Lecky revised the book minutely for the third edition, with help from his German translator. A few lines that had stirred angry argument were cut, and passages added where readers had misunderstood him.

His preface states the questions plainly. A historian of morals studies changes in the moral standard and in the moral type. The standard is how strongly the recognised virtues are enjoined and practised in an age. The type is the weight each age gives to different virtues. Volume one opens with the natural history of morals, then treats the pagan empire and the conversion of Rome. Lecky's book became a standard work of Victorian history, read for its wide learning and calm judgement.
39344-the-diplomatic-correspondence-of-t:
The Diplomatic Correspondence of the American Revolution, volume six, prints the letters of America's envoys abroad. Jared Sparks edited the set. Boston and New York publishers issued this volume in 1830. Congress ordered the publication in 1818. The letters come from the original papers in the State Department.

The title page lists the correspondents in full. Franklin, Deane, and Adams lead the names. Jay, the Lees, Izard, and Dana follow. The French ministers Gerard and Luzerne appear as well. This volume continues John Adams's letters. He writes from Amsterdam in May 1781. His subjects include Dutch defence measures and Prussian trade rules. He urges winning other powers to acknowledge independence before peace talks open.
39521-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Volume thirteen, slice two, of the eleventh Encyclopaedia Britannica runs from Hearing to Helmond. The transcriber's notes head the file, listing corrections made in articles from Heat and the Epistle to the Hebrews to the Hebrides, Hebron, Heine, the heliometer, helium and Hellenism. The slice forms part of the dictionary of arts, sciences, literature and general information, as the title page styles the whole work.

The articles listed for the slice mix the body, the map and biography. Hearing and Heart stand near Hearne and Hearn, that is Lafcadio Hearn, while Heidelberg town, the Heidelberg Catechism and Heidenheim follow. Heat, hearth and heart-burial sit beside the heifer in the usual alphabetical press.
39535-history-of-european-morals-from-au:
History of European Morals from Augustus to Charlemagne, by William Edward Hartpole Lecky, traces how the moral ideas of Europe changed across fifteen centuries. This is the second volume of the ninth edition, published by Longmans, Green, and Company of London in 1890. It holds chapter four, From Constantine to Charlemagne, chapter five, The Position of Women, and the index.

The volume opens by examining the moral ideal the new religion brought into Rome and the methods it used to realize it. Lecky warns against a common error at the outset. Men often set Christian teaching beside Marcus Aurelius or Seneca and call the gap the whole advance, yet pagan ethics belonged to a philosophy and Christian ethics to a religion. The book remains a standard Victorian history of morals.
39570-polly-s-first-year-at-boarding-sch:
Polly's First Year at Boarding School is a girls' school novel by Dorothy Whitehill. Barse issued it in New York in 1916. Charles Wrenn drew the illustrations. The story is set at Seddon Hall on the Hudson. The first chapter opens on the first day of school. Carriages from the train wind up the steep hill. Girls greet each other on the broad piazza. Suitcases and kisses fill the scene.

The contents run through a full school year. A paper chase and a welcome dance come early. Teams are chosen, and a Thanksgiving party follows. Betty's ducking and a cut lecture stir the middle. The indoor meet, field day, and a musical mark the spring. Polly's heroism earns its own chapter. Commencement day closes the year. School series of this kind had a wide girl readership.
39711-constitutional-history-of-england-:
Henry Hallam wrote the Constitutional History of England, from the accession of Henry the Seventh to the death of George the Second. This Everyman's Library volume one carries an introduction by Morgan. Hallam's work, first printed in 1827, was soon turned into German and French, Guizot himself doing the French.

Hallam traces how the English constitution grew: parliaments rising, prerogative checked, liberties won by statute and by struggle. He writes as a calm Whig, praising balance and law over crown and crowd alike. For a century his history was the standard account, read in schools and cited in debate. The Everyman edition put it in cheap cloth for the common reader.
40009-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Volume fourteen, slice five, of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica runs from the article Indole to the article Insanity. It is one bound portion of the dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information. A table lists the slice's articles in two columns, from Indole and Indore through to Inouye and Inquest.

The slice opens with Indole, or benzopyrrol, a substance first prepared synthetically and also got by distilling oxindole with zinc dust or by the reduction of indigo blue. Long articles follow on Induction and the induction coil, Indulgence, the Indus, Industry, Infancy, Infantry, and the Infinitesimal Calculus. Biographies of Ingres, Jean Ingelow, and Robert Green Ingersoll mix among geographical entries for Indre, Innsbruck, and Inowrazlaw. The slice closes with the Inquisition and a medical article on Insanity, whose chronic forms close the volume portion.
40301-sporting-society-or-sporting-chat-: A book of sport talk and sport thoughts forms this volume, of the kind its full head names: Sporting Society. The first pages shown are the lists of a print house of books for men of sport. Those lists name hunts in scarlet and silk, new tales of sport, trips and big game, and a poem of the chase with cuts. The lists show the world of print this book was made for: men who rode, shot, and fished, and who read of it by the fire.
40302-sporting-society-or-sporting-chat-: Sporting Society, or Sporting Chat and Sporting Memories, is a book of sporting pieces whose hosted opening is made up of publisher's lists and a title page. The title page promises stories humorous and curious, plus wrinkles of the field. An illustration called In Full Cry, by Caldecott, ornaments it. The front pages list other sporting books from the same house. On that evidence alone, the volume reads as a collection of field sports talk and memories.
40459-animal-intelligence-the-internatio:
Volume forty four of the International Scientific Series gathers the more important facts of animal intelligence into one resume. A note at the front deals with ants and bees. Sir John Lubbock was to bring out a work on those insects in the same series, the author says, so some ground would be told twice.

Facts will not lose their value from being twice told, the author argues. A complete account in this volume matters more than fresh ground. The series list shows shelf mates by Tyndall, Bagehot, Spencer, and Draper. Chapters sort what beasts, birds, and insects do that looks like thought, memory, and feeling, and weigh how far such acts prove a mind like man's.
40499-abridgment-of-the-debates-of-congr:
Abridgment of the Debates of Congress, volume one, gathers debates from 1789 onward, printed at New York in 1857. Appleton issued it. Its maker was Benton, author of the Thirty Years' View. The sources stand named on the title page: Gales and Seaton's Annals of Congress, their Register of Debates, and the reported debates by Rives.

Benton's preface vouches for those sources. They are authentic and sanctioned by resolves of Congress, he says. The compilers brought education, talent, and over forty years of personal connection with the debates as reporters and publishers. Gales especially reported on extraordinary occasions. The abridgment compresses decades of congressional speech into a run of volumes a reader can actually use.
40851-abridgment-of-the-debates-of-congr:
Abridgment of the Debates of Congress, Volume Two, is a record of the early Congresses by the author of the Thirty Years' View. Appleton of New York printed it in 1861. The work runs from 1789 to 1856. Its sources stand on the title page: Gales and Seaton's Annals of Congress and Register of Debates, and the official reported debates gathered by Rives.

This volume opens with the Fourth Congress, second session, at Philadelphia on December 5, 1796. John Adams, Vice President, presides over the Senate. The roll names the senators state by state: Langdon and Livermore from New Hampshire, Goodhue from Massachusetts, Bradford from Rhode Island, and the rest. Credentials are read, among them Goodhue's appointment in the place of Cabot, resigned. The abridgment condenses the vast debate record into a working history of Congress's first seventy years.
41387-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science for November eighteen seventy-seven is volume twenty, number thirty-three. J B Lippincott and Company entered the issue at Washington in eighteen seventy-seven. Tales, poems, travel, and reviews fill the number.

Lady Blanche Murphy closes a paper on Chester and the Dee. T Adolphus Trollope writes on Baden and Allerheiligen. A Kentucky duel by Will Wallace Harney runs in two parts. H James Junior sketches London at midsummer, and Rebecca Harding Davis serialises A Law Unto Herself. Monthly gossip, music of Russia and Turkey, and reviews follow. Parkman's Count Frontenac heads the book notices. Verse by Oscar Laighton and Epes Sargent adds light.
41640-the-diplomatic-correspondence-of-t:
The Diplomatic Correspondence of the American Revolution, volume 4, was edited by Jared Sparks and published in Boston in 1829. Congress directed the printing in 1818, from the original manuscripts in the Department of State. The set gathers the letters of the American envoys abroad during the whole Revolution, with the replies of Congress and the foreign secretary. The French ministers' letters to Congress appear in full as well.

This volume continues the letters of Benjamin Franklin. It opens in the peace autumn of 1782. The French foreign minister writes from Versailles on trade between France and America. A letter from Whitehall reports the king ready to treat with the commissioners on the footing of full independence. Franklin's own letters to Passy and London carry the talks toward settlement.
41833-the-diplomatic-correspondence-of-t:
The Diplomatic Correspondence of the American Revolution, volume five, gathers the letters of America's envoys abroad. Jared Sparks edited the set, issued at Boston in 1829. The letters are those of Benjamin Franklin, Silas Deane, John Adams, John Jay, and other named men. They concern the foreign relations of the United States through the whole Revolution.

With them stand the letters in reply from the secret committee of Congress and the secretary for foreign affairs. The whole correspondence of two French ministers with Congress is also included. The set was published by direction of the President, from the first manuscripts in the Department of State. A resolution of Congress of March 1818 ordered the work. Volume five carries that great exchange forward in date order.
41944-on-patrol:
Klaxon, the pen name of a naval officer, wrote On Patrol, published at Edinburgh and London in 1919. He had written an earlier book on a warship. Verses at the front speak for the women who watch the ships leave harbor for the greatest game of all, and wonder if they will come back across the greedy sea.

The contents mix short pieces: old women, chin up, sky signs, a battle-prayer, and submarines. Klaxon writes of patrol life in the Great War, the long watches and sudden peril of small ships at sea. His pieces are brief, salty, and tender toward the folk at home. The book is a sailor's keepsake of the war.
42149-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
The Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers print the profession's papers and debates, and this volume opens with paper number 1155. Its subject is the New York tunnel extension of the Pennsylvania Railroad, in particular the North River tunnels. Two members of the society, Hewett and Brown, presented it in June 1910.

Their section of the work ran from Tenth Avenue in New York to the great shaft at Weehawken, under the Hudson River. Shield driving, compressed air, and river silt fill the paper's tables and plates. The tunnels fed Penn Station and changed travel on the whole seaboard. Transactions volumes like this one are the bedrock record of American civil engineering at its boldest age.
42179-constitutional-history-of-england-:
Henry Hallam wrote his Constitutional History of England, running from Henry the Seventh to George the Second. This second volume appears in Everyman's Library, with an opening essay by Professor Morgan.

Chapter eight opens as Charles the First dissolves his third Parliament. Hallam follows the trials of Eliot and others for their conduct in the House. He tracks the king's means of raising money without Parliament. Compositions for knighthood and forced customs duties both appear. The road leads on to the meeting of the Long Parliament. Hallam writes calm, dense history of how crown and Parliament fought over the rules of English rule.
42355-the-diplomatic-correspondence-of-t:
Jared Sparks edited The Diplomatic Correspondence of the American Revolution, and volume three is this book, printed at Boston in 1829. The set was made by order of the President from the true papers in the State Department, under a vote of Congress of March 27, 1818. It holds the letters of the men sent abroad for the young States.

Franklin, Deane, Adams, Jay, and more wrote home on ties with France and other powers. Replies from Congress and the full letters of the French envoys Gerard and Luzerne stand with them. Students of the birth of the United States get the raw words that won friends and funds in war.
42413-the-diplomatic-correspondence-of-t:
Jared Sparks edits the record in The Diplomatic Correspondence of the American Revolution, volume twelve, from Nathan Hale and Gray and Bowen of Boston in 1830. The series prints the letters of Franklin, Deane, Adams, Jay, and the other envoys, with the replies of Congress and the French ministers. It was published from the manuscripts in the Department of State.

This volume continues Robert Morris's correspondence from the Office of Finance in November 1781. Morris pleads with the French minister Luzerne for money, congratulates Rochambeau on Yorktown, and presses the states for supplies. Washington writes him on paying the army's officers.
42553-excursions-and-poems-the-writings-:
Excursions and Poems forms volume five of the writings of Henry David Thoreau. Houghton Mifflin published the set at Boston in 1906. The volume was limited in its manuscript edition. Copyrights reach back to 1865. An introductory note explains the arrangement of the pieces.

The excursions lead the volume. A Yankee in Canada comes first. Essays on the natural history of Massachusetts follow. A Walk to Wachusett and A Winter Walk are included. The famous essay Walking holds a long place. Autumnal Tints and Wild Apples close the prose. Translations from Aeschylus and Pindar come next. Poems then fill the end of the book. A list finds verse scattered through the prose writings.
42961-the-house-with-sixty-closets-a-chr:
The House with Sixty Closets is a Christmas story for young folks and old children by Frank Samuel Child. Lee and Shepard published it in Boston in 1899. J Randolph Brown drew the illustrations. Child had written An Old New England Town and A Colonial Witch. The dedication names seven children, the Little Judge, and their merry friends.

The contents are built like the nursery rhyme of the house that Jack built. First the house, then the people, then the things that happened. The Judge built the house; Mrs Judge planned its sixty closets. In the chapters, portraits walk and talk. Closets talk and walk in their turn. A procession joins goat, dog, cat, bicycles, portraits, and closets. A party gives supper for seventeen, with toasts from a toasting-fork. Stockings are filled with music, rainbows, sense, and sunshine. Happy Day closes the fantasy.
4299-the-whirlpool:
George Gissing opened this novel with Harvey Rolfe dining with care at his London club. Rolfe knows good food without quite mastering it, and he enjoys the comfort his money now buys. He has known poverty, and London landladies' tables, and he values his present ease all the more.

The whirlpool of the title is London society itself, with its money, marriages, and restless talk. Gissing follows Rolfe and his circle through drawing rooms and clubs, tracing how ambition and affection pull people under. It is a large, patient novel of late Victorian London life.
43011-roy-blakeley-s-silver-fox-patrol:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh wrote Roy Blakeley's Silver Fox Patrol, issued at New York in 1920 with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. Howard Hastings drew the pictures. Fitzhugh had built a wide young readership with his Tom Slade books and the first Roy Blakeley tale. Roy tells the story himself, in the loose and funny voice his readers knew, as the Silver Fox Patrol stumbles on a letter and a puzzle.

The chapters move from a den meeting to a trip planned, a car started, and a brush with the law that lands the boys in suspense. A cliff descent in the dark and a grim sight by the way raise the stakes. It is scouting played for laughs and thrills at once.
43055-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
The Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers is a volume of papers from that body. A note at the head sets out the marks of the text. Bold parts are shown with equal signs, and one tied letter pair is rendered in brackets, as in the name of Phoenixville. A table at the front cross-indexes the papers of the society to the Gutenberg files that hold them.

The first rows of the table name the works in view. Paper 1150 is The New York Tunnel Extension of the Pennsylvania Railroad, by Charles W. Raymond. Paper 1151 is The North River Division, by Charles M. Jacobs. The table thus serves as a key to the society's papers in this ebook stock. The volume is a record of great works of American building: tunnels, rails, and the men who planned them.
43138-three-girls-from-school:
Meade wrote a school story, in an edition from Chambers dated 1907, with pictures by Percy Tarrant. Three friends share a low window sill on a July day. Priscilla Weir has dark hair and a grave, firm face. Mabel Lushington is big, laughing, and rich. Annie Brooke is small, golden, and full of questions.

The post has just come in, and two of the girls have letters. Priscilla reads hers, turns pale, and hides it in her pocket. Her uncle Josiah has made up his mind, she tells them. She must leave school and learn farming, dairy work and the running of a farm house. If she fails in six months, he will bind her to a dressmaker. Her friends cry out that she is a lady. The tale follows the three as school life breaks and new paths open.
43147-a-world-of-girls-the-story-of-a-sc:
Meade's A World of Girls, the story of a school, appears here in an edition from the New York Book Company dated 1910. The tale opens in a household in mourning, on the morning a girl of twelve must leave home.

Little Nan escapes her nurse and toddles through the house calling for Hetty, and finds her sister Hester in the small study. Hester, dressed in deep mourning, takes the child on her knee, feeds her biscuits and sugar, and tells her she is going away for months and months. The goodbye sets up the school world of the title, where Hester must make her way alone. Meade wrote many such boarding-school stories, and this one begins, as hers often do, with parting and pluck.
43334-jack-hardy-a-story-of-english-smug:
Herbert Strang wrote this tale of English smugglers in the days of Napoleon, printed by Bobbs-Merrill at Indianapolis with copyrights of 1906 and 1907. Rainey drew the pictures. Young Jack Hardy is bound for a warship, and trouble meets him on the road.

Jack rides the coach toward Wynport to join his frigate. Near the village of Luscombe live smugglers, French agents, and his mother's cousin at Bastable Grange. Chapters promise a market fight, a midnight excursion, signals, and close quarters. Jack is taken prisoner in France and breaks for freedom. A French ship is captured off Luscombe. Strang wrote history-flavored adventure for boys, and this tale mixes coast smuggling with naval war.
44050-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Volume eleven of The Works of John Dryden, now first collected in eighteen volumes, was printed in London for William Miller in eighteen oh eight. James Ballantyne and Company at Edinburgh did the printing. Walter Scott edited the set, with notes historical, critical, and explanatory, and a life of the author. This volume holds epistles, elegies, epitaphs, odes, songs, and lyrical pieces.

Epistles go to John Hoddeson, Sir Robert Howard, Dr Charleton, and the Lady Castlemain, among others. An epistle to Mr Congreve and one to Sir Godfrey Kneller show Dryden range of friends. Elegies mourn Lord Hastings, Mr Oldham, and Mrs Anne Killigrew. Eleonora mourns the Countess of Abingdon at length. An inscription under Milton picture and an epitaph in Westminster Abbey close the run in part. Poetry lovers get Dryden in his formal, public voice.
44106-the-confession-of-a-fool:
The Confession of a Fool is an autobiographical novel by August Strindberg, translated by Ellie Schleussner. Small, Maynard printed it at Boston in 1913. The German version had appeared as early as 1893, but it was mutilated and falsified. The attorney-general, misled by the translator's language, blamed the author and banned the book.

Schering's new translation tries to repair that wrong. Strindberg himself called the book terrible and regretted writing it. He never published it in Swedish, his own language. It gives a relentless account of his first marriage, too personal and too painful to face. He wrote it, the introduction says, before he could face death with composure.
44410-constitutional-history-of-england-:
Constitutional History of England, in its third volume, is the classic work of Henry Hallam. This issue belongs to Everyman's Library, edited by Ernest Rhys. Dent published it in London, and Dutton in New York. Professor Morgan supplied an introduction for the edition.

Hallam's history runs from Henry the Seventh to George the Second. This volume opens with a chapter on the state of the constitution. Its detailed contents range across the press, the courts, and parliament. Restrictions on printing before and after the Restoration are weighed. Licensing acts and political writings checked by judges follow in the analysis. The passing of the Habeas Corpus Act earns close attention in the text. Differences between Lords and Commons thread the whole discussion. Juries, their fines, and their right to a general verdict are treated in turn.
45680-flying-the-coast-skyways-or-jack-r:
Flying the Coast Skyways, or Jack Ralston's swift patrol, is a boys' air adventure by Ambrose Newcomb, copyrighted at Chicago in 1931. Newcomb's other sky tales crowd the title page: wings over the Rockies, sky pilots, sky detectives, and eagles of the sky. The contents open with a flight by air line to Atlanta. A cipher letter and a leech that hangs on follow fast.

Perk, the hero's mate, has an adventure of his own, and the pair escape by the skin of their teeth. Charleston by air, ships passing in the night, and a readiness to strike fill the middle heads. A black water bayou, a lonely camp, and a mother ship raise the stakes late. A motor truck caravan and a ghost boat ride close the list of thrills.
45735-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
Volume seventy of the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers came out in New York in December 1910. The society, founded in 1852, printed papers read by its members, with the talk that followed each one. The views are the authors' own, not the society's, as a note makes clear.

Papers here deal with how pipes swell with heat, tests of timber soaked in creosote, and hard points in the design of steel-set concrete. One long paper covers the water supply of a rail line in New Mexico. A further paper reports on federal work on mine blasts, building stuff, and fuels. Each paper is paired with remarks from other engineers who read it.
46047-tales-and-legends-of-the-tyrol:
Tales and Legends of the Tyrol is a folklore volume collected by the Countess von Günther. Chapman and Hall published it in London in 1874. The dedication honours those who dare the unfrequented mountain paths. Her preface calls Tyrol the wonder garden of the world. It is often visited but little known, she writes. Many dangers and weary walks went into gathering the tales.

No railroads run in those mountains, and cart tracks are few. The hidden beauty must be earned on foot, she insists. The strange dialect of the inhabitants bars most foreigners from their stories. Thousands of sightseers pass yearly, at a loss to satisfy their curiosity. The countess crossed that barrier to collect the legends. Grand, gorgeous, shocking, and terrible things meet at every step, she promises.
46212-the-covenant-of-salt-as-based-on-t:
Clay Trumbull, who had already written on the blood covenant and the threshold covenant, turns here to salt. The book came out in New York in eighteen ninety-nine. Its full title promises to ground the covenant of salt in the meaning and symbolism of salt in primitive thought.

Trumbull first fixes what a covenant is, then gathers the Bible passages that name a covenant of salt. Bread and salt shared at a table stand for a bond of life itself. Salt, he argues, could stand for blood, and salt and sun join as signs of life and light. Later chapters treat salt in sacrifice, in driving out evil, and in telling fortunes. To break faith with salt was a deep shame. A supplement reads the Ten Commandments as a covenant of love.
46404-mimi-at-sheridan-school:
Anne Pence Davis wrote Mimi at Sheridan School, held in 1935 at Chicago by the Goldsmith Publishing Company. Davis gives the book to Kay and Diane, who still have all the fun of school ahead. Twenty five chapters carry the school tale. Home leads the plot and Miss Jane's Wedding follows.

Sheridan My Sheridan, Follow the Leader, and Tumble Inn build the early fun. Green Cap Week, an accident, and a bid for Mimi come next. Clorissa's secret and Betsy's surprise fill the middle. A Thanksgiving game, a lake that freezes, and a horse show press the pace. Tennis, a roof garden party, and death bells mark the late turns. Chapter One shows Mimi rude for once on a train home from camp. She shoves and crowds in her haste to be home.
46491-journal-of-the-proceedings-of-the-:
The fourth zoology volume of the Journal of the Proceedings of the Linnean Society was printed in London in eighteen sixty by Taylor and Francis. Its list of papers shows Victorian natural history at work in a learned society. Huxley leads with a study of the skin armour of the jacare and caiman, with notes on the crocodile family, a paper that grew from his inquiry into a strange extinct reptile.

Other papers cover the moulting of the common lobster and shore crab, and the habits of the aye-aye of Madagascar. Garner writes on shell-bearing molluscs, and Hanley on a Linnean manuscript. Walker catalogues the two-winged flies that Wallace collected at Makessar in Celebes. Wallace himself closes the volume with the zoological geography of the Malay Archipelago.
46944-the-golden-maiden-and-other-folk-t:
Folk tales and fairy tales told in Armenia fill these pages, set in English dress in 1898. A. G. Seklemian told the tales, and Alice Stone Blackwell had a hand in the book. The first pages state why the field is new. A famed English student of folk lore is quoted: Armenia gives a rich field, as yet near untouched, to the man of lore. The script of the land has kept its tales shut from the men of Europe.

One set of tales of the land, made by a bishop, could be read in the West through a rare and poor German dress alone. A second man of the land had begun a set for an American friend of the work, but his death cut the work short.
47197-sevastopol:
Count Leo Tolstoy wrote these sketches of the siege of Sevastopol, and Isabel Hapgood turned them into English. The authorized edition came out in New York, with copyright in 1888. Tolstoy had served as a young artillery officer in the Crimea, and he wrote from inside the besieged city.

Three pieces mark the siege: Sevastopol in December 1854, in May 1855, and in August 1855. Tolstoy walks the reader through the bastions, talks with the soldiers, and shows wounds, boredom, and bravery without flinching. The sketches made his name in Russia while the war still raged. Readers get war writing of unmatched honesty, from a man who saw glory and filth in one view.
47289-abridgment-of-the-debates-of-congr:
Abridgment of the Debates of Congress, from 1789 to 1856, volume four, was compiled by the author of the Thirty Years' View, Thomas Hart Benton. Appleton published it in New York in 1860. Its sources are the Annals of Congress, the Register of Debates, and Rives's reported debates, as the title page states.

This volume opens with the second session of the Tenth Congress. The Senate met at Washington on November 7, 1808, with Vice President George Clinton in the chair. Senators from New Hampshire and Massachusetts head the roll. Readers get early Congress in its own words: speeches and votes that shaped the young republic, shortened for use.
47383-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
The Works of John Dryden, Volume Thirteen, belongs to the first collected edition of Dryden in eighteen volumes. William Miller of London published the set in 1808. Walter Scott edited it, with notes historical, critical, and explanatory, and a life of the author. James Ballantyne of Edinburgh printed the volumes.

This volume holds Dryden's verse translations. An essay on satire, addressed to the Earl of Dorset, opens the set. The first, third, sixth, tenth, and sixteenth satires of Juvenal follow. All six satires of Persius come next, each with its notes, the fifth inscribed to Doctor Busby. The works of Virgil, translated into English verse, close the volume, with the names of the subscribers to its cuts. Dryden's Juvenal and Persius were the standard English satires of their kind for a century. Scott's edition is the monument that kept them standing.
47430-fanny-campbell-the-female-pirate-c:
Maturin Murray Ballou wrote a tale of the Revolution dated 1844, about a woman pirate captain. His preface argues that all books should have a preface, as a private word between author and reader. He places great weight on first impressions. The tale, he says, is romantic but no more so than real incidents of the Revolution.

Ballou claims some expense in ferreting out the events. Chapter one is set at Lynn, Massachusetts, about ten miles from Boston. Lynn's Pirate's Cave, Lover's Leap, and Robber's Dungeon stand near each other there. William Lovell, Fanny Campbell, and Captain Ralph Burnet of the Royal Navy are introduced. A lover's jealousy is promised in the chapter heads.
47498-birds-and-all-nature-vol-4-no-1-ju:
Birds and All Nature, volume four, is a monthly serial from the Nature Study Publishing Company of Chicago, copyrighted in 1898 and illustrated by colour photography. The introduction promises each number at least two birds, three or four animals, and plates of insects, flowers, and other natural subjects.

The contents open with a poem, Squirrel Town, about the squirrels in the oaks. They go on to Wilson's snipe, the black wolf, an armadillo kept as a pet, and the red squirrel. Shorter pieces treat African folk lore, the prairie hen, the butterfly trade, the passenger pigeon in Wisconsin and Nebraska, the American rabbit, and the ocelot. The publishers boast that the parent magazine was read by over one hundred thousand persons. The number mixes verse, animal lives, and camera studies for home readers.
47533-the-forest-farm-tales-of-the-austr:
Peter Rosegger grew up on a forest farm in the Austrian Tyrol, and his tales draw on that hard mountain life. The stories here include My Father and I and Christmas Eve, pieces rooted in the work, faith, and seasons of a peasant household. Rosegger writes about his father's labor, the family's poverty, and the woods that shaped his childhood, in prose that made him one of the best-loved Austrian writers of his day.
