The 1912 Vineyard Press edition opens with an appreciation by Maude Egerton King and a short account of the author's life by Julius Petersen. Together they frame the tales for English readers meeting Rosegger for the first time. The stories that follow stay close to the farm and the village, finding large feeling in small events.
47567-birds-and-nature-vol-11-no-1-janua:
Birds and Nature, volume 11, number 1, is the January 1902 issue of a monthly nature magazine edited by William Kerr Higley and published in Chicago by A W Mumford. Each issue offered forty illustrations by color photography and served as a guide in the study of nature for general readers.

Contents mix verse and short studies: the golden-crowned kinglet, the king rail, the brown-headed nuthatch, and the sharp-shinned hawk. Other pieces take up quartz, berries of the woods, Irish moss, the cardinal flower, and the Greenland whale. A new year poem opens the number. The magazine belonged to a period when color plates first let city readers study birds closely without leaving home, and schools used such issues as teaching aids.
47597-deering-of-deal-or-the-spirit-of-t:
Latta Griswold wrote Deering of Deal, or The Spirit of the School, first published in nineteen twelve. Deal is a boys' boarding school, and Deering is its central figure. Griswold gave the book to six school friends, in memory of happy days at school.

Chapters move through a school year of games, scrapes, and tests of honour. A hazing bee, a midnight lark, and the night of the bonfire bring trouble and fun. The Boxford game and a gating stir strong feeling. Later chapters turn on the head prefectship, a protest, and self-sacrifice. The last term closes the story in the chapel.
47614-when-sarah-went-to-school:
Elsie Singmaster wrote When Sarah Went to School, printed in Boston in 1910. The book is dedicated to the memory of her grandmother, Sarah Mattern Singmaster, whose girlhood it recalls. Drawings by Wilson Dexter show Sarah sure it is not right for her to go, and standing on thresholds of new rooms.

The dress parade opens the tale, and the normal school, where teachers are trained, is Sarah's goal. She loses her temper, explains herself, and saves the day once more, as an earlier book had her do. Professor Minturn runs an experiment whose result fills a later chapter, and a Christmas carol is staged. In the end the state board hears the case, and the chairman makes a speech. It is a warm tale of a country girl and a new kind of schooling.
47641-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Walter Scott edited the works of John Dryden, first collected in eighteen volumes with notes and a life of the author, printed at London in 1808. This fifteenth volume holds the end of Dryden's Aeneid in his celebrated translation: books eight through twelve, each with notes, and a postscript to the reader.

Poems ascribed to Dryden follow: an essay upon satire, the art of poetry, and pieces on the young statesmen. Then come Dryden's original prose works, led by the Essay of Dramatic Poesy, his great dialogue on the drama. Scott's edition was the first serious monument to Dryden, the Restoration's master poet and critic, and his life of the author set the pattern for literary biography.
47679-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Volume eight of the works of John Dryden holds four plays and some added prose. Walter Scott put the full set of eighteen volumes in order and wrote a life of Dryden for it. The set came out in London in 1808. Scott added notes on the past, on the text, and on hard points for the reader.

The plays are Amphitryon, King Arthur, Cleomenes, and Love Triumphant. Each play comes with the note Dryden sent to a lord when he gave him the work. Cleomenes also has a life of its hero drawn from Plutarch in Thomas Creech's English. A short masque and songs for The Pilgrim close the volume.
48030-birds-and-all-nature-vol-6-no-1-ju:
Birds and All Nature, volume six, number one, is the June 1899 issue of a monthly serial in natural colours. Marble edited it at Chicago, where Mumford published it. Forty pictures by colour photography fill each volume, and the set ran two volumes a year. The June contents open with My Neighbor in the Apple Tree.

A Day in June, the western yellow throat, and Charley and the angleworm follow. The myrtle warbler, Taffy and Tricksey, and a suggestion to egg collectors fill the middle pages. There are pieces on a fly catching plant, bats in Burmese caves, and a metal bird's nest. Pet animals as causes of disease and curious trees widen the net. Such magazines taught nature study to families and schools at the turn of the century. Their colour plates of warblers were wonders of the printing of the day.
48141-birds-and-all-nature-vol-6-no-4-no:
Birds and All Nature, volume six, number four, dated November 1899, is an issue of an American nature magazine illustrated by colour photography. The contents page runs to some thirty short pieces, mixing bird and plant studies with stories and verses for younger readers. Titles include a rare humming bird, the towhee, the canary and the Carolina paroquet.

The issue opens with an account of taming a humming bird in California. The writer tells how he crept closer day by day, whistling softly, until the bird let him take it in his open hand. The piece notes that humming birds are found only in the Americas and shine like living gems in field and grove. The magazine's mix of observation, natural history and poems shows popular nature study for family readers.
48377-bill-bruce-on-forest-patrol:
Bill Bruce on Forest Patrol is a boys' aviation novel by Henry Arnold of the Air Corps. Burt of New York published it in 1928, in the Aviator Series, adventures of a pilot for boys of twelve to sixteen.

This book opens on vacation, fishing the McKenzie River in the Oregon woods. A fish takes Bill's line while he lazes on the bank. Chapters move through wood lore and the forestry service to a forest fire. Bill is drafted to fight the fire, then returns to duties with the artillery. The aerial fire patrol follows, with narrow escapes and a mountain lookout. A firebug hunt and the end of the fire season close the book.
48540-birds-and-nature-vol-08-no-3-octob:
Birds and Nature, a magazine illustrated by color photography, issued this number in October 1900. It is the third number of the eighth volume. A poem on October's bright blue weather opens the issue, with sonnets on October and autumn beside it.

Contents mix birds, flowers, and fish in the magazine's friendly way. The ruffed grouse, the bob white, and the American redstart stand among the birds. Blue gentians, columbine, and sunflowers carry the plant side, while baby lions and the rainbow trout widen the net. A piece on the geological succession of fishes adds deep time. Readers get a charming period nature magazine at its autumn best.
48951-dotty-dimple-at-school:
Dotty Dimple at School is the fifth of the Dotty Dimple Stories by Sophie May, printed at Boston by Lee and Shepard in 1869. May also wrote the Little Prudy Stories, where Dotty first appeared. The set was to be completed in six volumes at seventy-five cents each. This volume is illustrated, and dedicated to Attie Starbird and Katie Wheeler.

Twelve chapters follow Dotty to school. Her sister Prudy owns the accident gently, and Dotty's storm passes. Dotty and Tate, Doing a Lie and Dotty and Her Mother work the small moral cases of childhood. The Screw-Up Pencil, Dotty and Lina and Blowing Away follow. Is Your Name Solomon, A Long Night and Safe at Home lead to Bosom Friends and The Dear Little School.
49221-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Walter Scott edited the works of John Dryden in eighteen volumes, with a life of the author. Volume nine appeared in London in 1808, printed by Ballantyne at Edinburgh. Historical, critical and explanatory notes by Scott run through the poems in this collected edition.

Poems historical and political fill this volume, the contents announce at the start. Heroic stanzas to the memory of Oliver Cromwell open the book, with long notes by Scott. 'Astrea Redux,' a panegyric on the coronation and a New Year poem to Lord Chancellor Hyde follow, before the great 'Annus Mirabilis' and 'Absalom and Achitophel' later on.
49290-the-year-nine-a-tale-of-the-tyrol:
Year Nine is a tale of the Tyrol by the author of Mary Powell. Arthur Hall, Virtue, and Company printed it in London in 1858. A Latin motto vows that the vanquished fell for liberty itself. Chapter heads trace a rising: storm, inn kitchen, shooting match, and first success. Innsbruck and the Berg Isel fights mark the heart of the tale.

Later chapters turn to guerilla war, courtship, and winter on the mountains. Reverses and danger crowd the close of the long chapter list. The year in the title points to the Tyrolese stand of 1809. Readers follow small folk caught in a war for their home valleys. Home, feast, and fray mix in the chapter by chapter march.
4940-grace-harlowe-s-senior-year-at-high:
Grace Harlowe's senior year at high school begins on a sunny October afternoon at Oakdale station, where Grace and her chums Anne, Nora, and Jessica say goodbye to Hippy, Reddy, and David. The boys leave for a four-year course at an eastern college, and the girls face a school year without them.

The novel follows Grace through her final year: friendships, school rivalries, and the small puzzles of growing up, including a puzzling resemblance that opens the story. The catalog record leaves the author unnamed. Readers get a warm school story from the series tradition, centered on loyalty among friends rather than on a single crisis.
50152-liverpool:
Liverpool, issued by Adam and Charles Black in 1907, pairs paintings with prose. Hamilton Hay painted the city. Dixon Scott described it. The book holds twenty-five full-page illustrations in colour. Scott warns readers what his book is not. It is neither guide-book nor history nor trade survey.

He offers instead the instant effect of the place on one observer. Writer and painter report what their own senses found. The town hall fronts the volume. The series put such colour books on Devon, Paris, and Jamaica too. A portrait of the great port at its Edwardian height.
50600-how-to-make-and-set-traps-includin:
Keene wrote a handbook of traps for Frank Tousey of New York, entered in 1902. The title promises hints on trapping moles, weasels, otter, rats, squirrels, and birds, and on curing skins. Chapter one is the mole. Dirt, Keene begins, is matter in the wrong place, and so with most creatures called vermin.

The little gentleman in black velvet is a fine coated fellow, he says, with courage, industry, and love of his young. Once in a garden, though, he turns into one of the most troublesome of pests and must be killed without mercy. Rats get the same mixed verdict: lithe, fond parents, yet without excuse when they sit in the wrong place. The book then gives its makes and settings in plain, pictured steps.
50637-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Volume eighteen of the Works of John Dryden closed an eighteen volume set printed in London in 1808. Walter Scott edited the set and wrote a life of the author. Notes here are marked as historical, critical, and explanatory. This last volume holds short prose pieces and letters. Contents list a preface to a dialogue concerning women first.

Other items treat St Evremont, Polybius, and Lucian. Dryden's letters fill a long stretch, from page 83 to the appendix. An index ends the set. Scott's preface praises Walsh, author of the dialogue, as a friend to Dryden in age and trouble. He also notes that Walsh backed the young Pope. The volume suits readers tracing Dryden's prose and circle.
50960-dave-dawson-on-convoy-patrol:
Dave Dawson on Convoy Patrol is a boys' war novel by Bowen. Saalfield of Akron issued it, with copyright in 1941. Seventeen chapters carry Dave through the Atlantic war. Secret orders open the tale. London is under the bombs in chapter one. Wave after wave of German raiders cross the city. Searchlights and guns answer from below. Spitfires and Hurricanes hunt the raiders down.

Many bombers fall in flames over the streets. Wardens and fire fighters hold their posts below. The contents promise Satan's agent and mystery wings. The dead don't fly, one dark chapter says. A midnight phantom and sky doom follow. Wings of victory close the list. Bowen's Dave Dawson books ran through the war years. They gave boys a hero of the sky war.
51154-fairlop-and-its-founder-or-facts-a:
Fairlop and Its Founder tells the history of Fairlop Fair in Hainault Forest. An unnamed famed first Friday fairgoer wrote the pamphlet. Charles Clark printed a small number at his private press at Totham in 1847. Memoirs, anecdotes, poems, and songs fill the little book.

The fair's founder was Daniel Day, born in 1683 in a brewer's family. Day made engines, pumps, and ships' blocks at Wapping for many years. He gave the great bell to his parish church at its founding in 1760. His yearly feast under the Fairlop Oak drew hundreds in his life. Thousands still gathered there after his death, the writer says. Day's curious will is printed here for the first time. The pamphlet keeps the memory of a tradesman's kindness.
5141-what-katy-did-at-school:
Susan Coolidge's school story sends Katy Carr away to boarding school after the events of the earlier book. It follows her first year among new friends, teachers, and rules. Chapters take Katy from a country excursion called Conic Section through the autumn term, a secret society for the suppression of unladylike conduct, and the long wait for spring.

Coolidge writes warmly about friendship, mischief, unfair blame, and growing up, with letters and Christmas boxes marking the school year. The book remains a favourite of classic girls' fiction, and it offers a gentle, detailed picture of nineteenth-century school life as Katy learns to balance spirit with self-control.
51453-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science for November 1880 was entered at Washington by the Philadelphia publishers that year. It opens with The Ruins of the Colorado Valley, a survey of the inscribed crag in New Mexico where Spanish names begun before Jamestown crowd a ruined fortress of a forgotten people.

The contents mix travel, fiction, and science. They include The Arts of India, chapters thirty-three to thirty-five of a serial novel called Adam and Eve, The Mistakes of Two People, Limoges and its porcelain, and Three Roses, a poem. A practical history of a play and a narrative of how she kept her vow follow. Heinrich Heine gets a critical essay, and an article on automatism in medicine closes the longer pieces. Departments of monthly gossip, a dialogue on people's houses, Literature of the Day, and Books Received round out the number.
51615-a-matter-of-protocol:
A Matter of Protocol, a story by Jack Sharkey, ran in Galaxy Magazine in August 1962. Schelling drew the pictures for the tale. First contact was always dangerous, the blurb says, but usually only to the man involved. The planet of the tale is called Viridian in the text.

From space, Viridian resembled a great green moss covered tennis ball. The spaceship arrowed closer to the lush jungle of its surface. No break showed in the green cloak of the world below. Ships were poorly built for long flight within an atmosphere, the tale notes. Sharkey turns diplomacy itself into the danger of the piece. A rule of protocol, missed or kept, decides who lives.
51652-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Walter Scott edited the works of John Dryden in eighteen volumes, with historical and critical notes and a life of the author. Volume ten appeared in London in 1808. It opens with Religio Laici, a layman's faith, with its preface. An argument from Dryden's own marginal notes sums up the poem's course.

Threnodia Augustalis, a funeral poem for King Charles the Second, follows. The Hind and the Panther, in three parts, takes the largest place. Britannia Rediviva marks the birth of a prince. Prologues and epilogues fill many pages. Mack Flecknoe, a satire against Thomas Shadwell, closes the volume with Scott's notes.
52033-william-mackay-on-t-w-robertson-s-:
Letters to the Times in January 1869 over Robertson's new comedy School are gathered with William Mackay's account of them. Mackay, then studying for the law, wrote his first published piece out of the row, and it led to his career in newspapers. A letter signed Veritas opens the file on January 20. The comedy School at the Prince of Wales's Theatre, Veritas charges, was played with great success at the principal theatres in Germany last year.

Robertson, he says, has only the merit of translation, and he himself has seen it acted in Hamburg and Cologne. Why does not Veritas give the name of the German play, the Times asks the next day. Veritas answers that he had forgotten to name it. If the charge is true, the morality of those concerned is hard to understand, the paper muses. Mackay's own piece follows the letters.
52165-transylvanian-superstitions-from-t:
Transylvania might well be termed the land of superstition, the writer of this survey says. Nowhere else does the curious plant of delusion flourish so persistently or in such bewildering variety. It seems as if the whole species of demons, pixies, witches, and hobgoblins, driven from the rest of Europe by the wand of science, had taken refuge within this mountain wall.

The survey sorts the beliefs by their three sources: the native superstition of the land, whose scenery fits it for monsters, and the traditions of the peoples who share the mountains. Vampires and werewolves live here in earnest, not in jest. The writer was Emily Gerard, whose work fed the Dracula legend. The piece is a cool, amused inventory of fear.
52566-the-diplomatic-correspondence-of-t:
Jared Sparks edited The Diplomatic Correspondence of the American Revolution, here in its second volume. Nathan Hale and Gray and Bowen published it at Boston in 1829. Congress had resolved on March 27, 1818, that the letters be printed from the original manuscripts in the Department of State. The President directed the publication. The letters are those of Franklin, Deane, Adams, Jay, and others who served the United States abroad during the whole Revolution.

The replies of the Secret Committee of Congress and the Secretary of Foreign Affairs stand with them. The correspondence of the French ministers Gerard and Luzerne with Congress is given entire. The second volume opens with Arthur Lee's correspondence. A committee letter to Lee of December 12, 1775, heads the run. It stresses the need to know foreign powers' dispositions, and the necessity of secrecy.
53774-the-mercer-boys-in-the-ghost-patro:
Capwell Wyckoff wrote The Mercer Boys in the Ghost Patrol, a boys adventure book from 1951 in the Mercer Boys series. The tale turns on the summer camp of Woodcrest Military Institute, a yearly event the Mercer boys and their friend Terry Mackson looked forward to with real excitement. Camp life gives the cadets drills, hikes, and plenty of time in the woods.

The title promises a ghost patrol, a mystery thread woven through the camp routine. Wyckoff wrote many books in this series, each built on school and camp life, friendship, and a puzzle to solve. Young readers get brisk action, clean humor, and a test of nerve for the cadet troop.
54129-sixteen-years-in-siberia-some-expe:
Leo Deutsch wrote his memoir of exile as a Russian revolutionary, and Helen Chisholm turned it into English. The third impression came out in New York in 1904, a year after the first edition. Deutsch spent sixteen years in Siberia, and his calm tone makes the hard facts stand out more.

The translator's preface places the tale beside George Kennan's work on the exile system. It points to the grim events in the state prisons at Kara after Kennan had left Russia. Readers get a first-hand account of arrest, travel, prison life, and the fate of friends, told with little show or heat.
54190-the-spirit-of-the-school:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote this school story, published by Appleton in New York in 1907. A list of Barbour's books fills the front page, priced in the publisher's catalogue as printed there. His school tales include 'The Half-Back,' 'Weatherby's Inning' and 'On Your Mark' among the titles named.

A front plate shows a youth described as a more harmless boy than one could easily find. School spirit, the pride boys take in their school and its teams, stands at the center of Barbour's world. Games, loyalty and rivalry give the tale its shape for young readers of his day.
54286-the-life-and-times-of-george-villi:
The Life and Times of George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham, volume one of three, was written by Mrs. Thomson from original and first-hand sources. It was published at London by Hurst and Blackett in 1860. The frontispiece is an engraved portrait of Buckingham, the favorite of James I and Charles I.

In the preface Thomson notes that no complete life of Buckingham had appeared before, save Sir Henry Wotton's sketch. That account, from a man who owed Buckingham much, reads more as praise than as a memoir. Thomson drew instead on letters in the State Paper Office, newly opened and arranged for writers, to build a fuller and more even record.
54287-the-life-and-times-of-george-villi:
Mrs Thomson wrote The Life and Times of George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham, Volume Two, issued at London in 1860 by Hurst and Blackett. Thomson had writ Memoirs of the Court of Henry the Eighth and a Life of Sir Walter Ralegh. The work runs to three volumes from original and authentic sources. Translation rights were reserved.

Chapter One treats anxiety in England over the Spanish Treaty. Charles the First was the first male heir for whom a marriage treaty had been set on foot since Henry the Eighth, the heads note. The Infanta is called the Rare Infanta for her qualities. Charles's personal excellence and elegance get praise. The alliance drew interest for its link to the Palatinate. Bars of the dispensation, fleet costs, and James's fears fill the chapter heads.
54288-the-life-and-times-of-george-villi:
Mrs Thomson wrote this life of George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham, from original and authentic sources, printed by Hurst and Blackett of London in 1860. Thomson had written memoirs of the court of Henry the Eighth, a life of Sir Walter Ralegh, and memoirs of Sarah, Duchess of Marlborough. The part held here is volume three of three.

Its contents run from the death of the Earl of Suffolk through vehement debates and the sending of Sir Dudley Digges and Elliot to prison. Buckingham's motives for war with France, his fear of losing influence, and the arrival of Soubise and Rohan fill the chapters. Letters from the Duchess and from his mother mark his road to Dover, Portsmouth, and the sailing for Rochelle in 1626 and 1627.
54345-abridgment-of-the-debates-of-congr:
Thomas Hart Benton, the great senator from Missouri, abridged the debates of Congress from 1789 to 1856 in this series. Benton hides behind his earlier title, the author of the Thirty Years' View. The third volume came out in New York in 1861.

The debates are drawn from the Annals of Congress, the Register of Debates, and the reported debates of a later age. This volume opens with the Eighth Congress, meeting at Washington in October 1803, with Jefferson as president. Benton cut and shaped the vast record so one reader could grasp the Republic's first arguments. Readers get the raw speech of the early Senate and House.
54361-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Volume twelve of Dryden's works, in the eighteen-volume set edited with notes and a life by Walter Scott, gathers his verse translations. William Miller published the set in London in 1808, printed at Edinburgh by Ballantyne and Company.

An appendix first gives Chaucer's own tales that Dryden had modernized, from The Knightes Tale to The Wif of Bathes Tale. Then come renderings from Ovid's Epistles and Metamorphoses, among them Canace to Macareus, Dido to Æneas, Baucis and Philemon, and Pygmalion. Selections from Theocritus, Lucretius, and Horace follow. The volume ends with Homer: the first book of the Iliad and the last parting of Hector and Andromache.
54498-the-wise-and-ingenious-companion-f:
The Wise and Ingenious Companion, French and English, was printed in London in 1700 in both tongues on facing terms. Boyer, author of the Royal Dictionary, gathered the wit of illustrious persons, ancient and modern: wise sayings, noble sentiments, sharp replies, jests, and pleasant stories. A Horace motto praises the writer who mixes use with delight.

An opening essay argues that sentences, replies, and jests have been prized by all civilized nations. Greeks and Romans collected and quoted them, Julius Caesar kept a book of his peers' jests, and Plutarch set down the wit of the men whose lives he wrote. The companion serves English readers and foreigners alike, teaching French through sparkle rather than drill.
55213-the-girl-scouts-at-miss-allen-s-sc:
The Girl Scouts at Miss Allen's School is a girls' series book by Edith Lavell. The Burt Company of New York published it in 1922. Companion volumes take the same scouts to camp and on a canoe trip. The story follows Marjorie through a school year of work and mischief.

Off for boarding school opens the contents, and a room-mate follows. The sophomore reception, a stolen meeting, and a sorority party come early. Pledge-day and outsiders divide the school into camps for the heroine. A hockey match, a house-party, and a dance fill the social middle. The Girl Scout troop itself forms in the eleventh chapter. A winter hike and a second-class test take the girls outdoors in earnest. A basket-ball game and a ghost at a cabin crowd the later chapters.
56018-business-administration-theory-pra:
Business Administration: Theory, Practice, and Application is a correspondence school textbook set of 1910, issued by a Chicago school of business in many volumes. The catalog dates the work 1910. The text books listed in front run from business economics and business organization onward through the whole course.

Such sets taught the new science of management by mail to clerks and foremen across America. Accounting, sales, advertising, and office system each got a volume. The transcriber notes chemical formulas in a later volume, where business meets manufacturing. The work catches the moment when business became a teachable profession rather than a knack. Its pages are earnest, practical, and full of the period's faith in system. The La Salle style home study movement sold ambition by the volume.
5602-the-boy-scouts-patrol:
Ralph Victor wrote The Boy Scouts Patrol, illustrated by Rudolf Mencl, as a boys' adventure about a patrol finding its feet. Chapters run from A Monkey Trick and Finding Money through Up the River, The Enemy Makes a Raid, and The Colonel, to Forming the Patrol, Organized, A Challenge, and A Defiance. Pepper takes a message, Pepper goes missing, and the message itself becomes a quest.

The story follows lads of about sixteen through river trips, raids, pursuits, and a judge's office, ending in a race and a conclusion. Victor writes outdoor adventure with teamwork at its center. Young readers get a lively early scouting tale, full of pranks, pursuit, and patrol spirit.
56097-the-ranch-girls-at-boarding-school:
Margaret Vandercook wrote The Ranch Girls at Boarding School in 1913. Bodine illustrated the tale for Winston at Philadelphia. Still as the Night opens the contents. In Disgrace and Getting into Harness follow. News and a discovery, and her temptation, come in the middle heads.

Primrose Hall stands not far from the region of Sleepy Hollow. A clock there struck three, then four, then five solemn strokes. A girl in a big bare room lay awake through them. No glimmer of light announced the coming of morning to her. Frieda's mistake and the house of memory follow. The appeal to Olive and the true history of Olive follow. Jean and Frieda return to Primrose Hall near the end of it. Election day and New Year's Eve crowd the year. Vandercook gives ranch girls a school of polish and secrets.
56594-head-of-the-lower-school:
Head of the Lower School, a school story by Dorothea Moore, was issued at New York and London by Putnam in 1920. A front plate shows a girl named Joey at a chink, listening. School tales of this kind follow one term of tears and triumphs. The head of the lower school holds a small throne among small girls.

Moore wrote many stories for girls in school and camp settings. Her heroines learn loyalty, pluck, and fair play under mild perils. A lower school head must rule her form and win its trust. Friendships, feuds, and games fill the term in such tales. The book is a clean sample of the girls’ school story between the wars. It prizes pluck over prizes, and kindness over rank.
56695-the-radio-boys-with-the-border-pat:
Gerald Breckenridge wrote this volume of the Radio Boys series for Burt, with copyright in 1924. Jack Hampton's father keeps a radio shack on a Southwestern ranch, and the book opens with a landing. Captain Cornell, an army flyer of the Laredo flight of the Border Patrol, comes down on the Hamptons' terrace. Radio brings word that Jack will arrive in ten minutes. Father and captain walk out to the field together.

The contents promise border trouble. Don Ferdinand disappears, word comes from him, and the boys go off to Laredo. A bull fight, a house of mystery, and a novel call for help follow. The villain is named in a chapter title: that devil Ramirez. There is a tunnel, a trap, and a rescue at the end. The series mixed the wireless craze with the older Western, and boys read both hungers in one book.
57393-journal-01-1837-1846-the-writings-:
Henry David Thoreau kept a daily journal for most of his grown life. Bradford Torrey put this first journal book in shape for print. It came out in Boston in 1906 as part of a twenty-book set. The set was a small run for buyers who paid in advance. This book holds the years from 1837 to 1846.

Inside are notes on walks, books, work, and the life of the mind. Thoreau used these notes later in his more shaped works. Short bits first came out in books on spring, summer, winter, and fall. Here readers can read the notes in date order, whole.
5760-two-trips-to-gorilla-land-and-the-c:
Richard Burton recounts his first volume of travels in Gorilla Land, published in London in 1876. Chapters land at the Rio Gaboon, depart through a tornado, survey the geography of the Gaboon, and meet minor tribes and the Mpongwe people. Later chapters visit Sanga-Tanga, village life in Pongo land, the river journey upward, a specimen day with the Fan people, and Mr, Mrs, and Master Gorilla.

Burton writes as an explorer and observer, mixing geography, language notes, and firsthand encounters with humor and bluntness. Modern readers should note that his language about African peoples reflects Victorian attitudes and needs critical reading. As a travel record, the volume preserves a vivid, detailed picture of the Gaboon region before later colonial change.
5761-two-trips-to-gorilla-land-and-the-c:
Richard Burton's second volume of Two Trips turns from the Gaboon to the Congo, published in London in 1876. Chapters sail from Fernando Po to Loango Bay. They visit Sao Paulo de Loanda and celebrate a festival with a trip to Calumbo. Cruising along shore, they enter the Congo River and pass factories and a slave depot. Boma outfits the party for the interior, and the march leads through Banza Nokki toward the Yellala cataracts.

Burton records river navigation, trade posts, and peoples met along the way with an explorer's detail and a Victorian traveler's bluntness. Modern readers should read his descriptions of African peoples critically, as products of their era. As a record of the Congo before later upheaval, the volume offers geography, incident, and a hard-won route toward the cataracts.
58338-the-life-and-correspondence-of-sir:
Louis Fagan wrote The Life and Correspondence of Sir Anthony Panizzi, and volume one of the American edition came out in Boston in 1881. Fagan worked in the British Museum, where Panizzi had been principal librarian. Panizzi was also a senator of Italy, his native land, from which he had fled as a young man.

Letters and life together tell how an exile rose to run the great library in London. Henry Stevens adds a third volume of his own memories of Panizzi and the Museum from 1845 to 1865. Reform Club men and Museum staff fill the pages with talk of books, prints, and politics. The set is a record of a famed keeper of books.
59089-the-powers-of-europe-and-fall-of-s:
A popular history of the Crimean War by a British officer. Higgins and Bradley published it at Boston in 1856. A panoramic map of the seat of war fronts the volume. The author admits the work is partly a compilation. He also acted in many scenes himself. Authentic sources supplied the rest, sometimes condensed.

His aim is a readable book of reference. Minute details give way to a full survey of the ground. Earlier sieges at Saragossa, Gerona, and Badajoz allow comparison. Sebastopol's long siege is the centrepiece. Photographs, then a novelty, illustrate the text. American readers of 1856 wanted the great European war explained plainly. This volume met that demand while the guns were barely cold.
59378-carpet-beetles-and-their-control:
Farmers' Bulletin No. 1346, from the United States Department of Agriculture, gives this guide to carpet beetles and their control. The catalog credit is garbled, but the title page is clear. The bulletin calls these pests buffalo moths and links their damage to that of clothes moths. Their grubs feed on wool, silk, hair, fur, and feathers.

The guide tells how to guard clothes and furniture in tight chests and trunks. It names crystals and fumigants in use at the time, and warns that some gases are risky. It also notes where fumigation of a whole house may be wise, and who should do it. Homeowners fighting damage to rugs and stored clothes were its readers.
59552-the-life-and-correspondence-of-sir:
Volume 2 of The Life and Correspondence of Sir Anthony Panizzi, by Louis Fagan of the British Museum, was issued in an American edition at Boston in 1881. Panizzi, an Italian exile, rose to be chief librarian of the British Museum and a senator of Italy. A third volume of memories by Henry Stevens of Vermont is added to this edition.

Chapters in this volume cover the choice of a new chief librarian, debates in the House of Commons, and gifts such as the Temple collection. Later parts treat the revolt of 1848 in Naples, visits by Gladstone, and Panizzi's wide web of letters. Fagan uses the letters to show how one man shaped a great library and its public role.
60061-the-century-illustrated-monthly-ma:
The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine for September 1913 is an issue of a leading American monthly. It is number five of volume eighty-six. The Century Company held its copyright that year. A sculpture of the American polo team fronts the issue. That team had won the world title in England in 1909. It defended the title in 1911 and again in 1913.

The contents mix art, verse, story, and comment. A Daumier painting faces the opening pages. A tale called The Book of his Heart appears within. Cartoons treat a bathing dress and lighter themes. An editorial states the spirit of the magazine. A Sargent portrait of Choate faces its page. Such monthlies set the taste of the reading middle class. The Century was among the most richly illustrated of them.
6063-the-bobbsey-twins-at-school:
Laura Lee Hope sends the Bobbsey twins to school, opening on a circus train where Nan asks how much longer they must ride. Bert offers to sit by the window and watch telegraph poles and trees go by, and their father smiles, seeing Bert has two thoughts for himself and one for Nan.

Chapters follow Snoop gone, a queer dog, Snap doing tricks, Danny Rugg mean, a scare, a children's party, Thanksgiving, first snow, a night alarm, and a confession. The fat lady's letter and Snap and Snoop close the book. School days bring tricks, questions, and small mysteries for the twins.
60653-car-pool:
Rosel George Brown wrote Car Pool for Worlds of If in July nineteen fifty-nine. A tag line teases the tale: certainly alien children ought to be fed, but to human kids? A flying car pool full of children opens the story in mid-song. All sing happy birthday except Gail, who is still screaming.

The driver sings jovially on, glancing at the other air traffic. Singing seems to work: the children stop swatting each other with lunch boxes. Her trained ear notes that Gail is now forcing her screams. Billy starts a song of Davy Eisenhower, and Jacob takes up the alphabet. Little Meli sings of a red and blue helicopter on the airways. Brown hides her aliens inside a school run.
61048-the-girls-from-fieu-dayol:
The Girls from Fieu Dayol is a science fiction story by Robert Young, first printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction in September 1961. The head note calls the girls lovely and quick to learn, with only little faults. Herbert Quidley, the hero, is a man who loves old books, old wood, old wine, and young girls.

In a library, inside a history of English literature, Quidley finds a sheet of copy paper covered in typing drills and a strange coded message. The name Fieu Dayol hides in the gibberish. Then a girl walks in who looks as Helen of Troy must have looked. Young builds a playful tale of messages, time, and desire from that find.
61303-magnetation-methods-of-birth-contr:
Magnetation Methods of Birth Control is a pamphlet by Margaret H. Sanger, closing her series on national methods of birth control. Earlier pamphlets covered English and Dutch methods, which repeated much of her Family Limitation. Sanger judged the French methods so close to those that she gives instead a list of French League books and pictures of goods sold at its Paris rooms.

She notes that methods in many lands were shaped by the English and Dutch leagues, the two oldest. She still holds the pessary named in Family Limitation to be the best, safest, cheapest, and handiest device. The pamphlet ends with her account of the magnetation method itself.
61388-sebastopol:
Count Leo Tolstoi wrote Sebastopol, here in an English version made from the French by Frank Millet, printed in New York in 1887. Howells, the American novelist, adds an introduction. A portrait of Tolstoi, as the name was then spelled in English, fronts the book.

Howells owns a sense of lunar remoteness in the Russian's far-off home at Yasnaya Polyana. Yet no author, he says, has written more faithfully of the life common to all men. The tales themselves come from the siege of Sebastopol in the Crimean War, where young Tolstoi served as an officer. His scenes of the bastions, the hospitals, and the men under fire made his first fame. They are war writing without varnish, close and true.
61495-dutch-methods-of-birth-control:
Dutch Methods of Birth Control is a pamphlet by Margaret Sanger, printing the methods of the Neo-Malthusian League of Holland. The methods are taken from the League's own pamphlet, Methods Used to Prevent Large Families, translated from the Dutch. Sanger adds a short history of the League. The Council of the League states its sole object plainly: the prevention of conception, and not the causing of abortion.

The history begins in 1877, when Annie Besant and Charles Bradlaugh were prosecuted for publishing The Fruits of Philosophy. That book presented the facts of birth control, and the trial lasted several days. It aroused more interest in the subject than had been known since Malthus. Over a hundred petitions went to Parliament asking freedom of discussion. Meetings of thousands filled the large cities, and a strong League was formed.
61878-the-manor-school:
The Manor School is a girls tale by Mrs Meade, out in nineteen three. Christian Mitford, age thirteen, leads the tale from its first part. She is tall, pale, and fair haired, with a will of her own by all counts. Her home is a great house in Russell Square with vast high rooms. The attics of that house are hers by right of long claim.

She took those attics at age seven or eight for her true life den. Part names hint at a hid thing, a wild scheme, and six long years. A slum night, play acts, and a school start fill the mid scheme. A purse, a bill, a note, and a clew to the hid thing come late. A tool house jail and a good will win close the long part list.
62094-the-middle-five-indian-boys-at-sch:
The Middle Five, Indian Boys at School, by Francis LaFlesche, was copyrighted in 1900. Small, Maynard published the Boston edition of 1909 from that copyright. LaFlesche, an Omaha, wrote from his own school days in this account. A dedication offers the book to the universal boy at the front.

The Mission opens the contents as chapter one of the school tale. Brush, Edwin, Little Bob, and Warren follow as chapters named for boys. Lester and a chapter on the splinter, the thorn, and the rib come next. Fraudulent holidays and a chapter named for General Sherman fill the middle heads. A runaway, a new study, and Ponka boys close the listed contents. A little boy crying on a porch bench opens the mission school scene.
62223-plain-parochial-sermons-preached-i:
Plain Parochial Sermons is a volume of sermons preached in the parish church of Bolton-le-Moors by James Slade, vicar of Bolton and prebendary of Chester. It was printed in London in 1831. Slade dedicates the sermons to the congregation of the parish church of Bolton, with affectionate regard, as their pastor and friend.

His advertisement explains a long delay. Friends had urged him for years to print his sermons. He feared that the interest his discourses raised from the pulpit would not revive in print. He feared it would impress only those who had heard them. He also thought the Christian world had sermons enough already. At last he yielded. Parish sermons of this kind were the weekly bread of the Church of England. They are plain teaching on plain texts, addressed to a known flock, and kept in print as a record of one incumbent's ministry.
62360-adele-doring-at-boarding-school:
Grace May North wrote this girls' novel, issued by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard in Boston in September nineteen twenty-one, with pictures by Florence Liley Young. It belongs to the Adele Doring series, after Adele Doring of the Sunnyside Club and Adele Doring on a Ranch. The dedication thanks the many girls of that Sunnyside Club in California who wrote to say how dearly they loved Adele and wished to be like her.

The contents run from a new Sunnysider's arrival through the ogre, two surprises, and a letter from Carol to the departure for boarding-school. Apple-Blossom Alley, a Thanksgiving dinner party, a tame Katrina, and a string of pearls keep the school terms busy until old friends arrive.
62528-to-a-youth-at-school:
To a Youth at School is a religious tract addressed to a schoolboy. Applegath printed it in London, and Davis and Nisbet sold it. It is number eighteen in its tract series. The writer asks leave to present a paper for the boy's best interest. Your parents regard you with tender affection and anxious hope, he writes. If God spares the boy's life he will add to one of two sums. He will increase the mass of sin and misery in the world. 

How desirable to increase the latter, the tract urges. Man is born ignorant of everything, it teaches. His parents placed him under teachers by duty to God and him. Next to Christian ministers, teachers hold the highest office, it says. The tract is a penny sermon for the schoolroom.
62891-the-medals-of-creation-volumes-1-a:
Gideon Algernon Mantell, a doctor and fossil hunter, wrote The Medals of Creation, or First Lessons in Geology and the Study of Organic Remains. The two volumes are combined in the hosted text. Mantell opens with Sir Humphry Davy's words: if broken columns and temples stir us, how much more the rocky tombs of a former living world.

Fossils, in that image, are the medals of creation, older and grander than any coins of Greece or Rome. The contents promise fossil vegetables and the remains of past life, set out as first lessons for beginners. Mantell had won fame with The Wonders of Geology and with his finds of great fossil reptiles in Sussex. His lessons taught general readers to read the earth's story in its buried bones and shells.
63450-course-of-study-of-the-oakland-hig:
Course of Study of the Oakland High School is an official curriculum booklet issued at Oakland, California, in July 1912. It sets out the subjects taught, the order in which pupils take them, and the two main courses the school offered, both preparing students for the University of California.

An index lists algebra, botany, chemistry, civics, composition, drawing, economics, and history among many subjects. Languages include Latin, Greek, French, and German, and the outline adds music, public speaking, hygiene, and gymnasium work. Course one aims at the colleges of letters, social sciences, and natural sciences, while course two also serves the engineering colleges. Booklets of this kind let parents and pupils plan four years of schooling subject by subject.
63475-the-brides-of-ool:
The Brides of Ool is a science fiction story by M A Cummings. It appeared in Planet Stories in the summer of 1955. Commander Ool wakes on the first morning of his honeymoon. Marriage services were out of date, but Loris had wanted both wedding and honeymoon. His hand finds the form beside him smooth and cold as marble. Loris, his beautiful bride, is dead.

Ool then reports back after weeks without word. The captain orders him up at once; the Old Men want his story. Two weeks are gone from Ool's life without memory. He had floated in space, unconscious, while Loris lay dead beside him. He wonders whether he could have killed her without knowing it. His memory runs perfect up to the Invasion, when the untested Gilkite rays screened civilisation. Ool alone stood at the machines after Gilk, the froglike Martian inventor, ran.
64053-calling-world-4-of-kithgol:
H B Fyfe wrote Calling World Four of Kithgol, printed in Planet Stories for January nineteen fifty two. A head note tells that Yorgh sent off into space a grim two hundred year old message by accident. He lived to see his dead world meet the busy future, it adds. Yorgh is a hunter on a sand swept world. He rides a six legged beast called a wolly.

The star was obscured by blowing sand, and Yorgh could not see much of the world. His wolly snorted in panic at the howl of the sandstorm. He swung down and dragged the beast by the guide rope, seeking trees he passed that morning. Sand filled his short golden beard. He had given the Sea People two dozen copper arrowheads for his dark red tunic. A tale of a lost world calling its colony follows.
6416-entertainments-for-home-church-and-:
Frederica Seeger, edited by Theodore Waters, offers entertainments for home, church, and school in a practical handbook. Household games open the book, with Going Shopping, Hit or Miss, a game of rhymes, and a most improbable story. Animated art, guessing character, and tongue twisters follow, with French rhymes, Ant and Cricket, and a spoonful of fun.

Church and school socials bring charades, including Cicero, Attenuate, and charades on the Grecian islands. Optical illusions, table games for adults, outdoor games, and holiday games complete the set. A note on staging adds that a royal crown need only be golden on the side toward spectators, and cotton velvet reads as silk through gauze. Seeger writes for hosts who want fun without fuss.
64337-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Volume fourteen of The Works of John Dryden was printed in London for William Miller in 1808. The eighteen-volume set carries notes historical, critical, and explanatory, and a life by Walter Scott. This volume is given to Dryden's translations from Virgil.

It opens with the Georgics in four books, preceded by Dryden's dedication to the Earl of Chesterfield and an essay on the Georgics by Addison, and followed by notes. The Aeneis follows, dedicated to the Marquis of Normanby and Earl of Mulgrave, its books and notes filling the rest of the volume. Dryden tells Chesterfield he hid his longing to appear before him for seven years. The wait was as tedious as the voyage of Aeneas before he reached Italy. He lays the best poem of the best poet at his patron's feet.
64971-the-rising-son-or-the-antecedents-:
The Rising Son is a history of the African race by William Wells Brown. The Boston edition of 1882 is the thirteenth thousand. Brown was a doctor and a noted Black author. He also wrote Clotelle and The Black Man. His preface admits the scant stock of materials. He aimed at a faithful account, faults not hidden. Some lives are brief for want of sound facts.

A publisher's note boasts of the book's sales. Twelve thousand copies had already been sold. Demand in the Southern states had doubled in two years. The work joins early history to lives of note. It traces the race from old Africa to America. Brown had escaped slavery and knew its weight. His histories argued the case for full manhood rights. The verse motto calls a historian of the race to come forth.
65081-life-of-charles-t-walker-d-d-the-b:
Life of Charles T Walker, called the Black Spurgeon, is a biography by Silas Xavier Floyd, printed at Nashville in 1902. Walker was pastor of Mount Olivet Baptist Church in New York City. Robert Stuart MacArthur wrote the introduction. A portrait shows Walker at forty-four years of age.

MacArthur opens with the difficulty of biography. Biographers are tempted to magnify the virtues of their subjects, or at other times to minify their vices. The biographies of Holy Scripture, he says, are the models: they neither extenuate defects nor set down aught in malice. A biography is the history of the life, actions, and character of a particular person. Carlyle's saying is quoted, that history is biography, and the history of a nation the story of its great men. Floyd's life tells of a famed Black preacher whose voice won him his nickname.
65171-the-conchologist-s-first-book-a-sy:
Edgar Allan Poe, of all people, published The Conchologist's First Book at Philadelphia in 1840, a school textbook on shells. Poe arranged the system of testaceous malacology for classroom use, following Cuvier, and he added many new species. Two hundred and fifteen shell pictures show a type of each genus.

Poe took the job for money, working over an English conchology by Thomas Wyatt. The book sold well enough to need a second edition within the year, the only one of his books to do so in his lifetime. Scholars still argue over how much of it is truly Poe. Either way, it is the strangest item in his bibliography: the poet of the Raven, teaching shells.
65174-the-new-year-s-carol:
The New Year's Carol is a Swiss tale by Johanna Spyri for children. Alice Howland Goodwin turned the German tale into English for this copy. Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York held the rights in 1924. Grace Edwards Wesson drew the pictures, a coloured frontispiece among them. Green meadows lie near the fortress of a little Swiss village.

That village stands above Altdorf, with fragrant grass and fresh flowers. A foaming brook rushes through the meadow over rocks in its course. An old ivy-covered tower marks the end of the village there. A great old nut tree shades the path by the brook side. Barty and his little sister Franzelie stand at the tale's heart. Their boy was born on Saint Sebastian's day and took his name. Summer grass cutting on high slopes fills one pictured scene. A card found by Franzelie grows the wonder of the tale.
65205-the-bravest-girl-in-school:
Ethel Talbot wrote The Bravest Girl in the School. Cassell and Company issued it at London in 1924. Four pictures in color and black-and-white aid it. The book goes to Hilda Skae. Twenty-one chapters carry the school tale. A Secret opens the action at page one.

Going to School and New Arrivals follow fast. Scrambled Eggs and Rules fill the early terms. The Hope-Scott Prize enters at chapter six. Hermits and Horses and plans for bravery come next. Mainly About Hockey fills the ninth chapter. A Holiday Adventure and To the Rescue build it. The House on the Cliff stands at twelve. The Hockey Match decides much at fourteen. Sybil Returns and Margot's Story come late. News for Gretta and the shield close it. Helen's brilliant stroke wins one match by a goal. School story courage here is hockey, loyalty, and a cliff house secret faced down.
65271-gloria-at-boarding-school:
Gloria at Boarding School is a girls' novel by Lilian Garis, author of Gloria: A Girl and Her Dad. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York in 1923. The frontispiece shows Gloria and Trixy examining a mysterious package. The first chapter, Mixed Baggage, opens with a dark-haired girl chuckling on a cretonne couch.

So this is boarding school, she says to the empty room. Chapters follow the talisman, a sudden departure, and a rescue from icy waters. Steppy finds a clue at the Rookery tea room, and the tale closes with the lure of boarding school itself. Garis wrote many series books for girls in this brisk, cheerful vein.
65424-more-about-teddy-b-and-teddy-g-the:
More About Teddy B and Teddy G, the Roosevelt Bears, is volume two of a children's verse series by Seymour Eaton, writing as Paul Piper. Stern published it at Philadelphia in 1907, with pictures by Culver. The bears were born, Eaton says, in the autumn of 1905.

Eaton brought the two bears out of a Colorado mountain den for a tour of the East. His aim was to teach children that animals have human like feeling. Bears, he argues, are not made only for hunters' sport. The welcome from boys and girls proved the lesson took, he writes. This volume depicts their further travels and adventures. Readers get rhymed bear travels tied to the teddy bear craze.
6575-the-purple-parasol:
George Barr McCutcheon opens with young Rossiter on a fast train north, hating the task his firm has set him. He must watch a young, lovely wife of seventy-year-old Wharton, and the job feels like police work, not law. Rossiter grumbles that he never wanted to be a cop, and that Wharton got just what he might have expected.

From that sour start grows a tale of love, age, money, and a parasol that marks its heroine. McCutcheon writes with wit and a light touch, letting Rossiter's gruff voice carry the comedy. The Purple Parasol is a smart, old-style romance of a man who takes a shabby job and finds his heart in it.
65808-pecan-diseases-and-pests-and-their:
Pecan Diseases and Insects and Their Control, numbered MP-313 and dated November 1958, came from the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station and the Texas Agricultural Extension Service at College Station. It is a field guide for growers, built around keys. A grower matches what he sees on leaf, nut, root, or bark against short entries, and each entry points to a page for the full account.

Leaf troubles come first: scab with its olive spots, downy spot, brown leaf spot, vein spot, and rosette with its crinkled yellow leaflets. Nut diseases add pink mold, and the roots add crown gall and cotton root rot. Lichens and Spanish moss get a place as growths that harm by crowding. A second key sorts the insects, from the pecan nut casebearer and hickory shuckworm to weevils, stink bugs, aphids, and mites, with the control for each.
65925-patrol:
Patrol is a science fiction story by Richard Nelson. It was printed in Imagination, a magazine of stories of science and fantasy, in October 1952. The tag line sets the puzzle: MacMartree knew that Man was omnipotent, master of the universe. But could he expect his patrol to fight and conquer an invisible enemy?

The story opens on a small planet where night comes fast. The patrol makes camp high on the breast of a gently swelling hill. Far out on the grass-covered plain their ship stands gleaming like a slender candle in the sunset. Cole asks if the screen is not useless. The younger men are bored to death by the quiet life. Nelson builds his tale on that boredom, and on what the screen may really be for.
65933-all-wool:
Tuttle wrote All Wool, a tale of the sheep country. Zeb Whitney lays the ace of diamonds on a rock and grins at Ricky Saunders: play that little old jack, and it will put me out. Ricky lays his cards down and peers over Zeb's shoulder instead. Look at that sheep, Zeb; what do you reckon ails him?

Zeb will not turn round and be fooled out of the jack. Then a shot rings out: sping, a bullet ricochets off their card-table rock and whines away down the foothills. The two young sheep men dive for the pine tree. Somebody is shooting at them, and danged good shooting too. Western fans get a Tuttle tale at full tilt.
65939-fortune-s-fool:
Rafael Sabatini wrote Fortune's Fool, a novel printed in Boston in 1923. The author of Scaramouche and Captain Blood sets this tale in Restoration London, where the Duke of Albemarle keeps an antechamber of suitors and the Duke of Buckingham disposes as he pleases. The hostess of the Paul's Head tavern opens the story.

A mercenary soldier is the fool of the title, drawn into the court's games by George Etheredge and a woman scorned. The shadow of the gallows falls, a sedan-chair is stopped, and an abduction leads to a parley and a battle. Under the Red Cross the tale reaches its crisis, in the plague year of the old king's London. Sabatini's hand with costume, courts, and swordsmen is at its practised best.
66193-the-phantom-rider-or-the-giant-chi:
Rolfe wrote The Phantom Rider, a tale of the old Dahcotah country published in New York in 1872. Vinnie, a young girl in a lone log cabin in the great North-west, is in peril from the first chapter. Clancy Vere, the Maybob twins, and a phantom warrior enter the story. A giant chief's fate hangs over the plot.

Storm, a fall over a cliff, and time lost in the forest raise the stakes. Vinnie is taken prisoner, scouts search for her, and the Phantom Rider appears at last. Rolfe also wrote a Pocket Novel called The Man Hunter. Readers who like frontier tales of danger and rescue will find a fast, tense story here.
66644-the-origin-and-ideals-of-the-moder:
Francisco Ferrer wrote an account of his Modern School, turned into English by Joseph McCabe and issued in London in 1913. Ferrer had fought in the revolt years of Spain and lost faith in mere party change. Fifteen years in Paris, through the Boulanger and Dreyfus storms, taught him that schooling was the key lack.

His school taught boys and girls as one, and rich and poor as one, with no prize and no blame as tools. Chapters cover clean rooms, teachers, Sunday talks, a school sheet, and the forced shut of the school. A last part guards his name and holds up the clear mind of the child.
67497-the-fool:
David Mason wrote The Fool, a science fiction story printed in Infinity Science Fiction in August 1956. Its headnote calls the Tarchiki the worst pupils in the universe and Duncan, their teacher, a first-rate carpenter at the wrong trade.

A veteran agent tells the tale of Duncan, who served on the planet thirty years before, Earth time. Duncan looked able, even bright, yet did everything the wrong way round. Knowing him, the narrator says, was a real education: do the opposite of Duncan, and you will be right. The Tarchiki cut each other's throats freely, which shortens every lesson. Mason builds a dry, funny parable about teaching the unteachable.
67552-the-history-of-the-manners-and-cus: Volume one of a history of the manners and customs of ancient Greece sold for thirty-one shillings and sixpence. A notice at the front warns the lending libraries of the day. The new Copyright Act, it says, barred them from lending single copies of foreign editions of English works. The book treats Greek daily life, home, dress, food, and custom in full.
67637-the-history-of-the-manners-and-cus:
The History of the Manners and Customs of Ancient Greece is a three-volume work by St John, and this text is volume two. It was published in London by Richard Bentley in 1842. The volume carries book three to its end and book four. Chapters treat marriage rites, the state of married women, dress, and ornaments.

Book four turns to private dwellings and household furniture. The work aims to show daily life among the ancient Greeks, not just their wars and politics. It draws on classical authors and on the remains of Greek art. For its time it was a standard popular guide to Greek private life.
67707-the-history-of-the-manners-and-cus:
John St John wrote a history of the manners and customs of ancient Greece in three volumes, and volume three is this book, printed in London in 1842. A copyist's note says the index here points to all three books. Slaves fill the first part of this volume, then the serfs of Sparta, Crete, and Thessaly.

Trade and work come next, with the state of the poor, millers, bakers, wine men, and markets. Day-to-day Greek life, not just wars and kings, is the theme. Students of the old world get a full, close view of how Greeks ate, worked, bought, and lived at home.
68083-a-day-at-happy-hollow-school:
Lettie Cook Van Derveer wrote this school entertainment, published in Ohio in 1910 by a house that specialized in such pieces. It is built as a play in acts, not a story. The setting is an old-fashioned schoolroom, with chairs in rows, a teacher's desk, and a blackboard.

The severe teacher, in eyeglasses, rings her bell, and the scholars troop in. They wear gingham aprons and carry baskets, bags, and tin dinner pails, hanging their wraps on hooks and backs of chairs. Hair is in pigtails or curls tied with ribbons or shoestrings. Readers get a ready-made school program, written for country schools to perform.
68781-trichocosmos-notes-historical-sthe:
Trichocosmos is a book of notes on the hair and beard, from a London house of Fleet Street. Its title page stacks its fields in a row: the past, taste, the lore of peoples, the build of the body, tales, and the craft of the barber. A verse couplet at its head sings how fair locks snare the race of men.

Its parts take the charm of hair first, then the styles of the old world and the freaks of vogue. Wigs get a long part of their own. Barbers, their shops and their lore, come next. The close turns to hard facts: the build, growth, and hue of hair in man. No part of the head, it seems, was too small for this fond survey.
68815-galactic-patrol:
Galactic Patrol is a science fiction novel by Smith, first run in Astounding Stories from September 1937 to February 1938. It opens at Wentworth Hall, a ninety story tower of chromium and glass. There the Tellurian candidates for the Lens of the Galactic Patrol live and train.

Graduation day fills the top floor with tense movement. Class Five must report to Room A, the commandant's dreaded office. Cadets summoned there alone vanished from the corps, the tale says. The Lens, a jewel of great power, marks those chosen to police the galaxy. Readers get the founding tale of the Lensman saga, space opera on the grandest scale of its age.
68845-the-story-of-the-thirty-eighth-reg:
The Story of the Thirty-Eighth Regiment of Massachusetts Volunteers, by George Powers, was printed at Cambridge in 1866. Powers entered the book for copyright in 1865. His preface promises a plain, linked account of the regiment's movements in the field.

Powers says he did not set out to paint armies or whole campaigns. He keeps to the part his own regiment played, and to the small matters of its daily life. Names of men seldom appear, since all did their duty alike. He was with the regiment for thirty-two of the thirty-five months he records. His notes were made day by day for friends at home. The Shenandoah campaign, where he was parted from the unit, is the chief gap in his own witness.
69517-the-ocean-wireless-boys-of-the-ice:
Wilbur Lawton wrote a boys' sea tale of the wireless age that Hurst copyrighted in 1915. Charles Wrenn drew the pictures. Jack Ready serves as wireless man on the Cambodian, a brand new freighter bound from New York for Rotterdam with no cargo aboard. Jack had hoped for the post on a great liner and grumbles at his berth, till work on a faulty detector lifts his mood.

The chapters promise ice and peril from the start. They bring a man overboard, a spell as prisoners, and a marooning on an iceberg. Jack saves the captain, boards a ship called the Polly Ann, and meets a plot and a treasure hunt. Skull Island and Cedar Island mark the far points of the cruise. The Polly Ann is wrecked, yet a joyous message comes by wireless near the end, and a crash in fog leads on to the treasure.
69773-the-long-patrol:
Albert Treynor wrote The Long Patrol, a novel published by Dodd, Mead, with copyrights of 1924 and 1926, and reissued by Grosset and Dunlap. Treynor had written The Trail from Devil's Country. Thirty-nine chapters carry the story, and their titles map a manhunt: the ambushed trail, knights of the law, find the woman, the doorway of dread, and the man-trap. The patrol is the mounted police of the Canadian north.

The tale opens on a snowy mountainside near dusk. A drab object lies barely defined against the white waste, a speck ninety-nine travellers in a hundred would pass unseen. The one man of a hundred rides by at that moment. Treynor wrote northwesterns of pursuit and endurance: runaway girls, voluntary prisoners, avalanches, and dangerous waters, all under the honour of the service. The novel belongs to the shelf of Mountie fiction sold throughout the nineteen twenties.
70097-a-new-note-in-the-christmas-carol:
Clara Wood Mingins wrote a Christmas tale issued in New York in 1913. A girl born on Christmas morning eight years past sings a carol in a clear child voice. Her father sits in the library with wet eyes as the song floats in and wakes fond thoughts.

The house had long kept rich Christmas ways: stockings, a huge tree, gifts for each child friend, food for the birds, and a lit candle in the window. Six short chapters move through growth in grace, plans, a girl named Maddie, and a search for Dorothy. Candles at Christmas close a tale built on gifts to sad hearts.
71124-the-radium-pool:
Ed Earl Repp's The Radium Pool came out as a book from the Fantasy Publishing Company of Los Angeles in 1949, though the title tale had first been copyright in 1929. Beneath volcanic sands, the jacket copy says, lies a hidden world with a gem-crusted cavern and a pool of shimmering matter, guarded by beings from outer space. Two men follow the trail of a vanished girl into that cavern land.

The searchers meet the weird Jovians in their workshop under the Valley of Death and learn what the pool can give, even immortality. Two shorter works share the volume: The Phantom of Terror, a scientific detective story, and The Red Dimension, long praised by readers as Repp's best short tale. The book is pulp science fiction of the early magazine age, bound up for the postwar market.
71711-tales-out-of-school:
Tales Out of School is a story book for young readers by Frank Stockton. Scribner first held the rights in 1875, and a new edition appeared at New York in 1916. In a playful preface Stockton owns that telling tales out of school is not thought proper. He invites the Arabs, tigers, and cabmen of his tales to complain in person if they dislike it.

The contents mix adventure tales with short nature pieces. One story follows a colonel's hunting in Africa and India, where he fears he has shot too many buffalo. Other pieces treat a sugar camp, silver plating, and very ancient animals. Readers meet luminous insects, sponges, kangaroos, and a voyage to the lower Amazon. A lady narrator from an earlier book tells some of the tales. The range suits the book's aim of varied, lively reading.
71821-beyond-our-control:
Beyond Our Control is a star tale by Randall Garrett from the January nineteen fifty eight Infinity. Craft flaws on Satellite Four turn a threat to all Earth in its tag. A great house in New York bears a glow atom mark on its roof at night. That mark stands for Earth ringed by robot moons that beam world shows. It is the sign of Circum Global, the firm that links those moons.

The top twenty floors hold a vast spark brain that plots each moon path. Four floors of watch rooms pick and set the world shows there. A new chief in Johannesburg speaks hard words to a lens in the tale. His speech beams by tight ray to Satellite Nine in that sky. Seam faults in that chain are the dread seed of the plot.
721-the-birds-christmas-carol:
Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote this Christmas tale about Carol Bird, a frail child known as a little snow-bird, who longs to give joy to others. Though she is often confined to her room, she plans a Christmas carol party for the poor Ruggles children next door, with food, gifts, and song. Her family helps her carry out the plan.

The tale is tender without being mawkish, and it turns on Carol's wish to share what little strength she has. Wiggin writes the children's world with warmth and humour. The book has lasted as a gentle holiday story about giving, kindness, and the light one small life can cast.
72213-the-sexagenarian-or-the-recollecti:
The Sexagenarian, or the Recollections of a Literary Life, was printed in London in 1817, in two volumes, and this is volume one. Its subject is a man of sixty with a whimsical character, shown first through a pile of ready-made dedications found in his papers. Some are solemn and addressed to great men, ministers, and bishops.

Others are lighter, meant for old college friends, and the mix sets the book's tone: fond, gossipy, and a bit sly. The tale looks back over a life spent among books, patrons, and the trade of writing. Readers get a portrait of literary London in the age of patrons, written as if from a long insider's memory.
72214-the-sexagenarian-or-the-recollecti:
The Sexagenarian, in its second part, is a set of tales of a life in letters by a man of sixty years. It came out at London in the late years of the great war with France. A Latin tag at its head warns of an old skin kept and a fox hid in the breast.

Its first part turns to a new shape in its hid notes. The man, it says, must be an aim of guess work. Yet his marks are most strange, and the shifts of his cast and acts so great, that some readers may find sport in the look back. They may try to find, from the past five and twenty years, to whom the notes will fit. His school days in a great house stand first in the tale.
7235-the-bride-of-fort-edward-founded-on:
Delia Bacon's Bride of Fort Edward grows from an incident of the Revolution, yet Bacon warns readers at once that it is not a play. She chose dialogue in scenes arranged for the reader alone, wholly unadapted to the stage. That form best suited her purpose: presenting anew the passions and events of a day long buried in the past.

The preface guards against misconception with care, insisting that the work be judged as reading, not as theatre. Its scenes let voices from the Revolution speak in their own heat, while the author shapes the whole for private reflection. Bacon's little book thus joins history to drama without ever asking for footlights.
7283-short-stories-and-selections-for-us:
Emilie Kip Baker compiled and annotated these short stories and selections for secondary schools, with questions for study. Her table runs from Louise de la Ramee's Leaf in the Storm and Maurice Hewlett's Cats through Balzac, Axel Munthe, and Richard Jefferies. Herman Melville's Taboo, George Sand's school days at the convent, and Louisa Alcott in Brittany complete the set.

Each piece comes with notes and questions, so that pupils can read a story and then think hard about it. Baker mixes famous names with lesser-known work, favouring tales that teach by feeling as much as by craft. The volume serves as a classroom reader with a critic's guidance built in.
73570-the-mutual-influence-of-christiani:
The Mutual Influence of Christianity and the Stoic School is a prize essay. James Bryant wrote it at St John's College in Cambridge. It won the Hulsean prize there for the year 1865. The book came out in London and Cambridge in 1866.

Bryant first sets out what the Stoic school of Greece and Rome taught. He then lays that creed side by side with the Christian faith. Two long parts trace the sway each had on the other. One asks how the faith changed the last years of the school. The next asks how Stoic thought shaped the early church in turn. A short close draws the sum of the two-way debt.
737-the-bobbsey-twins-at-school:
Laura Lee Hope took the Bobbsey twins, Bert, Nan, Freddie, and Flossie, back to school for a new term of lessons and play. Class work, games, and small rivalries fill their days, while pets and friends add comic trouble. The twins learn to help classmates, own up to faults, and keep their spirits up when plans go wrong.

The tale is gentle and orderly, with each chapter bringing a fresh schoolroom scrape or kindness. Hope writes for young readers in plain, cheerful prose, and the twins' good humour carries the book. It stands as a classic school story of its era, valued for its warmth and its simple lessons in fair play.
73930-ross-s-adventures-of-the-first-set:
Ross's Adventures of the First Settlers on the Oregon or Columbia River is a fur trade narrative of the years 1810 to 1813, reprinted at Cleveland in 1904. It forms volume seven of a series of early western travels, edited with notes by Reuben Thwaites. That editor had also handled the Jesuit relations and other border chronicles, the front pages note. A preface by the editor opens the volume.

The adventures themselves tell of the expedition fitted out by John Jacob Astor, the contents explain. Its aim was to plant a Pacific fur company on that far coast. An account of the Indian tribes on the Columbia stands within the tale. Alexander Ross, its author, was a clerk of that company who wintered among those tribes. His book is one of the root records of the American north west.
74645-bessie-at-school:
Bessie at School is a story for children by Joanna H. Mathews, printed in London by George Routledge and Sons. Bessie Bradford is a small, delicate girl in a warm home with her sister Maggie, baby Annie, and a mother who has been very ill.

The chapters follow Bessie into school life with her schoolmates. Readers meet Belle, share a party, and face small trials like a hurt foot and a broken clock. One chapter turns on a confession, and another on a lost-and-found episode. Prizes and an award close the school term. Mathews writes gentle lessons about truth and kindness into daily scenes that child readers of the time would know well.
75261-frank-and-andy-at-boarding-school:
Frank and Andy at Boarding School is a tale for boys by Vance Barnum. Its second title runs Rivals for Many Honors. Barnum was the author of Frank and Andy Afloat and Frank and Andy in a Winter Camp, and of the Joe Strong books. The tale came out from Whitman Publishing Company of Racine, Wisconsin. The first chapter is called In Trouble.

Frank and Andy Racer are on the deck of a river steamer on its way up a fair stream. Andy asks if they ought to be there soon, and Frank says the captain called it a short trip. Andy turns to what Riverview Hall will look like, and what sort of a school it is. Frank is a bit at a loss: it must be a good school, or their parents would not have picked it. Yet neither of them saw the place first, Andy notes.
75343-a-day-in-mary-carrow-s-school:
A Day in Mary Carrow's School is a children's story issued by the American Sunday-School Union. It was entered for copyright in 1848, at Philadelphia. An illustration shows Anne Lyle on her first day, standing by her father.

The Union's committee of fourteen, drawn from six denominations, sanctioned every book it published. No book could pass if any member objected. The tale follows a day in Mary's school. After roll call the little ones say their lesson first, spelling two-syllable words. Camel, peacock, hen-coop, parlour, and tea-cup are given out. Then questions are allowed, and Harry Linn asks what a camel is. Mary fetches a book and shows the class its picture.
76845-the-golden-pool:
Austin Freeman wrote The Golden Pool, a story of a forgotten mine, printed in London in 1905. Freeman, later famous for the detective Thorndyke, begins in the first person. His narrator makes the acquaintance of Captain Bithery, sets out for Africa, and hears strange stories and vague rumors on the way.

He visits a graveyard, meets a blind man, and finds a curious relic. The journal of Captain Barnabas Hogg, an old slaver's log, points the way. The golden pool itself, the Aboasi mine, a robbery assisted in, and a flight fill the later chapters. Freeman writes a West African treasure tale with a surveyor's care for place and process.
76952-the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first:
Walter Scott edited The Works of John Dryden, the first full collection in eighteen volumes, printed in London in 1808 with notes and a life of the author. The text here is volume seventeen. Scott's edition gave Dryden, the great poet and critic of the Restoration age, a monument on the scale of a classic.

This volume holds prose and translation rather than poems. It opens with Dryden's Life of Plutarch and part of his History of the League. A long section prints the controversy between Dryden and Stillingfleet over a paper by the late Duchess of York, paper, answer, and defence in turn. The volume closes with Du Fresnoy's Art of Painting in Dryden's English, with his own preface setting a parallel between painting and poetry. Scott's notes made such mixed volumes readable as literature and as history.
77010-a-second-day-in-mary-carrow-s-scho:
Mary Carrow's School tales came from the American Sunday School Union, with the second day book filed in 1849. The union had shops at Philadelphia, New York, Boston, and Louisville. A front note says no book went out without the nod of a board of fourteen. That board drew from six church groups.

No more than three board men could share one group. No book could pass if one man said no. The tale opens on a cool, rainy morning. Boys and girls come in thick shoes with coats and shawls. Mary is glad the rain did not keep them home. A front print shows Carry Deacon and her small sister with ducks. The tales teach faith and good acts in a school frame.
77093-a-silver-pool:
A Silver Pool is a volume of lyric poems by Beulah Field. Moffat, Yard and Company published it in New York in 1922. Some fifty short poems fill the table of contents. Inspiration opens the book and gives it its title image. The poet bridles her soul and waits for peace. Then she makes her heart a silver pool of melody. Stars come down at night and bathe in it.

Beggar-Man, Thief follows, contrasting a beggar's laurel with a merchant's tarnished gems. Carnival, Branded, and Pierrot strike darker notes. Branded hymns a darkling mistress of opal fire, hurricanes, and jungle screams. The Wayfarer, Wind of the Sea, and The Dead Lover recur to travel and loss. Other poems address friends by name or turn devotional. The poems are brief, musical, and steeped in sea and star imagery.
77937-children-of-the-old-masters-italia:
Children of the Old Masters, Italian School, an art book by Alice Meynell, was published by Duckworth in London in 1903. Meynell writes on how the painters and sculptors of old Italy showed children.
