Plates from works by Filippino Lippi and many others support the text. The book is addressed to young readers, as playmates.

Chapters move from the child in early art to Tuscan sculpture and enamel. Two chapters treat the Florentine painters, and one treats portraits. Siena, Umbria, and outlying schools follow, then Raphael and after, then the Venetians. Donatello, Luca della Robbia, Botticelli, and Ghirlandajo appear among the plates. The book teaches looking at old art through one clear theme.
78324-a-third-day-in-mary-carrow-s-schoo:
A small church school book tells of a third day in Mary Carrow's class. The American Sunday-School Union put it out in 1849. Its shops stood in Philadelphia, New York, Boston, and Louisville. A board of fourteen from six church kinds passed each book. A plate shows a glad group of small boys and girls.

Mary's scholars are the heart of this third day's tale. Lessons, songs, and kind talk fill their hours with her. Each child brings a small trial or joy to the room. Faith in plain words is the book's clear aim. Such books taught the young in homes with no school near. Brief and warm, it fits small hands.
78800-the-six-books-of-proclus-the-plato:
The Six Books of Proclus on the Theology of Plato survives here in Thomas Taylor's translation from the Greek. It forms the second volume of a two-volume edition printed for the author at London in 1816. A seventh book is added to supply the deficiency of another book on the subject that Proclus wrote but which has since been lost.

The volume also carries Taylor's translation of Proclus's Elements of Theology and his treatise on providence and fate. Extracts follow from the Ten Doubts Concerning Providence and from the treatise on the subsistence of evil. Book Six opens with the eternity of the intellectual gods, celebrated through the mystic conceptions of Plato. Taylor's Proclus proceeds from the demiurge and father of wholes, to whom all things are converted and by whom they are perfected.
78896-a-fifth-day-in-mary-carrow-s-schoo:
A Fifth Day in Mary Carrow's School was entered in 1852 by the American Sunday-School Union of Philadelphia. A front plate shows harvesters in a field; another shows Eddy at the window, just up. The tale takes its little readers over to Eddy Forester's cottage on a fine morning. Eddy has opened his window and is glad to find the sun shining.

His first thought on waking was the mowing-party to be held at Linn's. The Union's committee of publication, drawn from six denominations, had to approve every book it issued. No book could pass if any member objected. Tales of this kind taught country children their lessons through a school day: work, weather, Scripture, and kindness, told in short, plain scenes for Sunday reading at home.
79133-fate-and-a-fool:
Fate and a Fool is a western story by Tuttle, author of A Bull Movement in Yellow Horse. It opens at an alkali spring in the hills. A ragged old man scoops up bitter water and gives thanks. I am Fate, he announces to the narrator who rides up. The narrator answers that that is just what he figured. The old man looks like the pictures of Jerusalem herd riders. His shoes are tied on with strips of gunny sack.

His whiskers are about all that is visible on his head. The narrator tells his horse the pose would make a picture called Destiny. He is a sorrowing one named Wetherbee, he says. He seeks his mate as the tale begins. Tuttle mixes desert comedy with a touch of scripture talk.
79325-thoughts-of-a-fool:
Evelyn Gladys wrote Thoughts of a Fool, published by Rosenthal and Company in Chicago and London in 1905. The book is a set of comic essays spoken by a self-confessed fool. Chapter titles give the flavor: My Genealogy, How Smart I Am, and Shoes, Pigs, and Problems.

In the first essay the fool refuses to blame her parents for her foolishness. Her notions, she insists, are all her own, though her ancestry shines with wise men of every era. Other essays treat democracy, success, occultism, boiled cabbage, and free love. The closing piece is called It Is Finished. The humor is dry and sideways, in the manner of the newspaper column: short takes on life, dressed as the wisdom of a fool.
911-tales-of-the-fish-patrol:
Jack London wrote these tales of the Fish Patrol on San Francisco Bay, a water so large that storms often hide its far shore. The patrolmen chase oyster pirates, smugglers, and poachers, in boats that race the tide and the law. White and Yellow, the opening tale, sets the scene of bay, fog, and hard men.

London draws on his own youth on the bay, and his stories carry the salt, danger, and humour of that life. The patrol tales praise courage and fair play, while showing the rough code of watermen. The book is a lively set of sea adventures, and a fine introduction to London's California years.
9590-margaret-smith-s-journal-and-tales-:
Volume five of Whittier's works pairs Margaret Smith's Journal with his Tales and Sketches. The journal paints New England hearths and homes in the 1600s, in the voice of a young woman of the time. Its editor warns of small slips in persons, places, and dates, yet praises its lifelike picture of the past. Secretary Rawson and his kin figure large in the record.

Tales and sketches beside it include The Little Iron Soldier, The Opium Eater, Yankee Gypsies, and Patucket Falls. Other pieces treat charms, fairy faith, and witch folk with a storyteller's ease. A reader gets Whittier's prose at its most vivid, with history made homely and strange at once.
a-christmas-carol: Charles Dickens tells the Christmas story of Ebenezer Scrooge in five staves. Marley's ghost visits first, followed by the spirits of Christmas past, present, and yet to come. Each spirit shows Scrooge a part of his life and of the world he has shut out. The final stave brings repentance, generosity, and a merry Christmas at last.
a-slave-girl-s-story-being-an-autobiogra: Kate Drumgoold tells her own story in this autobiography, published in Brooklyn, New York, in 1898. Once a slave girl, she writes not something dry but the interesting thoughts her mind is full of. She writes for the good of those who wrote and prayed that slaves might be freed. Schools and books, learning to read and write for themselves, stand at the heart of her answer to their prayers.
big-and-little-sisters-a-story-of-an-ind:
Theodora R. Jenness wrote this story of an Indian mission school, opening on a Saturday morning in December in Dakota. Two Sioux girls, Hannah Straight Tree and Cordelia Running Bird, climb the stairs to their cleaning with aprons thrown over their heads against the draft. The great unplastered mission building is chilly throughout the winter, and the halls are drafty from the wind off the plains.

Christmas wishes carry the girls' world in miniature. Cordelia would buy a big doll for Susie, a red silk handkerchief for her father, and a blue one for her mother, and hang them on the Christmas tree. A prudent ten-year-old objects, and jealousy stirs among girls whose people can hang nothing. Jenness, who taught in such schools, writes assimilation's pressures gently: friendship, envy, and generosity among children between two worlds.
britannica-1911-alcohol:
Alcohol is treated in a long chemical and commercial article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In commerce the name means spirits of wine. In systematic organic chemistry it carries a wider sense, naming a whole class of compounds called hydroxy hydrocarbons. Ordinary alcohol, ethyl alcohol in particular, stands as that class's typical member, with the wider family handled under Alcohols.

The word itself is Arabic in origin, from al and kohl, the fine powder used in the East for painting eyebrows. For centuries alcohol meant any fine powder at all, and Paracelsus and Libavius still used it that way. Its use for the liquid distilled from wine is comparatively recent, though Paracelsus also wrote of alcool vini, burning wine. Later sections take up the law, since manufacturers pressed for freer use of absolute alcohol in industry, and a British committee of 1905 and an American inquiry of 1896 are reported.
britannica-1911-algol:
Algol, a variable star, is treated scientifically in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name is Arabic, signifying the Demon, and it belongs to the star Beta Persei, of the second magnitude. Montanari noticed in 1669 that its brightness fluctuates. John Goodricke in 1782 fixed the period of the change at about two days and twenty-one hours. He suggested the true cause: recurring eclipses by a large, dark companion star.

The star's light holds steady for close on fifty-six hours, then fades to nearly a quarter of its normal amount and returns by the same steps. Having no flat interval at its dimmest proves the eclipse partial, not a full ring eclipse. Pickering investigated the conditions from light measurements in 1880. Vogel's spectroscopic measures in 1889 finally proved the eclipse real. The star's motion matched the fading and brightening. A later theory making the system triple is reported as still on trial.
britannica-1911-allyl-alcohol:
Allyl alcohol is a chemical compound found in very small amounts in wood spirit. The entry gives three ways to prepare it. Moist silver oxide can act on allyl iodide. Acrolein can be reduced. Glycerin can also be heated with oxalic acid and a little ammonium chloride. In that last method an intermediate compound forms first. It breaks down as the heat rises.

The pure substance is a colourless, mobile liquid with a pungent smell. It boils at 97 degrees. It is an unsaturated compound, one with unused combining power in its structure. So it joins readily with the halogens. Strong oxidation turns it first into its aldehyde, acrolein. Further oxidation gives acrylic acid. Gentle oxidation with potassium permanganate can instead turn it back into glycerin.
britannica-1911-baliol:
Baliol was the name of a family that played a large part in the history of Scotland. Its founder in England was Guy de Baliol, a Norman baron who came over with William the Conqueror and gained lands in the north from William II. His heir Bernard built the fortress in Durham around which the town of Barnard Castle grew.

The 1911 Britannica entry traces the family through its English and Scottish branches, down to John and Edward Baliol and their failed hold on the Scottish crown. A late tradition, called dubious by the entry, says the name fell into such disgrace that its owners dropped it for the form Baillie.
britannica-1911-benzoin-ketone-alcohol:
Benzoin, in chemistry, is a ketone-alcohol, a compound carrying both kinds of oxygen group at once. It can be made by boiling benzaldehyde in alcohol with potassium cyanide, by reducing benzil with zinc and acetic acid, or by oxidising hydrobenzoin. Three roads to one substance make it a neat case for the laboratory.

The solid is colourless and crystalline, dissolving freely in alcohol and ether, and melts and boils at set, high heats. Because it gives up its oxygen easily it works as a reducing agent, throwing down red cuprous oxide from Fehling’s solution even in the cold. Chlorine and nitric acid push it back to benzil, while stronger treatment yields benzoic acid and benzaldehyde.
britannica-1911-benzyl-alcohol:
Benzyl alcohol, also named phenyl carbinol, is an alcohol found ready-made in several natural scents and balms. It sits in Peru balsam as a benzoic ester, in Tolu balsam as a cinnamic ester, and in jasmine oil and storax in other bound forms. Nature, in short, makes it widely but always in company.

Chemists can build it by reducing benzoyl chloride, by treating benzylamine with nitrous acid, or by boiling benzyl chloride with potash solution. The Cannizzaro reaction gives it too, splitting benzaldehyde into benzoic acid and the alcohol at once. The liquid is colourless with a faint sweet smell. Nitric acid turns it back to benzaldehyde, and chromic acid carries it on to benzoic acid.
britannica-1911-blackpool:
Blackpool is a seaside resort and borough on the Lancashire coast, 46 miles north of Liverpool. It grew very fast in the late 1800s, from 23,846 people in 1891 to 47,346 in 1901. Two railway companies served the town, and the council ran an electric tram service.

Seafront pleasure is the whole point of the place, as the entry presents it. Three piers, theatres, ballrooms, and a tall tower modelled on the Eiffel Tower are listed among its draws. Long promenades rebuilt by 1905 gave it a sea front said to match any English resort. Its beach is sandy with good bathing. The borough dates from 1876 and became a county borough in 1904.
britannica-1911-broach-tool:
Broach is a word for pointed tools of many kinds, drawn from the French broche and Latin brocca for a pointed thing. Its doublet brooch took a special sense of its own, while broach stayed with the workshop and kitchen. Bodkins, wooden needles for tapestry work and spits for roasting meat all fall under the name.

One shop use stands out: a broach, also called a rimer, works with a wrench to enlarge or smooth holes in metal. From tapping casks with such a tool comes the phrase to broach, or tap, a cask. Building gives the word its oddest sense, the broach-spire, found only in England. Sloping stone roofs fill the gap between a square tower and the eight-sided spire rising from it, and their meeting line forms the broach.
britannica-1911-carbazol:
Carbazol is a chemical found in coal-tar. It also occurs in crude anthracene. This 1911 Britannica article gives its making and properties. Its formula is written C12H9N in the article. It can be got from anthracene by fusion with caustic potash. That process turns it into a potassium compound. The anthracene is then distilled off to free it.

Several laboratory routes to carbazol are set out. Diphenylamine vapour passed through a red-hot tube yields it. Heating certain diphenyl compounds with acid or lime yields it too. Brucine and strychnine give it when distilled with zinc dust. The article describes the pure substance in detail. It dissolves easily in common organic solvents. It crystallizes in plates that melt at 238 degrees. It is very stable and sublimes with great readiness. Melted with oxalic acid it gives carbazol blue. In strong sulphuric acid it forms a clear yellow solution.
britannica-1911-carol:
Carol is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a hymn of praise, above all the songs sung outdoors at Christmas. The word's origin is unclear: the entry links it with chorus and with corolla, a garland, and notes that its earliest sense seems to be a ring or circle dance. Stonehenge itself was often called the Carol, or the Giants' Dance. Christmas hymns in Latin were written to dance tunes.

The entry traces how carolling, the joined practice of dance and song, passed from pagan ritual into the church. Councils at Toledo in 589 and Avignon in 1209 tried to ban dancing and secular songs in churches, yet the custom held on. Strictly, the word belongs to lyrics written for dance measures, though common use ties it to Christmas songs. Readers get both a word history and a record of the church's losing fight against festive dance.
britannica-1911-carvacrol:
Carvacrol is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a chemical substance, also called cymophenol, with the formula C10H13OH. It occurs in the oil of Origanum hirtum, in oil of thyme, in oil from pepperwort, and in wild bergamot oil. Chemists extract it from Origanum oil by means of a ten per cent potash solution. The entry gives the substance as a thick oil that sets at minus twenty degrees into crystals.

The entry also lists ways to make carvacrol in the laboratory. Routes include fusing cymol sulphonic acid with caustic potash, acting on a named benzene compound with nitrous acid, and heating camphor with iodine. Its crystals melt at zero degrees and the liquid boils near 236 to 237 degrees. Oxidation with ferric chloride turns it into dicarvacrol, and phosphorus pentachloride turns it into chlorcymol. The account is a compact bench note on sources, preparation, and behaviour.
britannica-1911-chodkiewicz-jan-karol:
Jan Karol Chodkiewicz, a Polish general, was born in fifteen sixty as a castellan's son. He was schooled at the Wilna academy, then went abroad to learn war. He fought in Spanish service under Alva and under Maurice of Nassau. In fifteen ninety three he wed a wealthy wife, Sophia Mielecka, in Poland. His first service at home was against a Cossack rising as a lieutenant.

Chodkiewicz then helped in a victorious campaign in Moldavia for his country. Honours and posts were showered on him in the years that followed. In sixteen hundred he became acting commander in chief of Lithuania. In the war against Sweden for Livonia he took fortress after fortress. He beat Swedish generals twice and won the grand baton of Lithuania. His crown deed was the great victory of Kirkholm in sixteen o five. With barely five thousand men he destroyed a far larger force.
britannica-1911-col:
A col, from the French word for neck, is a marked dip in a high, rugged divide between waters. Passage over it from one valley to the next is easy. The Col de Balme gives the type. It lies between the Trient and Chamounix valleys. There a smooth curve breaks the great wall of peaks below Mont Blanc. A footpath crosses with ease.

Most cols form in one plain way. The head-waters of a stream eat back into the divide. That action lowers the ridge at the head of the valley. The entry adds two notes on use. Armies in early campaigns always marched over a col. Roads in high mountain country still lean on such passes. Trade gains from them as well. The entry keeps to form, cause and use, with no list of named passes.
britannica-1911-eugenol:
Eugenol is a scented oil part that gives oil of cloves its chief smell. Its science entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is also called allyl guaiacol and eugenic acid in the text. The oil occurs in many other scented plant oils as well.

The entry gives the oil as clear, with a spicy scent, and a high boil point. Strong agents turn it into vanillin and other named products in tests. Base agents shift it to iso eugenol, which then yields vanillin too. Vanillin is the scented part of vanilla, the entry points out. A test by acetyl work can gauge how much eugenol clove oil holds.
britannica-1911-faldstool:
Faldstool is a word for a fold seat, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica traces its parts in two old tongues. One part means to fold, and one part means a stool or a chair. The French word for an arm chair of the day comes down the same line. In strict use the thing is a fold seat for a bishop. He uses it when he does not sit on his throne in his own great church.

He uses it as well when he serves in a great church that is not his own. From that use the word came to name any move fold stool used to kneel at prayer in church rite. The small desk from which a set prayer is read at times bears the same name.
britannica-1911-ferrol:
Ferrol, a seaport of north-western Spain, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the province of Corunna, on an inlet of the Atlantic, twelve miles from the city of that name. Its people numbered 25,281 in 1900. With two other ports it ranks as a principal naval station of Spain, ruled by an admiral of high title.

The article praises its site and its harbour. The town sits on a headland ringed by rocky hills that hide it from the sea. Its harbour is deep, wide, and safe, by nature one of the best in Europe. The way in is a narrow strait two miles long that admits one ship at a time, guarded by strong modern forts. The town holds wide dockyards, quays, storehouses, and an arsenal, most of them built or renewed after 1875.
britannica-1911-fool:
Fool comes from Old French fol, from a late Latin use of follis, a bellows or air-filled ball, for a stupid person, a jester, a wind-bag. A fool is a buffoon or jester. The class of professional fools, the entry argues, reached its height of influence and its recognized place in society during the middle ages. Yet it seems to have existed in all times and countries, wherever communities kept men who lived by amusing others.

There have always been persons born to amuse, the article observes. Beside them stood a definite class who used their powers, or their weaknesses, as a regular living. Savage jugglers, medicine-men and even priests share much with the jester by profession. The long piece then follows fools through courts and households of many ages. The hosted file opens with the end of the Food Preservation article.
britannica-1911-gaol:
Gaol is the older British spelling of jail, and a brief entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces where both word forms came from. The two forms grew from twin forms in Old Central French and Norman French. Both go back to a medieval Latin word for a small hollow or den.

The entry notes that gaol still held a place in official use, as in the term gaol-delivery. Yet both spellings were said aloud in the same way, as jail. That shared sound, the entry argues, shows which form was the real living word. It points readers to the main article on prisons for the fuller topic.
britannica-1911-ibn-gabirol:
Ibn Gabirol, also called Solomon ben Judah, was a Jewish poet and thinker. He was born at Malaga in probably about the year ten twenty one. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. His early troubled life was spent at Saragossa, in Muslim Spain.

Both parents died while Ibn Gabirol was still a small child. Patrons Jekuthiel and then Samuel ha Nagid shielded him in youth. His fierce temper, sharpened by hardship, led to quarrels with Samuel later. He wrote poems at age sixteen and laments for dead patrons early. He first spread use of Arabic verse forms in Hebrew poetry widely.
britannica-1911-jehol:
Jehol was a city in China once used as a summer seat by the emperor, as a 1911 Britannica entry records. It lay about one hundred and forty miles north east of Peking on a good road. The town had one long main street with short streets branching off it. Shops were fine and the people were said to be well off.

The palace there was built in 1703 and called the mountain lodge for avoiding heat. A brick wall six miles round held gardens, temples, and halls on wooded heights. Lord Macartney came here on his famed mission in 1793. Lama temples stand near the town, the best known built on the model of Potala.
britannica-1911-methyl-alcohol:
Methyl alcohol is the simplest of the alcohols, and this 1911 Britannica entry treats it as a topic in chemistry. An impure form was sold as wood-spirit, since it came from heating wood in closed vessels. Boyle found it in 1661, Dumas and Péligot studied it with care in 1831, and Berthelot built it up from its parts in 1858.

Much of the text explains how the spirit is made and cleaned. Wood is distilled in iron vessels, and the mixed liquid that results is treated with lime and distilled again to clear out acids. More steps with calcium chloride and potash yield a purer product. The entry also covers tests for strength and for traces of other spirits, and notes that pure methyl alcohol is a clear, light liquid that boils at a low heat.
britannica-1911-parasol:
Parasol, a word built from Italian roots for shielding against the sun, names a light sunshade, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives a brief account of it. A parasol is a small form of umbrella, covered with coloured silk or other light stuff. In Japan and China, bright paper parasols stretched on bamboo frames are used by people of all ranks.

The entry stresses the parasol as a sign of rank in the East. Richly made and highly adorned kinds are carried over rulers, princes, and nobles as a mark of honour and office. In West Africa, chiefs keep large, solid parasols for themselves alone. Their size varies, the entry notes, and marks steps in rank.
britannica-1911-patrol: Patrol is a word article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It links the word to the French patrouiller and to patte, a foot. As a verb, to patrol is to move up and down over a set round or beat in a town district, a camp, or on a stretch of river or sea. The aim is to watch and guard the ground, or to scout the numbers and posts of an enemy. As a noun the word names the body of troops or police on that duty.
britannica-1911-physiocratic-school:
Physiocratic School is an economics article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a group of French thinkers of the eighteenth century. Its heads were Francois Quesnay and Vincent de Gournay. The seed ideas had been set out in 1755 by the merchant Richard Cantillon, whom Jevons held the true founder of political economy. The members called themselves les economistes; the name physiocrates, from Greek words for nature and rule, was coined by Dupont de Nemours, one of their own.

In politics the school held that all men own the same natural rights and know their own interest best. The social union is a contract that trims each man's freedom only where it collides with the rights of others. Government is thus a needful evil, to be kept to the least interference that keeps the contract.
britannica-1911-stool:
Stool, a low seat with no back and no arms, is the topic of a furniture entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The piece notes that stools are old, made when folk first wanted a seat they could move with ease, unlike heavy settles and benches. Chairs, by contrast, were then a sign of rank.

The text traces forms from the plain three legged joint stool to four legged, braced and carved types, and quotes lines from Cowper on how the shape grew. It tells of stuffed seats in rich cloth, of stools that served as small tables, and of the coffin stool name it calls a wrong one. Later parts deal with the footstool, the ducking stool used to punish scolds, and the stool of repentance, so the entry mixes craft, home life and old custom.
britannica-1911-symbol:
Symbol, a sign that speaks of more, is weighed in an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Greek word names a seen thing that stands for an unseen. The mind grasps that unseen thing by its tie to the sign. A palm branch stands for victory, an anchor for hope. Much early Christian sign craft grew from pagan roots, it notes.

The Good Shepherd with his lamb may come from Hermes' form. Orpheus with the beasts, drawn in the tombs, types Christ there. The fish was one of the first signs of the Saviour. Its Greek name hid the first marks of five holy words. A ship stood for the Church on the sea of life. Lamb, lion, and peacock each bear a set sense too.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce:
Bristol takes its origin as a diocese from measures aimed against the Church. Its Catholic history is very brief, with only one bishop acknowledged by the Holy See. It was one of six bishoprics Henry VIII tried to found by Act of Parliament in 1542. He built them out of the spoils of suppressed monasteries, beside Oxford, Westminster, Gloucester, Peterborough, and Chester.

The city, then a leading town and chief seaport, was chosen for the new see. Its Augustinian abbey church was saved from demolition by the king's order after the house was plundered in 1539. That house had been founded by Robert Fitzharding in 1133. At the dissolution the dedication changed from Saint Augustine to the Holy Trinity, and the arms of the see show three ducal crowns in gold on black.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faldstool:
A faldstool is a movable folding chair used by bishops at pontifical functions. When no throne stands in the church, the bishop sits on it. It is covered in cloth of red, green, or violet, matching the liturgical colour. The name comes from the folding stool it stands on.

Rich examples include a gold and jewelled chair given to Clement IV. Hugh Pudsey, bishop of Durham, owned a silver faldstool in the twelfth century. The article notes where the chair stands during Mass and processions. It also lists the ministers who carry and set it in place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liverpool:
Liverpool is one of the thirteen dioceses Pius IX set up for Catholic England in 1850, when he restored the hierarchy. It covers North Lancashire, western South Lancashire, and the Isle of Man, with Salford taking the eastern half of the south.

By 1910 the diocese counted about 366,611 Catholics, 184 churches and chapels, and 458 priests, plus some seventy convents holding a thousand nuns. Schools taught 74,100 children, and homes cared for the blind, the aged poor, orphans, and fallen women. Town tables show Liverpool itself with 143,000 Catholics, then Preston, St. Helens, Wigan, and the rest in turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-protocol:
Protocol, in this short encyclopedia entry, is a notary's word with three linked senses. First, it means the opening formula of a public deed. That formula names the reign, the time and the place. Second, it means the bound register where a notary enters each deed in date order. Third, it means the first draft itself, written small and kept by the notary. From that draft a larger fair copy is made for the parties.

Courts whose registrars still carry the name of notary keep the same usage for their own registers. Because public deeds must be trustworthy, only originals or certified copies count as proof. A copy gains its standing when the notary witnesses on its face that it matches the original. That guarantee goes by the Latin name fides instrumentorum, trust in documents. The entry cites Justinian's Novels and the 1910 rules of the Rota.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-joseph-:
Joseph Oriol, called the wonder-worker of Barcelona, was born there on 23 November 1650 and died there on 23 March 1702. He studied at the University of Barcelona and took his doctorate in theology in 1674. Ordained priest in 1676, he won a benefice in the church of Our Lady of the Pine after a visit to Rome in 1686.

His priestly life stood out for penance, deep humility, and wise guidance of souls. Longing for martyrdom, he set out for Rome in April 1698 to offer himself for the foreign missions, but fell sick at Marseilles and returned home. People who were dying, blind, deaf and dumb, lame, or paralysed were said to be cured by him at once. Pius VII beatified him in 1806, and Pius X canonized him in 1909.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-anchor-as:
Hope, pictured as an anchor, is the theme of this short entry on early Christian symbols. In the ancient world the anchor already stood for safety at sea, since ships depended on it in storms. Christians took up the familiar emblem and gave it a deeper sense: trust in salvation to come, not merely rescue in this life.

Hebrews chapter 6 supplies the key text, calling hope an anchor of the soul, sure and firm. Peter, Paul, and early Fathers use the same image, and the entry traces it through catacomb inscriptions and carvings, including a fragment from the cemetery of Saint Domitilla. For readers of early art, it explains why an anchor carved beside a name spoke of faith beyond death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tiraspol:
The Diocese of Tiraspol, in southern Russia, was one of the largest dioceses in the world, covering 462,504 square miles. Suffragan to Mohilev, it took in Saratov, Samara, Kherson, Ekaterinoslav, Taurida and Bessarabia. It held 350,000 Latin Christians, mostly descendants of German colonists in a hundred parishes, with 40,000 Armenian Catholics in fifty parishes and a small Chaldean community.

About 210 priests served the diocese, and the bishop lived at Saratov, where seminaries for priests and boys trained new clergy. Religious orders were not permitted. German colonists had settled the empty southern lands at Catherine II's invitation in the later eighteenth century, keeping their German village names. Bishop Franz Xaver Zottmann, appointed in the nineteenth century, built its cathedral and seminaries and made it one of Russia's best organized dioceses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zahle-and-for:
Zahle and Forzol is the Greco-Melchite diocese whose wandering title tells a story of mistaken geography. In the seventeenth century, Antioch's patriarch moved the diocese of Seleucia Pieria to Maaloula in Lebanon for safety. The reason was later forgotten, a phantom town of Seleucia Libani was invented and matched to Maaloula, though no such town ever stood. When the see moved from Maaloula to Forzol, the Seleucia title travelled with it, already borne by a Forzol bishop in 1760.

Since 1849 the bishop bears the titles of Zahle, Forzol, and Beqaa, residing at Zahle since 1768. Zahle itself dates only from the late seventeenth century, when Catholics fled there in crowds under Lebanon's emirs. Now about twenty thousand strong, nearly all Catholics, the town saw Druses destroy two thousand houses in 1860 and massacre Christians. The diocese counts thirty thousand Catholics, forty-seven priests, and thirty-three churches.
child-s-new-story-book-or-tales-and-dial: Short tales and dialogues for small children fill an anonymous story book dated 1849, with 1850 on its cover. A boy launches a cork ship in a basin and imagines Captain Cook sailing for the Friendly Islands. A little girl holds a shell to her ear, listening for the whisper of the sea and her uncle's promised return. Robert and John walk to school through lanes and a churchyard, and loitering John reforms on the road. Simple morals close each piece, in the plain style of early Victorian books for the nursery.
daddy-takes-us-to-the-garden-the-daddy-s:
A garden book for young children by Howard R. Garis fills this volume of the Daddy Series for Little Folks. M. A. Donohue and Company of Chicago and New York issued it, under a 1914 copyright held by R. F. Fenno and Company. Eva Dean drew the pictures.

Hal and Mab Blake make a garden with their father. Chapters treat upside-down beans, the first radish, the eyes of potatoes, and corn silk. Early tomatoes, white celery, and a children's market follow. Hail stones bounce on the path in one scene, and the children worry for their crops. A list at the front names ten Daddy books in all. The tale teaches plant lore by story.
david-lockwin-the-people-s-idol:
A political novel of Chicago fills David Lockwin, the People's Idol, by John McGovern. Donohue, Henneberry and Company of Chicago issued it under copyrights of 1889 and 1891. A frontispiece shows Lockwin on a balcony while a cheer rolls over the South Side.

Four books divide the tale, named for Davy, Esther Lockwin, Robert Chalmers, and George Harpwood. Primaries, fifty kegs of beer, and the night before election fill the first book. Corkey, a rough friend with a good heart, offers seven hundred cases in bar gold to see Lockwin in Congress again. Widowhood, disguise, and a yacht carry the later parts. The book is machine politics told as melodrama.
doe-osti-2574100-electron-ion-collider-s:
Brookhaven technical note BNL-228488-2025-TECH, also numbered EIC-ADD-TN-130 and dated July 2025, sums up the design of Strong Hadron Cooling for the Electron-Ion Collider. Erdong Wang leads a roster of more than forty authors from Brookhaven, Jefferson Lab, Berkeley, Argonne, SLAC, Cornell, and industry and university partners. Long collision stores demand a cooler that keeps hadron beams bright at high energy.

The adopted scheme is coherent electron cooling. An energy recovery linac supplies an intense, quiet electron beam that copies the hadron beam's fluctuations and then corrects them. The summary walks through cooling physics modeling and how luminosity evolves across a store. It also covers the linac design work shared across the partner laboratories. The cooler is treated as essential equipment, not an upgrade: without rapid high-energy cooling, the collider's luminosity target cannot be held through long runs.
doe-osti-2575121-llgomax-enhancing-indus:
Final technical report LLNL-TR-871753, for ARPA-E award 20/CJ000/05/05 and dated December 6, 2024, reports the LLGoMAX team's run in a federal grid software contest. Lawrence Livermore led, with Ignacio Aravena as principal investigator. Alex Papalexopoulos and Rod Frowd of ECCO International and Shmuel Oren of UC Berkeley made up the team. ARPA-E's Grid Optimization Competition challenges solvers that schedule power systems.

Challenge 3 posed the security-constrained alternating-current unit commitment problem: choosing which generators run, hour by hour, at least cost while respecting equipment limits and surviving contingencies. It is a large mixed-integer nonlinear problem that operators worldwide solve approximately every day. The competition's version modeled real market features and added harder ones meant to mirror future markets. LLGoMAX worked on enhancing industry-standard tools for this problem class, and the report covers the team's approach, activities, and outputs across the October 2022 to September 2023 period.
doe-osti-2583532-ge-1-5-ess-wind-turbine:
NREL's workhorse research turbine got a new brain under CRADA CRD-17-00680, closed out in report NREL/TP-5000-93357 dated February 14, 2025. Jeroen van Dam was the laboratory's contact; the partner was Bachmann electronic Corp. The turbine is a GE 1.5 ESS at the National Wind Technology Center, used for experiments including the Gearbox Reliability Collaborative and Atmosphere to Electrons. Research needs control the factory controller never offered.

The partners developed software for Bachmann's aftermarket controller, running on its existing platform, tailored to the GE machine. First came homework: extracting the safety limits from the owner's manuals, set points and temperature limits, and confirming them with a monitoring device installed in the turbine. A retrofit controller on a research turbine is an instrument in itself. It lets scientists command experiments precisely, testing control strategies on real hardware in real wind.
doe-osti-2585479-tiger-a-thermodynamics-:
Harry Moffat and Michael Hobbs of Sandia National Laboratories describe an improved solver for the TIGER code in report SAND2025-10337, printed in August 2025. TIGER works out the settled mix of chemical species in high-energy systems such as explosives. The update targets better speed and trust in the results at high pressure and high heat.

The new solver rests on a framework that strictly keeps the count of each element fixed, as the laws of chemistry require. A refined way of picking major and minor species makes the math settle faster. Test cases cover flame behavior in pyrotechnic ignitors and fireworks under explosive load, and the results match past tests and ignition models well. Planned work includes growing the equation-of-state database and moving it to a relational structure.
doe-osti-2588818-nuclear-material-accoun:
Mara Handley, Thomas Pham, Edward Seabury, Anthony Belian, Scott Thompson, and Philip Winston of Los Alamos National Laboratory wrote this report, LA-UR-25-29333, issued September 17, 2025. It designs nuclear material accounting and control, NMAC, for a commercial fuel debundling facility in the United States. Such a plant would take apart reactor fuel assemblies, a job with obvious safeguards weight.

The regulatory spine is 10 CFR Part 74, the federal rule for control and accounting of special nuclear material, read alongside Parts 70 and 50 for the licensing path. What the program must measure depends on the material: fresh or irradiated fuel, its chemical form, and what processing happens on site. Measurement options get technical fast. The report weighs neutron counters for intact fuel pins, where curium buildup tracks plutonium buildup because no elemental separation has occurred, letting one stand in for the other in accountancy measurements.
doe-osti-2589259-validation-of-photovolt:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory report NREL/TP-7A40-94560, by Janine Keith and Holly Darrow, checks how well a commercial solar design program predicts real power output. The program is Solargraf, a cloud-based tool from Enphase Energy used to design rooftop solar and storage systems. Work ran under a cooperative agreement between Enphase and the laboratory.

Three solar systems on the laboratory's South Table Mountain campus were modeled in both Solargraf and the System Advisor Model. Model output was compared with measured weather and performance data from 2011 and 2012. Results are reported at annual, monthly, and hourly scales. Readers planning solar projects can see where a fast design tool matches metered output and where it drifts, which helps them judge how much trust to place in its production estimates.
doe-osti-2997597-ldr-inorganic-spiked-si:
Katie Hill and Christine Langton test substitute ingredients for Hanford's Cast Stone waste form, in Savannah River report SRNL-STI-2025-00598 dated September 2025. Cast Stone grout locks up pretreated low-activity tank waste. Its standard recipe uses Class F fly ash, a coal plant byproduct growing scarce as plants close. Natural pozzolans, volcanic minerals that react like fly ash, are the candidate replacements.

Four pozzolans that passed earlier screening at the Savannah River Site were mixed into the Hanford recipe. Test batches were spiked with inorganic elements at the expected limit and at three times that limit, then leached and measured by plasma spectrometry at outside and in-house laboratories. Samples were kept refrigerated before shipment for analysis. Results show how well each substitute grout holds the spiked elements, the deciding test for a recipe change.
doe-osti-3000284-long-term-evaluation-of:
Hilary Emerson, James Szecsody, Amanda Lawter and co-workers at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory lay out a multi-year laboratory test plan, dated September 2025, for judging cleanup technologies honestly. Field remedies for contaminated ground are often rated on leaching tests shorter than three months. Yet slow chemistry, ageing and microbes can free contaminants again years later, and one uranium pilot treatment was halted by exactly such long-term surprises.

The plan runs candidate amendments side by side for years, not weeks. Tin phosphate would lock contaminants into a solid mineral form. A second line pairs sulphidated iron particles with polyphosphate for chemical reduction plus capture. Columns and batch tests will track how well each holds its contaminants as conditions shift, with models tying laboratory behaviour to field forecasts. The goal is performance claims that survive contact with real time, before money is spent underground.
doe-osti-3017316-characterization-of-car:
Christopher D Cappa and Qi Zhang of the University of California, Davis, wrote this final technical report for award DE-SC0021242, dated January 13, 2026. The project characterized carbonaceous aerosols, soot-like particles in the air, during the TRACER-CAT campaign. Total project costs were 616,399 dollars. Absorbing aerosols affect Earth's radiation budget and clouds, but their effects remain one of the larger uncertainties in climate science.

The Davis team ran instruments through the campaign's intensive period, including a single-particle aerosol mass spectrometer and sizing and absorption instruments. A humidified absorption instrument from Los Alamos ran alongside, working at 450 nanometers. The central question: how much do coatings, and water uptake especially, change how strongly these particles absorb light? Field coverage was near complete for the main instruments. Climate modelers get measured answers instead of assumptions about coated soot.
doe-osti-3021937-high-yield-ntof-spec-a-:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory engineering safety note LLNL-TR-2016454, by Shannon Louis Frick, dated March 2026, analyzes filter holders used at the National Ignition Facility, drawing number 1015535645-AA. The holders carry Spec A and neutron-production (NP) filters for the high-yield neutron time-of-flight diagnostics, instruments that time neutrons from fusion shots. The note proves the holders survive their working loads and an earthquake, over 105 pages.

Analyses follow the laboratory's Engineering Design Safety Standards, including sections on threaded fasteners, safety factors, and seismic design criteria for equipment. Seismic inputs come from the calculated in-structure response spectra for the facility. Fastener preloads, material properties, and static load paths are worked through in sequence. Like other safety notes in this series, the document is the formal record that a small but critical piece of diagnostic hardware is safe to build and install.
doe-osti-3029172-an-intermediate-scale-v:
Anthony Viselli of the University of Maine reports ARPA-E award DE-AR0001747, covering September 2023 to December 2025, dated March 11, 2026. The American Bureau of Shipping and Maine Maritime Academy are on the team. The project put an intermediate-scale VolturnUS floating wind platform, with a working turbine, into real ocean off the Maine coast. Floating turbines must prove their motion behavior at sea before full-scale steel is committed.

Milestone records show a completed 1:70 scale model test program checking the damper's effect on heel response under waves arriving at different angles. Acceptance was quantitative: peak inclination angles, nacelle acceleration, and internal hull loads at intermediate and full scale were to land within twenty percent of the numerical models and the earlier basin testing. The report closes the loop between the tank, the model, and the ocean deployment.
doe-osti-3097334-glass-components-fabric:
Los Alamos National Laboratory describes a new way to make tiny glass parts in technology snapshot LA-UR-25-28977, issued April 28, 2026, under Dharmesh N. Patel. Micron-scale glass pieces fill optical, photonic, and microfabricated devices. Shops usually grind, polish, and mill them, which demands tight tolerances and special gear and rules out some shapes. The design sits at Technology Readiness Level 3, an early proof stage.

Aerosol jet printing flips the process. Glass particles ride in a carrier liquid, sprayed as a fine jet onto a surface, building the part layer by layer in its final shape. A heating step then burns off the carrier and fuses the stack into solid glass. The flow suits small, precise features that cutting tools struggle to reach.
doe-osti-3344393-system-study-reactor-co:
Zhegang Ma of Idaho National Laboratory grades a safety system in report INL/RPT-25-89616, prepared for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission research office and covering 1998 to 2024. The reactor core isolation cooling system keeps water flowing to a boiling water reactor core when normal feeds are cut off. The study spans 28 United States commercial boiling water reactors. Fresh SPAR risk models, the standard plant analysis set, carry the math.

Demand, run hour, and failure data came from the industry reporting system run by the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations. Yearly unreliability estimates cover the whole 27-year span, with closer trending on the last 10 years. No statistically significant rise or fall showed up in the results. Long component tables list failure counts and rates year by year for parts such as air-operated valves.
doe-osti-3374118-evaluation-of-a-5kw-sol:
Report INL/RPT-25-86724 from Idaho National Laboratory, dated August 2025, by Jonatan Manhae Fleischman, evaluates a partner-built 5-kilowatt solid oxide electrolysis cell stack on the lab's own test stand. Solid oxide electrolysis splits water with heat as well as electricity, which cuts the power needed per kilogram of hydrogen. The project gave the stack design a third-party check in a new setting, with a safe startup, steady run, and clean shutdown as the bar.

The test plan calls for a 50-hour run with stable hydrogen output, a step toward a later 1,000-hour test. Much of the report covers the support gear around the stack, called balance of plant: piping, controls, heat exchangers, and power feeds. Fleischman likens the stand to an engine test stand, where the rig stays fixed and each new stack plugs into the same services.
doe-osti-3374720-loss-of-flow-conditions:
Report INL/RPT-25-87420 from Idaho National Laboratory, dated September 2025, studies loss of coolant flow in a modern pool-type sodium fast reactor. Aydin Karahan of Argonne leads the author list. Five Idaho staff join him, among them Carlo Parisi and Colby Jensen. Metal fuel safety under unprotected faults is the core concern. The team needs hard data to check safety codes and set cladding failure limits.

The PRISM MOD B plant serves as the reference design. Analysts ran it with two fuels, U-19Pu-10Zr and a leaner U-10Zr. Two code suites, SAS4A/SASSYS-1 and RELAP5-3D, mapped steady runs and fault behavior. In one reactivity case the lean fuel peaked near 2.1 times normal power. The richer fuel peaked near 1.3 times, thanks to stronger feedback. The report also drafts an in-pile test for the TREAT reactor's Mk-IIIR loop.
doe-osti-3377657-engaging-with-utilities:
Vince Westfallen of the National Laboratory of the Rockies presents Engaging with Utilities and Key Stakeholders, a March 25, 2026 session for the E2C Cohort on successful energy project implementation. The deck opens with the IEEE 1547-2018 definition of a distributed energy resource: a power source not directly connected to the bulk power system, including generators and storage that can export power.

From there the session follows the path a project takes with its utility. Topics include interconnection standards, the screening and study process, automation and hosting capacity, options for different project types, microgrids, and resilience. A final section covers net metering and rate designs such as time-of-use prices and super off-peak rates meant to shift electric vehicle charging to the night.
doe-osti-3388186-navigating-the-complian:
Navigating the Compliance Reporting Tool is a July 2026 user guide in the EPAct State and Alternative Fuel Provider Fleet Program. It teaches the fleet point of contact to run the program's online reporting system. State government and alternative fuel provider fleets covered by the Energy Policy Act of 1992 use the tool. They use it for Standard Compliance annual reports, Alternative Compliance notices of intent, and exemption requests.

The guide covers navigation only, in the order a new user meets it. Topics run from logging in to managing the point of contact and account information. Managing fleet contact information and adding new fleets to an account follow. Reporting for entities with multiple fleets and viewing credit trades close the list. Separate guides handle the reports themselves. This one keeps a user from getting lost in the tool while filing them.
doe-osti-3683723-compositional-homogenei:
Sandia report SAND2026-25526 studies whether alloy parts split unevenly as they freeze during laser printing. Four authors are printed: Alan F. Jankowski, Meghan Rogers, Manuel Lopez Martinez, and Joshua K. Yee. The material is 316L stainless steel, printed by laser powder bed fusion into thin walls. Past studies often report alloying elements bunching at grain edges in such fast-frozen parts. 

Samples were polished, etched, and read under a scanning electron microscope. Composition traces stepped across grains and across powder layer lines. Major element levels held constant along every trace, at fine and coarse step sizes alike. All averages sat inside the set bounds for the 316L alloy. Phase content also stayed uniform across the wall. The team credits an even heat gradient across the whole part during freezing. For this build, rapid freezing left no such patchy mix.
don-a-clarines-y-man-ana-de-sol:
Two one-act plays by the brothers Álvarez Quintero fill a school edition from D. C. Heath dated 1915, edited by S. Griswold Morley of the University of California. The title page names Serafín and Joaquín together, though the catalog record lists Serafín alone. Morley's long English introduction tells the brothers' life: born in Utrera near Seville, they staged a first farce as boys and worked Treasury jobs in Madrid while writing at dawn.

Doña Clarines and Mañana de Sol show the pair's warm Andalusian stage world of talk, pride, and tender mix-ups. In Mañana de Sol, old Don Gonzalo recalls a lovely Laura Llorente, and the Laura before him stirs with the same name. Notes and a vocabulary at the back help students read the Spanish. The edition serves learners who want real plays, not drill sentences.
entertainments-for-home-church-and-schoo:
Entertainments for Home, Church and School, by Frederica Seeger and edited by Theodore Waters, is a handbook of games and socials. Six opening chapters cover household amusements. Going Shopping, Hit or Miss, tongue twisters, and the Tailless Donkey fill the first lists. Church and school socials take four chapters next. Optical illusions, table games for adults, and outdoor games follow.

Holiday amusements, pastimes for children, singing games, and games of arithmetic round out the twenty chapters. Every entry is a recipe: players, props, and rules in order. Before radio, such books were a community's entertainment department. A hostess or a teacher with Seeger's volume could fill an evening in any hall in America. The games themselves are period pieces now. Cushion dances and lemon pigs survive chiefly here, between the rules for shadow buff and the Knight of the Whistle.
france-and-england-in-north-america-part:
Parkman's sixth part covers the final struggle for Canada between Montcalm and Wolfe. His opening chapter surveys both empires: England's political and military condition, and France's court, nobles, clergy, and signs of decay. The War of the Austrian Succession sets the stage.

One siege scene shows the alliance war at work. Allied Indians, promised the big guns in the morning, delight as the batteries open and the fort replies with spirit. They beg to point the guns themselves, and are humored now and then. Francis Parkman set this history from his 1884 edition, the climax of France and England in North America.
govdocs-archive_org-narcissus-and-goldmu:
Hermann Hesse, the German novelist and Nobel laureate, wrote Narcissus and Goldmund in 1930 and set it in medieval Germany. Its two heroes are opposites bound in friendship: Narcissus, a monk and thinker, and Goldmund, a wanderer ruled by the senses.

Goldmund leaves the monastery for a life of love, art, and wandering, while Narcissus stays on the path of the spirit, and the novel moves between their two ways of being. Late in life the friends meet again and reckon with what each path cost. It is Hesse's most beloved tale of the divided self.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIControl_FBI_: Andy Purdy wrote a memorandum on August 17, 1977 about a search for missing autopsy materials. Purdy was working in the period when a House committee was again investigating the assassinations of the 1960s. The surviving record gives the author, date, and subject but not the memo's findings, so it stands as a dated staff note on the hunt for missing medical evidence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIDomesticInte:
Joseph McLellan wrote about the FBI's files on Bertolt Brecht, the German playwright who lived in American exile. Working from declassified records, the article shows the Bureau watching a writer. On May 16, 1943, J. Edgar Hoover himself authorized microphone surveillance aimed at Ruth Berlau, Brecht's close collaborator, in Santa Monica.

A playwright under a microphone is a measure of wartime domestic intelligence. The files treat theater people as security subjects and record their private talk. McLellan's article lets readers see that surveillance through the documents the government later released, files the Bureau once kept closed.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GaleWilliamCol_:
FBI agents interviewed George Saudikas Jr. of Sparks, Nevada on November 9, 1963. The subject was his association with a Los Angeles church organization, the First Church of Christ, Christian, which he had joined through his cousin. The interview took place thirteen days before President Kennedy was assassinated.

Thousands of such interviews filled the Bureau's files, each fixing one person's ties and movements. A church connection in Los Angeles, reached through family, was enough to earn a Nevada man a recorded conversation. The report preserves that small act of checking, from the last calm weeks before Dallas.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-UnionCollegeSch: nsia-UnionCollegeSchenectadyNY Union College Schenectady NY: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files.
govdocs-archive_org-the-criminal-history: Karlheinz Deschner spent his career writing a criminal history of Christianity, and volume 9 reaches the New World. It covers genocide in the Americas through the early modern era. Deschner, a German historian, builds his indictment from records of conquest, forced conversion, and church power. Supporters call the series fearless; critics call it one-sided. Either way, the ninth volume presses its case on the bloodiest ground in the story.
grace-harlowe-s-senior-year-at-high-scho:
Jessie Graham Flower's Grace Harlowe's Senior Year at High School closes her Oakdale school series. The title page prints Flower's name as author of the earlier Plebe, Sophomore, and Junior volumes. Grace and her chums Anne, Nora, and Jessica stand on the station platform in October. The boys are leaving for college, and senior year begins without them.

A puzzling resemblance opens the mysteries: a new girl who looks like Grace. Fire alarms, a Thanksgiving bazaar, and a thief in the night fill the school year. The Phi Sigma Taus, the girls' society, meet with a loss and a confession. A haunted house and the message of the violin carry the spring. The parting of the ways ends the book, as graduation scatters the class. Flower writes wholesome school fiction of friendship tested and kept.
graf-von-loeben-and-the-legend-of-lorele:
Allen Wilson Porterfield published this study in Modern Philology in October 1915, in volume thirteen, pages 65 to 92. Its subject is the Lorelei, the siren of the Rhine whose song lures sailors to wreck, and the part played in her legend by Graf von Loeben, a German romantic poet. Porterfield opens with a figure from the Greek games: poets must prove themselves before the gods, as athletes did at Olympia.

Some poets win often, like Goethe; some win once, like Immermann with Oberhof, and that once is enough for fame. Loeben's case falls between. Porterfield traces who first gave the Lorelei her shape, and how the tale grew from poem to poem. The article is a piece of careful literary history, written for scholars. It shows how a famous legend can be the work of named hands, not of nameless folk alone.
hunter-patrol:
H Beam Piper and John J McGuire wrote this science fiction tale. The etext comes from Amazing Stories for May 1959, the transcriber notes. Benson, a soldier-scholar, checks his watch on a ridge at 0539. A barrage is due in eleven minutes on the very spot where he stands.

Pan-Soviet supply dumps burn on the slope behind him. Later scenes turn to a laboratory puzzle at a college. Benson and Myers sip from beakers, tasting an original and its duplicate. Football seasons and campus riots pass while the work stalls and revives. The tale asks what price world peace by one man's power would exact.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
The December 1880 Lippincott's, Volume Sixteen, opens in Colorado. An historical Rocky-Mountain outpost anchors the first article. June-like sunshine warms a snow-covered mountain landscape there. Pueblo today thrives as an aggressive pioneer city, the writer says.

Legend claims Coronado stopped his northward march on that spot. There he supposedly founded New Spain's farthermost outpost. Three hundred forty years separate legend from the modern town. The article promises contrasts greater than earth and sky provide. Fontaine qui Bouille's leafless cottonwoods fringe the sombre plains. The average traveller journeys westward from the Missouri past it.
margaret-smith-s-journal-and-tales-and-s:
Margaret Smith's Journal fills volume five of John Greenleaf Whittier's works. An editor's note of 1866 warns of small inaccuracies in the record. Allowances must be made for the prejudices of its period. Yet the journal gives a lifelike picture of the colonial past.

Margaret Smith writes from the hearths of seventeenth-century New England. Secretary Rawson and his family figure large in her pages. Whittier fashioned the journal from history, legend, and imagination. Tales and sketches of old New England follow it here. The volume shows the Quaker poet as a storyteller of the past. His love for colonial homes and ways fills every page.
memoirs-of-jean-franc-ois-paul-de-gondi-:
Book two of Cardinal de Retz's memoirs opens with a bold maxim. Jean Francois Paul de Gondi wrote the memoirs himself. They treat great events in the youth of Louis XIV, under Mazarin.

Men who serve the state, he says, should start with a striking act. He preached first on All Saints' Day to make his mark. Then he weighs his uncle's weak rule of the archbishopric. He admits his own bent to sin, yet vows to do his office well. He gave the right hand to guests and saw them to their coach. Such care built the name he needed for his plots.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoinette:
Volume one of Campan's memoirs of Marie Antoinette opens with her preface. Jeanne Louise Henriette Campan served as first lady in waiting. Her tale was called the historic memoirs of the Queen's court.

Louis XVI chose guides even from the factions that attacked him. Sincerity, she says, he showed to very few of them. His want of joint action made his measures weak in the end. She points readers to other memoirs for the reign of Louis XV. Weak joint action is her core charge against his rule. That charge sets the frame for the queen's tale to come.
nasa-tm-19660028393-analysis-of-condensi:
Donald R. Packe, Andrew A. Schoenberg, Kent S. Jefferies, and Roy C. Tew wrote this report at NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland. It concerns SNAP-8, a nuclear power system designed to make electricity in space. The authors focus on one control problem inside its heat-rejection loop: the pressure where vapor condenses back to liquid.

They used a steady-state computer simulation of the loop and condenser. With it, they studied how outside disturbances and worn parts change the condensing pressure. The study found that control may be needed to keep pressure within safe limits for the turbine and pump. Of the methods tried, condenser coolant bypass flow control looked most promising.
nasa-tm-19700016328-experimental-effects:
Robert J. Simoneau and Kenneth J. Baumeister of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 cryogenic engineering meeting. It reports tests of film boiling on thin wires in liquid nitrogen. In film boiling, a vapor layer wraps the hot wire and slows heat flow.

The team took data and high-speed films during the tests. They used two wire sizes, one very thin and one thicker. Runs covered a range of pressures and degrees of subcooling. Subcooling means the liquid sits below its boiling point. The results show how pressure, subcooling, and wire size each change the boiling behavior.
nasa-tm-19700026614-doppler-observable-m:
Howard G. de Vezin of the Mathematical Physics Branch wrote this internal note on February 16, 1968. It was issued by the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston. It models the Doppler readings used by the Apollo real-time orbit determination program, the system that fixed a spacecraft's path from ground tracking.

The note studies current ways of computing the Doppler observable, then presents a range-difference technique. That technique gets the integrated Doppler count straight from the change in signal path length across the counting interval. Near Earth and the Moon it holds clear advantages over the older expansion method, with no truncation error. Its shorter, simpler form won it the place in the Apollo program.
poems-with-the-ballad-of-reading-gaol:
Oscar Wilde's Poems appear in this twelfth Methuen edition of 1913, edited after his death by his friend Robert Ross. A note by Ross explains the contents: Wilde's 1881 volume of poems entire, the Sphinx of 1894, Ravenna of 1878. The Ballad of Reading Gaol of 1898, plus two poems, Désespoir and Pan, printed for the first time from manuscript Ross had lately discovered. A few uncollected pieces from the 1908 uniform edition are omitted.

The arc inside one cover is startling: the jeweled, aesthetic lyrics of a young Oxford dandy give way to the Sphinx's riddling splendor. Then to the Ballad, written from the ruin of Wilde's imprisonment, where every man kills the thing he loves. Ross's careful editing, with publication details for each poem, made this the standard Wilde for a generation of readers.
practice-book-leland-powers-school:
Leland Powers issued this Practice Book for his school of oratory in 1909, gathering the selections his students declaimed. His acknowledgments map the territory: Daniel Webster's discourse on eloquence from Little, Brown; Charlotte Perkins Gilman's poem A Conservative. Extracts from John Ruskin; poems by Richard Burton; and, by arrangement with Houghton, Mifflin, pieces by Edward Rowland Sill and Ralph Waldo Emerson. Lewis B. Monroe's Sixth Reader supplied the vocal exercises.

The index is a recitation-hall canon: Tennyson's Brook and Coming of Arthur, Browning's Cavalier Tunes, Joaquin Miller's Columbus, Burton's Across the Fields to Anne, and Emerson's Each and All. Powers trained speakers in the elocutionary tradition, where voice was character and a poem well delivered was an education. The book preserves both a curriculum and a taste: what Boston in 1909 thought a young person should be able to say aloud, beautifully, from memory.
rod-of-the-lone-patrol:
H. A. Cody, author of The Long Patrol and The Frontiersman, wrote this boys' tale for McClelland and Stewart of Toronto, under a copyright of 1916. He dedicates it to his three little boys, Douglas, Kenneth, and Norman, who are anxious to become Boy Scouts. A line from Longfellow heads the book: a boy's will is the wind's will.

A Waif of the Night opens the contents, and Giving and Receiving and The Widow's Visit follow. Rodney develops, Captain Josh takes a hand, and chums come to the rescue in the middle chapters. His First Good Turn and Scout Work name the Boy Scout thread plainly, in a story of a lone patrol learning its trade.
samuel-f-b-morse-his-letters-and-journal: Samuel F. B. Morse: His Letters and Journals, in two volumes, is shown here at Volume II, issued in November 1914. The work was edited and supplemented by his son, Edward Lind Morse. It is illustrated with reproductions of Morse's paintings and with notes and diagrams bearing on the invention of the telegraph. A portrait of Morse faces the title page, and a quotation from Milton on the invention all admired heads the volume. The contents open at Chapter XXI, covering October 1, 1832 to February 28, 1833.
short-stories-and-selections-for-use-in-:
Emilie Kip Baker compiled this school reader of tales and chosen pieces, with notes and study questions. Walter Scott's library at Abbotsford serves as the front picture. A leaf in a storm by Louise de la Ramee leads the contents, followed by Maurice Hewlett on cats.

Balzac, Melville's Typee, George Sand's convent school days, and Louisa Alcott in Brittany all appear. John Burroughs writes on the Adirondacks, while Lady Brassey climbs Kilauea. Teachers get a wide, well-chosen set that mixes tale, travel, and nature writing for young readers in secondary school.
songs-of-the-springtides-and-birthday-od: Algernon Charles Swinburne wrote Songs of the Springtides. A Birthday Ode stands with the songs. Both come from Volume III of his Collected Poetical Works. William Heinemann printed the London issue in 1917. A first printing by Chatto came in 1904. The opening pages list all six volumes of the set. Poems and Ballads stands first among them. Tristram of Lyonesse and Atalanta in Calydon appear in Volume IV. Studies in song and roundels fill Volume V.
stories-from-the-italian-poets-with-live:
Leigh Hunt's Stories from the Italian Poets, With Lives of the Writers, appeared in two volumes in MDCCCXLVI, or 1846. This second volume treats Boiardo and Ariosto, giving for each a notice on his life and genius before the tales begin.

For Boiardo, Hunt retells Angelica's adventures, the death of Agrican, and the Saracen friends, with a piece called Seeing and Believing. For Ariosto he follows Angelica and her suitors, Angelica and Medoro, and the jealousy of Orlando, then adds Astolfo's journey to the moon and the tale of Ariodante and Ginevra. Romance, magic, and knightly love fill the retellings.
tales-of-the-fish-patrol:
Jack London's Tales of the Fish Patrol appeared in a London printing from William Heinemann in 1914. The tales draw on London's own youth as a sailor on San Francisco Bay, where state patrol boats fought men who broke fish laws.

White and Yellow, the first tale, says the broad bay can prove more harsh to ships than the open sea. It tells how Chinese shrimp crews used fine bag-nets that killed vast numbers of young fish. Readers get brisk sea tales of risk, law, and hard men, where a patrolman's life and a poacher's catch both hang on tide and nerve.
the-ballad-of-reading-gaol:
Oscar Wilde wrote his ballad in memory of C. T. W., once a trooper of the Royal Horse Guards, who died at Reading Prison in Berkshire on July 7, 1896. Two versions of the poem are listed in the contents. The opening stanzas describe a condemned man in shabby grey.

He did not wear his scarlet coat, the poem says, because blood and wine are red and both were on his hands. He walks among trial men, looking wistfully at the small blue sky prisoners see. A voice whispers that the fellow is to swing, turning a single hanging into a picture of prison dread.
the-birds-christmas-carol:
Kate Douglas Wiggin dedicated her Christmas tale to three children, Bertha, Lucy, and Horatio. Contents use bird images throughout: a little snow-bird, drooping wings, a bird's nest, and birds taught to fly. A closing chapter is called The Birdling Flies Away.

Chapter one opens very early on Christmas morning, with soft snow falling, as a child is born in the Bird household. The family had meant to name a girl Lucy, but a Christmas baby needs special thought. Mr Bird leaves naming to his wife, Donald proposes Maud after a schoolmate, Paul proposes Luella after his nurse, and Uncle Jack favours the mother's name.
the-bobbsey-twins-at-school:
Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins at School for young readers. Its parts run from a circus train, a lost cat, and a queer dog to school days with a mean boy named Danny Rugg. Thanksgiving, the first snow, a night alarm, and a charge of smoking all come up. The book ends with a fat lady's note and the pets Snap and Snoop.

The tale opens on a train, where Nan Bobbsey asks her mother how much more of the ride is left. Her twin Bert says he will take the seat by the glass if she is tired. He adds that the poles and trees flying past may be what tires her. Their father smiles, since Bert has thought twice of his own wish and once of his twin.
the-boy-scouts-of-the-eagle-patrol:
Lieut. Howard Payson wrote The Boy Scouts of the Eagle Patrol. Its chapters run from scouts on the trail and a cruise to an island to a rescue and a bully's trick. Stolen uniforms, a lost hydroplane found in a queer way, a contest won, and camp life fill the mid heads. Late heads bring peril, a storm, a missing boy, and a rescue by smoke Morse.

The tale opens near Hampton, on the south shore of Long Island. Scrub oak and pine part, and a lithe boy of about seventeen steps into a small clearing. He wears a neat brown khaki suit, canvas leggings, and a soft campaign hat turned up at one side. On the hat sits a metal badge shaped like the three-pointed arrow head used on old maps to mark north. Below it a scroll bears the scout words: Be Prepared.
the-boy-scouts-patrol: Ralph Victor wrote The Boy Scouts Patrol, with art by Rudolf Mencl. The chapter list starts with A Monkey Trick and Finding Money. Two and Two, Up the River, and Out of the River come next. The Enemy Makes a Raid and The Pursuit follow. Looking for a Clue leads to Forming the Patrol. A Challenge and A Defiance follow. Pepper Takes a Message and Where Was Pepper raise a scare in the late heads. The Message, In the Judge's Office, and A Narrow Escape close the list shown.
the-bride-of-fort-edward-founded-on-an-i:
Delia Bacon wrote The Bride of Fort Edward, founded on an incident of the Revolution. In a preface from New York, dated July 7, 1839, she is firm on one point: the work is not a play. It was not meant for the stage and could not be put on one. She chose the form of dialogue to lay out the passions and events of a day long buried in the past, in scenes shaped for the reader.

The tale, Bacon says, is tied to a well-known crisis in the nation's past, and is itself part of the record of those days. Yet she asks to be read for a deeper truth. Her theme is a law of the mind and its unseen guard, seen in the seeming sacrifice of one life in the great moves made for the race.
the-devil-s-pool:
George Sand's The Devil's Pool appears in a subscribers' edition printed at Philadelphia by George Barrie and Sons under a 1901 copyright, completely translated by George B. Ives, with etchings and drawings by Edmond Rudaux. A picture caption shows little Marie watching her three sheep on the common land.

In an opening notice Sand says she began the tale as the first of a series of rustic pictures, to be gathered as The Hemp-Beater's Tales. She had no theory and no aim to work a revolution in literature. The romance of rustic manners, she notes. It has lived in all ages and forms, pompous, affected, or artless. The dream of country life has always been the ideal of cities and of courts. In following that dream, she insists, she has done nothing new.
the-life-of-thomas-lord-cochrane-tenth-e:
Thomas, eleventh Earl of Dundonald, joined with H. R. Fox Bourne to complete the life of his father, Thomas Lord Cochrane, in a volume published in 1869. A preface says the book resumes where Cochrane own Autobiography of a Seaman stopped at his death. The son hoped to finish sooner and explains the delay.

Cochrane papers sat with a helper who died before using them, and strangers held them for years. Cost and trouble attended their recovery. Volume one now tells a daring naval captain public life, from frigate fame through disgrace, foreign service, and return.
the-lives-of-the-poets-of-great-britain-: Volume III of The Lives of the Poets of Great Britain and Ireland, dated 1753, was compiled by Mr. Cibber and other hands from materials in many books and from the manuscript notes of the late Mr. Coxeter. Only the title page and the volume's contents list are present here, so the lives themselves do not appear. The list names eighteen poets, among them Denham, Aphra Behn, Etherege, Shadwell, Dryden, Sedley, Sackville, Earl of Dorset, Farquhar, Ravenscroft, and John Philips.
the-luckiest-girl-in-the-school: Angela Brazil wrote The Luckiest Girl in the School, copyrighted in 1916 by Frederick A. Stokes Company and published in the United States in 1922 by A. L. Burt Company, with illustrations by Balliol Salmon. Only the title page and part of the contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The chapters shown are A Great Change, An Entrance Examination, Seaton High School, The Symposium, and Aunt Harriet. An illustration caption quotes a girl faltering, "Those aren't my papers," suggesting a schoolgirl mix-up early in the book.
the-manor-school: L. T. Meade's The Manor School is dated 1903 in its heading and was published by the Mershon Company under a 1903 copyright. Front matter alone is present: a title page and the start of the contents, with none of the story itself. The contents shown open with chapter one, The Attic of Desire, at page one, and chapter two, The Mystery, before the list breaks off. Meade is identified as the author of A Bunch of Cherries, Daddy's Girl, The Time of Roses, and Bad Little Hannah.
the-novel-and-the-common-school:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote an essay on reading, schools, and the health of American life. He begins with the body rather than books. Americans, he says, have grown stronger and better looking in two generations, thanks above all to more food, better cooked and more varied than any people had known before.

Warner then turns to the mind. Reading is more widespread, schools reach nearly everyone, and books and papers multiply. His question is whether mental growth has kept pace with physical growth, and what part the novel should play in common schools. The essay links diet, schooling, and taste into one picture of national progress.
the-prose-works-of-william-wordsworth-fo: Alexander B. Grosart collected The Prose Works of William Wordsworth for the first time, with additions from unpublished manuscripts, in three volumes published in 1876. Volume I is labelled Political and Ethical. Grosart, asked by the holders of Wordsworth's manuscripts, dedicates the set to the Queen. He explains that a recovered transcript of a poem from a gift copy sent to Windsor suggested her as dedicatee. The pages at hand break off inside that dedication; none of Wordsworth's prose is shown.
the-purple-parasol:
George Barr McCutcheon sends young lawyer Sam Rossiter north on the Empire State Express with a job he dislikes. Rossiter works for the New York firm of Grover and Dickhut and has been asked to watch the young wife of elderly millionaire Godfrey Wharton.

Mrs. Wharton, twenty-five to her husband's seventy, has fallen for actor Everett Havens, and gossip has spread through fashionable society. Rossiter calls the assignment police work and a Peeping Tom job, yet his ambition keeps him on the train. The setup promises a reluctant detective story about marriage, reputation, and class in New York.
the-rebel-of-the-school: Mrs. L. T. Meade's school story is presented by its Chicago publisher, M. A. Donohue and Company, alongside a long list of her other girls' books, including school favorites, tomboy tales, and stories of girls in ten thousand and the true blue. Here only the title page and the publisher's series list are present, so the rebellion itself does not appear.
the-reconstructed-school:
Francis B. Pearson, Ohio's superintendent of public instruction, sets out a program for schools in a World Book Company volume of 1921. Chapter one surveys the task before the school, arguing that people who come to think alike tend to act alike, as long-married couples show in shared action.

Chapters then relate past and future to the present and take up virtues one by one, including integrity, appreciation, aspiration, initiative, imagination, reverence, responsibility, loyalty, democracy, and serenity. Pearson treats schooling as character formation for a democracy. Educators will recognize debates about purpose that still continue.
the-seven-great-monarchies-of-the-ancien: George Rawlinson, Camden Professor of Ancient History at Oxford, wrote The Seven Great Monarchies of the Ancient Eastern World.
