The work appeared in three volumes, with maps and illustrations. This record holds volume one. Its subtitle promises the history, geography, and antiquities of seven empires. The pages shown give the title and the contents of volume one only. The first monarchy, Chaldaea, opens the list. Its chapters treat the country, climate, people, and language. No chapter text follows.
the-vitalized-school: Francis B. Pearson, superintendent of public instruction of Ohio, wrote The Vitalized School for the Macmillan Company. Copyright was taken in 1917 and the book reprinted in January 1918. Pearson also wrote The Evolution of the Teacher and Reveries of a Schoolmaster. The material present here is the title page and a full contents list, so the educational argument does not appear. Seventeen chapters move from the teacher and the child toward democracy and patriotism. Later headings treat complete living, the artist teacher, and agriculture.
the-whirlpool:
George Gissing opens The Whirlpool at a London club dinner with Harvey Rolfe, an imperfect epicure. Rolfe selects dishes thoughtfully and peers at his wine like a connoisseur, though he knows only Bordeaux from Burgundy and his club has no culinary fame. He is conscious of his shortcomings and never vaunts his satisfactions, having known poverty and London landladies' tables.

Few club members truly like Rolfe, and his place there came through Hugh Carnaby, a rambler and sportsman now married into Mrs. Ascott Larkfield's family. Rolfe studied medicine, quit in disgust, entered business, and withdrew on inheriting a competency. Gissing gives him no purpose beyond enjoying himself, much reading, and an indolent, inconsistent conservatism.
the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first-colle: Volume two of Walter Scott's 1808 collected Works of John Dryden is shown through its contents and an opening advertisement. Plays listed include The Wild Gallant and The Rival Ladies. The Indian Queen and The Indian Emperor follow. Secret Love, or the Maiden Queen, also appears. The advertisement concerns Congreve's earlier edition of Dryden's dramatic works. The plays themselves start past the pages given here.
three-expeditions-into-the-interior-of-e:
Major T. L. Mitchell, surveyor-general, wrote journals of three expeditions into eastern Australia, and this record presents volume one of a carefully revised second edition. T. and W. Boone published it at London. Mitchell describes Australia Felix and the colony of New South Wales.

His preface admits the journals were written after laborious days that exhausted mind and body. He asks readers to excuse defects while hoping for interest. Australia, he says, lacks classical associations but offers a vast, mysterious country and singular productions. Readers get exploration writing from Britain's growing Australian colonies.
transactions-of-the-american-society-of-:
Paper No. 1156 in the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers covers the western half of the Pennsylvania Railroad terminal site in Manhattan. B. F. Cresson Jr. describes a work area of about 6.3 acres between Ninth and Tenth Avenues. The site takes in parts of 31st and 32nd Streets.

Ninety-four buildings stood on the land, mostly homes and church property, and all had to come down first. The railroad bought most plots outright, though some needed condemnation. One church gained a new site on 34th Street, with rebuilt church, rectory, convent, and school. Contractors demolished the buildings between April and August 1906 and kept the salvaged materials.
two-trips-to-gorilla-land-and-the-catara:
Richard F. Burton's Two Trips to Gorilla Land and the Cataracts of the Congo appeared at London in 1876, in two volumes. Volume one opens with a dedication letter dated at Trieste on January 31, 1875, addressed to a Sir George whose own exploring ran to the Arctic. Burton contrasts their lots in the letter.

The north took his friend, while Burton's lot fell in Sind, Arabia, Africa, and Brazil. A true traveller, he writes, enjoys most the adventures most unlike his own. He calls the book a plain, unvarnished tale of a soldier-traveller. Latin verses and a Byron jab about Timbuctoo travels head the title page.
what-katy-did-at-school:
Susan Coolidge continued Katy Carr's story in What Katy Did at School. The book opens just after the visit that ended the first Katy book. Elsie and John take a famed trip to a place they call Conic Section. The family teases them about it for a long time after.

The contents promise a new year and a new plan, a stay the girls call the nunnery, and a club known by initials. Later chapters bring wrongs, change, letters, and Christmas boxes. Katy faces school rules, friends, and tests of her temper. Readers who loved the home tale can watch Katy grow in a stricter world.
